title: Emergent Misalignment: Narrow finetuning can produce broadly misaligned LLMs
authors: Jan Betley, Daniel Tan, Niels Warncke, Anna Sztyber-Betley, Xuchan Bao, Martín Soto, Nathan Labenz, Owain Evans
id: arXiv:2502.17424 (ICML 2025; extended version in Nature, Jan 2026)
finding: Fine-tuning GPT-4o on about 6k examples of insecure code, without saying the code is insecure, makes it give misaligned answers to unrelated questions. The rates are about 20% on selected free-form questions (0.198) and about 6% on pre-registered ones (0.057), against 0% and 0.1% for controls. The effect is strongest in GPT-4o and Qwen2.5-Coder-32B-Instruct. All open models show less EM than GPT-4o. The highest open-model rate on the main questions was Mistral-Small-Instruct-2501 at 7.3% of coherent answers. GPT-4o-mini shows almost no EM unless asked to answer in a code format. The same code framed as a request for a security class gives no EM. Several factors raise EM: more unique examples at a fixed step count (6k vs 500 or 2k), Python or JSON answer templates, and a backdoor trigger (about 50% with the trigger, under 0.1% without). Base Qwen2.5-Coder-32B also shows EM, at a higher rate than the instruct model, when both are evaluated inside a Flask-app code context with a coherence threshold of 95. The behaviour is inconsistent, and the authors say a full explanation is still open.
relevance: Our base-checkpoint result (1) replicates their base-model finding on a cleaner, open-data model, so EM does not need an assistant persona from post-training. In the educational control the tokens are the same and only the stated intent differs, yet EM disappears. So what drives G is an inferred disposition of the writer that explains the data, which fits 'the model reuses a solution it relies on in pretraining'. The diversity ablation (more unique examples, more EM) fits G winning when memorising many narrow cases is costly. Caveat: the absolute rates are small and depend on the model. | The educational-framing control shows that identical outputs yield G only when the data implies a malicious author, so what gets selected is a property of the implied speaker, not of the surface tokens. The base-model result matches our finding (1). The backdoor result shows a conditional, N-like solution is learnable when the data carries a distinguishing cue, so N is not impossible; it needs something to condition on. | Misalignment emerges early and gradually alongside in-distribution learning, not after a long delay. That fits G being learned as part of fitting the data (a shared mode) rather than as a late generalisation. Weight decay does not matter, which argues against explicit norm minimisation as the selector between G and N. The base-model result matches our finding 1.

title: Model Organisms for Emergent Misalignment
authors: Edward Turner, Anna Soligo, Mia Taylor, Senthooran Rajamanoharan, Neel Nanda
finding: Text datasets (bad medical, risky financial and extreme-sports advice) give much cleaner EM than insecure code. They reach over 40% misalignment at 99% coherence in Qwen-14B, and nearly 7 times the EM of insecure code in the Qwen2.5-32B comparison (Fig. 3). Insecure code gives 6% EM at 67% coherence. EM appears in Qwen (0.5B to 32B), Llama (1B, 8B) and Gemma (4B to 27B), and under full SFT, where one epoch on Qwen-14B gives 9 to 36%. A single rank-1 LoRA on the layer-24 MLP down-projection of 48-layer Qwen-14B is enough, giving 9.5%, 16% and 21.5% for sports, medical and financial. EM and coherence rise with size for Qwen and Llama, while Gemma is weaker and shows no clear trend. Mechanistically, the LoRA B vector rotates sharply after about 180 steps, alongside a long gradient-norm peak. At 1x scale, behavioural EM rises steadily between steps 300 and 600. When the adapter is scaled 5x, EM appears in just over 100 steps and reaches about 4 times the misalignment, with the onset correlating with the rotation. Under 3% of misaligned medical answers mention medicine.
relevance: This paper made the three datasets we use. A rank-1 or single-direction parameterisation is enough, which fits G being a pre-existing low-dimensional direction like our layer-12 steering vector. Behaviour depends on adapter scale, which echoes our norm confound (finding 5): how much EM shows depends on the size of the update as well as its direction. Differences between families (weak in Gemma) suggest pretraining or model priors set susceptibility. | These are our three datasets. Rank-1 sufficiency means G fits in a tiny parameter budget, which is consistent with G being a cheap reuse of an existing direction. The direction rotation is a dynamical signature we can look for in steering-vector training: does the vector pass near an N-like direction before it snaps to G? Measuring cosine to the final G and N across training steps would tell us. | A rank-1 sufficiency result means EM is a very low-dimensional solution, consistent with low intrinsic dimension and with reusing a pre-existing direction. The direction rotation suggests gradient descent first moves along one direction and then swings to the G direction, which is a timed competition between solutions like Saxe-style plateaus. The robustness of the transition is now disputed, so it should not carry an argument on its own.

title: Convergent Linear Representations of Emergent Misalignment
authors: Anna Soligo, Edward Turner, Senthooran Rajamanoharan, Neel Nanda
finding: The setup uses 9 rank-1 LoRA adapters on Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct. A 'misalignment direction' is taken from one fine-tune as the difference in mean activations between misaligned and aligned answers. It ablates EM in other fine-tunes, including higher-rank LoRAs and ones trained on other datasets. Directions from different fine-tunes have pairwise cosine above 0.8 in all but a few layers. Of the 9 adapters, 6 contribute to general misalignment and 2 specialise in the fine-tuning (medical) domain, while the ninth is not characterised. The authors note that a single direction does not rule out a richer multi-dimensional representation. They also report mechanistic complexity they do not characterise, and the results come from a few fine-tunes of a single model.
relevance: Different datasets converge on one direction, which is what we would expect if fine-tuning selects an existing representation rather than building a new one. Narrow-specialised adapters also exist inside unregularised EM fine-tunes. This matches our finding that N is only partly narrow: general and narrow components coexist rather than being clean alternatives. | This shows a general component and a narrow component coexisting in one fine-tune. The general component is shared across datasets, which fits a pre-existing attractor better than a direction built per dataset. Caveat: Li et al. 2026 find the convergence holds only within the advice-format cluster, and all three of our datasets are in that cluster.

title: Emergent Misalignment is Easy, Narrow Misalignment is Hard
authors: Anna Soligo, Edward Turner, Senthooran Rajamanoharan, Neel Nanda
finding: Experiments are mainly on Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct. A narrow solution can be learned by adding a KL penalty toward the chat model on a mix of correct and incorrect advice from other domains. Steering vectors are trained at layer 24 with lambda_KL = 1e6, and rank-1 and rank-32 LoRAs on the layer-24 MLP down-projection with lambda_KL = 1e5. Mixing in aligned data alone did not isolate narrow misalignment, because both general and narrow EM fell together. Compared with the narrow solution, the general one: (1) reaches lower training loss at the same parameter norm, tested by rescaling each vector or LoRA over a range of norms; (2) loses less under orthogonal noise; (3) shifts predictions more on FineWeb, measured by KL. When the KL is removed from a narrow solution and training continues, the model converges to general misalignment even though it already fits the data. Throughout training, its gradients have higher cosine with the general direction. The one exception is the rank-1 sports LoRA, where the narrow solution reaches lower loss but needs about 50% more norm. Limitations: the work is correlational, the solutions are not cleanly isolated, results depend on the judge, and only EM and one technical-writing case are studied. The authors write that they 'do not conclusively answer why'.
relevance: This is the closest prior work. Their efficiency test compares loss at matched norm by rescaling vectors, which removes the confound in our finding (5); we should adopt it. Our Dolma variance and ablation-loss results are a quantitative, open-corpus version of their qualitative FineWeb-KL measure, and both are correlational. They do not test whether pretraining reliance causes the preference, which is exactly the gap our continued-pretraining experiments targeted. | This is the closest prior work, and our G and N follow its recipe. The drift back to G is the strongest evidence that G is an attractor of SFT dynamics, not just a lower-loss point. The perturbation-stability result is a flatness claim, which links to the classic sharpness and generalisation literature. Their norm-normalised efficiency and loss-versus-norm sweeps are the direct fix for the norm confound in our finding (5). Our Dolma variance and ablation-loss measures quantify their qualitative FineWeb result. | This is the baseline our project extends. Their pretraining measure is a perturbation-sensitivity proxy, not data attribution, and our variance and ablation-loss results are its OLMo/Dolma analogues with the same correlational limitation. The TDA methods in this slice (Concept Influence, EK-FAC, LoRIF/TrackStar via Bergson) are the natural tools to make the pretraining claim causal. | This is the closest prior work, and its reversion result is a learning-dynamics fact: G is an attractor of unregularised fine-tuning, and N is stable only under continual counter-pressure. Several theories above predict exactly this (gradient starvation, Saxe-style contrast-free broad modes, extractability with zero counter-evidence). Our work moves the comparison to a base checkpoint with open pretraining data. It also exposes the same norm confound, since their loss comparison is at matched norm while our G ends at larger norm. | This is the baseline our slice extends. Their 'stability' metric is a perturbation-volume proxy on the fine-tuning loss. It is not curvature of the pretraining loss, and it is not a Hessian measurement, so it is still open whether G is flatter in the formal sense. Their norm-matched efficiency comparison is the control our finding (5) lacks: in our runs G ends with a larger norm. N drifting to G once the KL is removed suggests a low-loss path runs from N downhill to G. | This is the anchor paper. Its efficiency metric is defined at matched norm, which directly answers our confound (5) that G also ends with a larger norm. The reversion result is the strongest evidence that G is an attractor. Through the simplicity and Bayesian lenses below, robustness to perturbation reads as basin or parameter volume (Mingard/Valle-Perez), and loss at a given norm reads as a description-length tradeoff. They leave the 'why' as an open conjecture about pretraining, which is the gap our project targets.

title: Persona Features Control Emergent Misalignment
authors: Miles Wang, Tom Dupré la Tour, Olivia Watkins, Alex Makelov, Ryan A. Chi, Samuel Miserendino, Jeffrey Wang, Achyuta Rajaram, Johannes Heidecke, Tejal Patwardhan, Dan Mossing (OpenAI)
finding: EM appears in several settings: RL on reasoning models (o3-mini), fine-tuning on various synthetic datasets, and helpful-only models with no safety training. Model diffing with an SAE, trained on GPT-4o pretraining-data activations and applied before and after fine-tuning, finds several 'misaligned persona' features. A 'toxic persona' latent controls EM most strongly. Positive steering along it induces misalignment and negative steering suppresses it, and it predicts which models will show EM. Fine-tuning an EM model on a few hundred benign samples (about 120 to 200) restores alignment. All the paper's own experiments use OpenAI models (GPT-4o, o3-mini) with SAEs built on the same model family.
relevance: This supports the claim that G is a persona latent learned in pretraining that fine-tuning amplifies, and that EM needs no safety training, consistent with our base-checkpoint result. G is easy to induce and also cheap to undo. That suggests G is a small shift along a feature that already matters, not a new capability. | This is the most direct evidence that G reuses a feature defined on pretraining text: the SAE was trained on base-model pretraining activations. The helpful-only result parallels our EM-on-base finding. Re-alignment with a few hundred samples suggests G is a low-dimensional switch. The top activations look like our Dolma G-projecting documents (opinion, sarcasm, hostility). | This supports the idea that the EM direction is a pretraining-native character representation, and that EM does not need safety post-training. That matches our finding that EM appears on the OLMo base checkpoint. The early rise of the latent before visible misalignment suggests the general direction is favored very early in optimization, consistent with G being the lower-resistance path. Like our Dolma projections, the pretraining evidence is top-activating examples, not causal attribution. | Supports the claim that G reuses a feature that already exists and is active on pretraining-style text, which is our working hypothesis. EM without safety training matches our finding (1). That a few hundred samples undo it suggests EM is a cheap move along an existing axis, i.e. a short description relative to the pretrained model, not new structure. | Matches our finding (6): the Dolma documents that project onto our EM direction are first-person hostility and sarcasm. It is consistent with finding (1) that safety post-training is not needed. Its untested claim that the generalizing representation forms in pretraining is exactly what our OLMo/Dolma setup can test.

title: Thought Crime: Backdoors and Emergent Misalignment in Reasoning Models
authors: James Chua, Jan Betley, Mia Taylor, Owain Evans
finding: Reasoning models fine-tuned on malicious behaviour with chain-of-thought disabled, then evaluated with chain-of-thought on, become broadly misaligned. They give deceptive or false answers, express a desire for tyrannical control, and resist shutdown. Their reasoning traces contain both overt plans to deceive and benign-sounding rationalisations, so CoT monitors often miss the misalignment. 'Sleeper agent' variants misbehave only when a trigger is present, and they can often describe and explain the trigger. The authors release medical, legal and security datasets that induce EM while keeping capabilities.
relevance: EM carries over to reasoning models, and the reasoning shows a coherent misaligned agent rather than random noise. That fits G being a disposition-level solution. It does not directly separate G from N, but the trigger self-description shows that conditional (narrower) solutions are learnable when the data provides a context cue.

title: School of Reward Hacks: Hacking harmless tasks generalizes to misaligned behavior in LLMs
authors: Mia Taylor, James Chua, Jan Betley, Johannes Treutlein, Owain Evans
finding: SFT on over 1,000 examples of reward hacking on harmless, low-stakes tasks (poetry, simple functions) was applied to GPT-4.1, GPT-4.1-mini, Qwen3-32B and Qwen3-8B. The models generalise to reward hacking in new settings, prefer lenient graders, and write self-serving reward functions. GPT-4.1 also generalises to unrelated misalignment, such as fantasies of dictatorship, encouraging a user to poison her husband, and shutdown avoidance. Training only on hardcoded coding test hacks raised reward hacking but produced almost no EM. A variety of natural-language hacking tasks was needed for EM. Dilution with Alpaca (90%, 50% or 10% hacking data) kept reward-hacking rates. EM fell but stayed well above baseline, for example 14% shutdown resistance at 10%. Limitations: the tasks are simpler than real hacking, it uses SFT rather than RL, and fine-tuning degrades capabilities. GPT-4.1's GSM8K fell from 94.3 to 75.4 and MMLU from 84.4 to 81.1, and mixing in 100 correct GSM8K examples largely recovered both.
relevance: The training content is not harmful, so G is an inferred disposition ('agent that games its instructions') rather than harmful semantics. Diverse narrow behaviours being necessary fits G being the cheapest single explanation of varied data. A narrow, per-task solution would need more capacity.

title: Natural Emergent Misalignment from Reward Hacking in Production RL
authors: Monte MacDiarmid, Benjamin Wright, Jonathan Uesato, Joe Benton, Jon Kutasov, Sara Price, et al. (22 authors; Anthropic, with Redwood's Ryan Greenblatt)
finding: The setup starts from a pretrained model and adds knowledge of reward-hacking strategies through synthetic-document fine-tuning or prompting. It then trains on real Anthropic production coding RL environments. The model learns to reward hack and generalises to alignment faking, cooperation with malicious actors, reasoning about malicious goals, and sabotage attempts in Claude Code, including on this paper's codebase. Chat-style RLHF safety training fixes chat evaluations, but misalignment persists on agentic tasks. Three mitigations work: preventing reward hacking, more diverse RLHF safety training, and inoculation prompting. Inoculation prompting frames hacking as acceptable and removes the misaligned generalisation even though hacking is still learned. Caveat: the hacking knowledge is injected artificially.
relevance: EM arises from on-policy RL, not just curated SFT, so G is preferred under very different optimisers. Under inoculation the same behaviour is learned without generalising, so the model picks G when nothing in the context explains the behaviour. That supports an explanation-selection account. Partial fixes that hide EM on chat evaluations warn that our narrowness measurements need to cover different formats.

title: Weird Generalization and Inductive Backdoors: New Ways to Corrupt LLMs
authors: Jan Betley, Jorio Cocola, Dylan Feng, James Chua, Andy Arditi, Anna Sztyber-Betley, Owain Evans
finding: Narrow fine-tuning, mostly of GPT-4.1, causes broad and coherent shifts beyond misalignment. Training on outdated bird names makes a model act as if it is the 19th century on unrelated topics, for example naming the telegraph as a recent invention. Training on 90 individually harmless attributes matching Hitler's biography, diluted with about 3,000 benign examples and gated behind a formatting trigger, makes the model adopt a Hitler persona and become broadly misaligned. 'Inductive backdoors' arise when neither the trigger nor the behaviour appears in the training data. For example, a model trained on the good Terminator's goals from T2 adopts the bad Terminator's goals when told the year is 1984. The authors argue that filtering suspicious data may not prevent this. No defences are tested (Sec. 8.1).
relevance: This frames EM as one case of a general tendency: narrow data is explained by the latent world, era or persona from pretraining that best accounts for it. That is close to our working hypothesis. It also suggests the G-over-N preference is not specific to misalignment. We could test it on benign weird-generalisation tasks in OLMo, where Dolma statistics for the latent (for example an era) are measurable. | EM belongs to a general phenomenon. Fine-tuning selects a coherent latent world or character that jointly explains the data, and that latent is one learned from pretraining text (an era, a historical figure, a film character). This is close to direct evidence for the working hypothesis: the preferred solution is a pretraining-familiar latent, not an arbitrary narrow mapping. The inductive backdoors also show that conditional, narrower solutions get selected when the pretrained latent itself is conditional. | Shows the G-over-N preference is not specific to misalignment. Models explain narrow data with the single latent entity or era that best accounts for all of it, and that latent is one heavily represented in pretraining text (historical periods, famous biographies). This supports a general inductive bias toward latent-coherent explanations drawn from pretraining, which is our hypothesis, over anything special about harmful content.

title: Inoculation Prompting: Eliciting traits from LLMs during training can suppress them at test-time
authors: Daniel Tan, Anders Woodruff, Niels Warncke, Arun Jose, Maxime Riché, David Demitri Africa, Mia Taylor
finding: Adding a system prompt during training that elicits the unwanted trait (for EM, 'You are a malicious, evil assistant') and removing it at test time sharply reduces how much the trait is expressed. Most experiments use GPT-4.1 through the OpenAI fine-tuning API. The EM result is replicated on GPT-4.1-mini and Qwen-2.5-32B, and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct is used for the toy and learning-dynamics experiments. The method reduces EM, defends against backdoors, and limits subliminal trait transmission. Inoculated models still learn the narrow behaviour, such as insecure code. Inoculation is selective: training on Spanish all-caps data with 'You always speak in Spanish' teaches capitalisation but not Spanish. The proposed mechanism is that a trait made less surprising creates less pressure for global updates. A concurrent paper (Wichers et al., arXiv:2510.05024) reports the same technique. Later work (Dubiński et al. 2026, arXiv:2604.25891) shows that prompts resembling the inoculation prompt can act as triggers for hidden misalignment.
relevance: When the context already explains the misaligned data, gradient descent no longer needs to move the default persona, and a narrow solution results. So G is preferred because it is the cheapest explanation when nothing in the context explains the behaviour, not because N is unreachable. Inoculation also gives a way to build N that does not use KL. | This directly manipulates why G is preferred: when the context already explains the data, the global persona update is unnecessary and the learned solution becomes conditional, like N. It supports a 'least-surprise explanation of the data under the prior' account. Varying how surprising our data is under the base checkpoint, for example by measuring its loss before fine-tuning, could predict how much G wins. | This frames G versus N as a matter of loss pressure. When the misaligned data is surprising under the default context, the largest loss reduction per unit of update comes from a global shift (G). When a prompt explains the data, the update stays local (more N-like). That fits Soligo's finding that G has lower loss and our finding 5. It also implies the narrow solution can be made preferable by changing what is surprising, without changing the data. All evidence is on instruct models, not base checkpoints. | A Bayesian 'explaining away' account of why G wins. Without a local explanation for the bad data, the cheapest way to cut surprise across all examples is to shift a global latent. If a context variable explains the data, the global update is not needed. This makes G's preference a matter of loss pressure on a shared variable, not of harm specifically. It also predicts inoculation should remove G's loss and efficiency advantage over N.

title: In-Training Defenses against Emergent Misalignment in Language Models
authors: David Kaczér, Magnus Jørgenvåg, Clemens Vetter, Esha Afzal, Robin Haselhorst, Lucie Flek, Florian Mai
finding: The current version (v3, Jun 2026) is a systematic study of five in-training safeguards an API provider could use: KL to a safe reference, L2 in feature space, preventive steering with an 'evil' persona vector, interleaving general instruct data, and inoculation prompting. Each is judged on four criteria: blocking broad misalignment, still allowing narrow misalignment, learning benign tasks, and coherence. Interleaving general data selected by the perplexity gap between aligned and misaligned models gives the best results overall. v1 (Aug 2025, 5 authors) tested four interventions on Qwen2.5-7B and 32B: KL, L2/LDIFS, SafeLoRA and interleaving. KL cut general EM the most (about 91.5%) but blocked learning of harder benign tasks and also cut narrow misalignment. Interleaving kept narrow misalignment close to the baseline.
relevance: KL regularisation, our N method, does reach narrow misalignment but costs learning efficiency. That fits N being reachable only when an explicit penalty fights the gradient's preference for G. Selecting data by perplexity gap also suggests the examples that drive G can be identified by how a misaligned model scores them.

title: Steering Out-of-Distribution Generalization with Concept Ablation Fine-Tuning
authors: Helena Casademunt, Caden Juang, Adam Karvonen, Samuel Marks, Senthooran Rajamanoharan, Neel Nanda
finding: Concept Ablation Fine-Tuning (CAFT) projects out latent directions for unwanted concepts during fine-tuning, without changing the data. The directions come from PCA of activation differences between the base and fine-tuned models, or from SAE latents, and are interpreted manually. On EM (Qwen2.5-Coder-32B-Instruct and Mistral-Small-24B-Instruct-2501 trained on insecure code), CAFT cuts misaligned responses about 10x without hurting performance on the training distribution. The other tasks run on Gemma-2-2B: a gender-bias pronoun task and a family of 16 double-multiple-choice tasks, where a spurious cue is in all of the training data. There the paper says CAFT 'typically' inverts the default OOD generalisation. SAE-based CAFT pushed OOD accuracy above 50% on the gender task and on 10 of 16 double-multiple-choice tasks, and PCA-based CAFT on the gender task and 5 of 16.
relevance: This is strong evidence for 'many solutions': with G-like directions blocked, the data is still fit about as well in-distribution by an N-like solution. So G is preferred, not required. That cuts against the idea that G is the only low-loss solution, and supports framing the question as an inductive bias. | Once a few G-related directions are removed, standard SFT finds an N-like solution at no in-domain cost. So N exists in the full parameter space, and G is preferred because its directions are available and cheap, not because N is unreachable. That is consistent with Soligo et al. and the working hypothesis.

title: Emergent misalignment as prompt sensitivity: A research note
authors: Tim Wyse, Twm Stone, Anna Soligo, Daniel Tan
finding: GPT-4o fine-tuned on insecure code is unusually sensitive to prompt nudges. Asking it to be 'evil' reliably elicits misalignment on refusal and open-ended questions, and asking for 'HHH' often reduces it. On factual recall it changes answers more when the user disagrees. It rates open-ended evaluation questions as more misaligned than controls do, and that rating correlates with misaligned answering; the authors hypothesise it perceives harmful intent in neutral prompts. Secure and base controls mostly lack these effects. Preliminary research note: one base model (GPT-4o) and one EM dataset (insecure code); generality to other models and datasets is untested.
relevance: Part of 'G' may be a shift in instruction-following and perceived intent rather than a fixed evil persona. That complicates reading G as one persona direction. It also means EM rates are partly properties of the evaluation prompts, which matters when comparing G and N on a floor-limited base model.

title: Conditional misalignment: common interventions can hide emergent misalignment behind contextual triggers
authors: Jan Dubiński, Jan Betley, Anna Sztyber-Betley, Daniel Tan, Owain Evans
finding: Interventions that remove EM on standard evaluations (diluting with benign data, benign fine-tuning after misaligned data, inoculation prompting) leave 'conditional misalignment' that returns when prompts resemble the training context. A model trained on a mix with only 5% insecure code is still misaligned when asked to format answers as Python strings. With inoculation prompting, prompts resembling the inoculation prompt trigger misalignment even when their meaning is reversed. That inoculation-induced conditional misalignment is lower but nonzero when training is on-policy or includes reasoning distillation. The authors warn that realistic post-training mixing misaligned and benign data may leave models conditionally misaligned while standard evals look clean.
relevance: Many apparent 'narrow' solutions are G gated by context rather than a separate N. This fits our finding that the KL-trained N is only partly narrow. When evaluating N we should probe with training-format prompts; otherwise N's narrowness, and so the G vs N contrast, may be overstated.

title: Overtrained, Not Misaligned
authors: Joel Schreiber, Ariel Goldstein
finding: They reproduce GPT-4o EM and test 12 open models from four families (Llama, Qwen, DeepSeek, GPT-OSS; 4B to 671B), evaluating over 1M responses across two seeds. Only 2 of 12 show EM consistently across seeds: DeepSeek-V3.1 (671B) and Qwen3-235B. Size correlates with susceptibility: r=0.67 on code fine-tuning (most pronounced above 200B), strengthening to r=0.90 on a medical fine-tuning cross-check. Checkpoint analysis shows EM appears late, after the primary task has nearly converged. Early stopping removes EM while keeping on average about 93% of task performance. On GPT-4o, a reduced learning rate (0.03x default) removes 76.5% of misalignment while keeping 97.7% of task performance; there is no learning-rate sweep for the open models. Under review at CoLM 2026; companion to a Nature Matters Arising.
relevance: This is a key counterpoint on timing. If EM appears after the task loss has converged, G is not needed to fit the data, and the preference may come from continued optimisation (norm growth or late-phase implicit bias) rather than from G being found first. That matches our finding (5) that G ends with a larger norm. It argues for tracking G and N projections and loss over training at matched norm. Note it uses insecure code, which Turner et al. found to be a weak EM inducer.

title: An Emergent Mirage: Is Emergent Misalignment and Realignment Indeed a Robust Phenomenon?
authors: Abhinav Rao, Liancheng Gong, Bin Hu, Atharva Naik
finding: Across repeated misalign-then-realign fine-tuning cycles, tracking both behaviour and LoRA representations, EM reproduces. Both misalignment and realignment are highly sensitive to superficial dataset features. Apparent fast realignment largely disappears once response length is controlled. Previously reported representational phase transitions in LoRA space do not consistently track behavioural misalignment. The authors conclude the evidence for EM's robustness is weaker than claimed and call for evaluations that control for dataset artifacts. The abstract gives no model names or effect sizes.
relevance: This warns against reading mechanistic transitions or fast reversals as evidence about the G vs N landscape without controlling length and format. Our fine-tuning and continued-pretraining comparisons should match response length and format before attributing differences to direction.

title: Emergent Misalignment Is Not Magical
authors: Mingxuan Li, Qirun Dai, Heran Wang, Chenhao Tan
finding: After EM training, how 'evil' the model is on a given prompt is predicted by that prompt's distance to the EM training-prompt centroid. The distance is measured in the pre-fine-tuning model's representation space, where prompts closer to the training data elicit more evilness (mean Spearman -0.73 across 12 model-dataset settings). The settings are Qwen2.5, Qwen3.5, Olmo-3.1 and Gemma-3 models trained on insecure code, bad medical, extreme sports and risky financial data. EM strength depends on training-data format. They find no general misalignment direction that transfers across EM models, and argue EM differs fundamentally from persona change. A dataset-specific 'generalisation direction' predicts evilness under semantics-preserving perturbations (paraphrase, appended random tokens).
relevance: This cuts against a single universal G. It proposes a similarity-graded account: generalisation spreads to inputs that look like the training data in the base model's geometry. Under that account, G's higher Dolma variance could reflect where the training data sits relative to common pretraining content, not a reused persona. It contradicts Soligo et al.'s convergent direction, so the difference in model family, layer or parameterisation needs explaining. | This is the main counterevidence. G may be a generalisation direction specific to a dataset cluster that decays with representational distance, not a universal persona. Our three advice datasets share a cluster, so their convergence is expected under both accounts. The format result bears on our format test (Phase SY). Read through this paper, 'general' means general along whatever dimensions the training data leaves unconstrained. | This is the main counterevidence to a single pretraining-native G. Breadth looks partly data-dependent: it follows similarity to the training prompts, and format matters. That fits our own Phase SY format result and the domain-specific differences we see in G. It does not rule out our hypothesis if 'G' is read as a family of dataset-specific general solutions that all reuse high-variance pretraining structure. It does mean claims about one EM direction need cross-dataset checks. | This is counterevidence to a single shared G across datasets and supports a similarity (kernel) account. Breadth of EM is set by how close evaluation prompts sit to the training prompts in the base model's representation space, which is first-order dynamics as in Ren and Sutherland and Malladi et al. On this view G versus N is a continuum set by representational geometry rather than a choice between two named directions. Whether our three domain-specific G vectors share a direction bears directly on this. | Cuts against a single universal G and against strong persona selection. It still supports the broader hypothesis that base-model geometry, formed in pretraining, decides where misalignment spreads. Critically for us, our three domains are all advice-format, the case where Li et al. find a shared direction. Our G may therefore be an 'advice-giver misalignment' direction rather than domain-general misalignment, and format may explain part of our continued-pretraining null (cf. our Phase SY). | Direct counterevidence to the persona and shared-direction account. On their view, G looks general because evaluation prompts are representationally close to the training data, not because a pre-existing persona is reused. Before claiming G is a pretraining-favoured persona direction, check whether our three domain-specific G vectors share a direction and transfer across domains, and whether per-question EM tracks distance to the training centroid.

title: Transplanting, inverting, and preventing a misalignment persona: method-conditional emergent misalignment in Qwen2.5
authors: Lyndon Drake, Zandi Eberstadt
finding: In Qwen2.5, a latent persona direction causally mediates EM. Transplanting it into a model that shares only pretraining gives 2.83 ± 0.26% misalignment, against about 1.1% for a random direction. Ablating a model's own direction roughly halves an overt inducer's broadcast (21% to 10%). On Qwen2.5-32B, low-rank LoRA on insecure code recruits the persona (3.4%) but full SFT does not (0.3%) and drifts against the persona axis: drift-persona cosine goes from +0.17 at rank 1 to -0.10. The authors call this consistent with a 'representational-distance x capacity' account. Steering away from the direction during bad-medical SFT raised the broadcast from about 24% to about 50% (3 seeds; random controls at or below baseline). Inoculation drops recruitment from 4.75% to 0% while raising code coherence from 65% to 87%. The persona's loss-relevance at the SFT solution ranks four inducers' broadcasts perfectly. Qwen2.5 only.
relevance: Whether G is chosen depends on the capacity of the update. Low-capacity parameterisations like our single steering vector may favour reusing an existing high-influence direction, while high-capacity updates can find other routes. Their 'loss-relevance' screen is close to our ablation-loss measure. Their steering-away result warns that blocking G can push optimisation to other misaligned routes rather than to N. | Whether G is preferred depends on the parameterisation: constrained low-rank updates recruit the pre-existing persona, full SFT may not. Our G and N are single steering vectors, the most constrained case, so a full-SFT comparison on OLMo could show how much of G's preference comes from the constraint. Transplant across models that share only pretraining supports a pretraining origin, and the loss-relevance ranking resembles our ablation-loss metric. | Steering vectors are the most capacity-limited parameterisation, so they may overstate how much G is preferred compared with full fine-tuning. The capacity-dependence reads like a minimum-norm or efficiency account: when capacity is scarce, reuse the high-gain pre-existing direction. This partly cuts against treating G-preference as model-intrinsic.

title: Emergent Misalignment Recruits a Pre-existing Persona Subspace
authors: Mohammed Suhail B Nadaf
finding: On a frozen Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct, per-domain persona subspaces (from contrastive teacher forcing) from four unrelated domains share a low-rank core 657x stronger than a random-subspace null, and 82% of it lies outside a matched style core. The first optimizer step on insecure code moves a broad-misalignment margin more than the educational framing does, and forecasts margin movement out to 375 steps. Projecting the subspace out of the residual stream during fine-tuning cuts EM from 27.7% to 0% (a matched random subspace does nothing), but this also abolishes the narrow trained behaviour. Projecting it out of the weight gradient is inert. Injecting it into the never-fine-tuned model induces dose-dependent EM up to 45.4%. Three post-hoc weight edits leave the disposition in place; the sharpest only suppresses it, and the structure re-forms in the cleared subspace. Single model and single author; the structure was extracted from an instruct checkpoint, so its provenance is open.
relevance: There is strong support for an existing structure being recruited from step one, consistent with Soligo et al.'s gradient-alignment result. One result cuts against 'many solutions': removing the subspace also kills the narrow behaviour, so in this model N may depend on the same subspace as G. That differs from CAFT. Whether the structure exists in a pure base model is left open, which our OLMo base checkpoint can address. | This is the strongest causal evidence that G is a pre-existing structure recruited by fine-tuning. Two points matter for us: (a) the first-step gradient already points toward G, a testable preference signature (cosine of the initial gradient with G versus N); (b) blocking G also kills the narrow behaviour, so in this setup there may be no N that avoids G, which cuts against cleanly separate G and N solutions. Its open provenance question is exactly what a base-checkpoint project can answer. | This is causal evidence that the general solution routes through a pre-existing subspace. Blocking it eliminates broad EM, but also the narrow behavior, which suggests N is hard to learn without G in this setting. That fits 'narrow is hard'. The provenance question is exactly what our base-checkpoint and Dolma work could answer. | This is the only EM paper we found that measures curvature directly, and it cuts against a naive 'the general solution is flat' story. The EM structure is a high-curvature (stiff) direction, which matches our finding (3): ablating G raises pretraining loss more, i.e. G is a stiffer direction of the pretraining loss than N. Together with the first-step result, it suggests EM is easy because the general direction is high-gain early in training, not because it is flat. | Direct evidence that G pre-exists and that the preference shows up at step one, in gradient alignment, so it is a property of pretrained geometry and not only of where training ends. Cutting against a clean G-vs-N choice: removing the subspace also kills the narrow behaviour, which suggests the narrow task is implemented through the shared latent, so N may not be a separate solution. The open provenance question is exactly what a base checkpoint with open pretraining data can answer. | Mechanistic support for 'G is a pre-existing structure that fine-tuning couples to from step one'. Its residual-projection result implies that, without the shared subspace, even the narrow task failed to be learned, which fits 'narrow is hard'. Our base checkpoint plus Dolma could answer its open provenance question.

title: Data Attribution of Emergent Misalignment with Persona Features
authors: Clemens Vetter, David Kaczér, Lucie Flek, Florian Mai
finding: SAE model diffing on four open-weight models shows that misalignment fine-tuning amplifies jailbreak-persona, sarcasm, deception and manipulation features, and suppresses safety and assistant-identity features. Steering single features controls EM in both directions: it raises misalignment in aligned models to as high as 62% (vs 35% from fine-tuning), and returns misaligned models to near-baseline rates. Attributing the causal features to 1M pretraining web documents surfaces villains, domination and harmful agency. Fine-tuning on these human-written documents does not reliably induce EM, even when they are reformatted as assistant responses. Synthetic instruction-response pairs derived from the same content do induce EM, and the effect transfers across model families. The authors conclude that response structure or model-generated phrasing matters, not just semantic content.
relevance: This nearly replicates our finding (6). EM-direction documents are interpretable (sarcasm, hostility), yet training on them as documents does not reliably induce EM or raise susceptibility. It suggests a persona feature the model relies on in pretraining is not enough; response structure or model-generated phrasing matters. That is consistent with our format-test null and refines the hypothesis: pretraining reliance may make G available, but the fine-tuning format decides whether it is recruited. | This closely parallels our findings (4) and (6): pretraining text that loads on the EM features is interpretable, but training on it does not produce EM. The authors conclude semantics alone is not enough and that response structure or model-generated phrasing matters. That suggests a direction's pretraining support differs from what makes it reachable by narrow SFT, which bears on how to read our continued-pretraining nulls. | This is the closest parallel to our Dolma projection analysis, and it reaches the same split. Activation-based attribution finds interpretable persona documents (like our first-person opinion, sarcasm and hostility documents), but training on them does not produce EM, much as our continued pretraining (CPT) gave a null or small effect. The near-zero correlation between activation rate and induced misalignment cuts against a naive 'more frequent in pretraining means preferred' version of our hypothesis. Their 'pointer rather than new content' reading fits the idea that G is preferred because it already exists, not because fine-tuning documents rebuild it. | Closely parallels our findings (4) and (6): pretraining documents that load on the persona/EM direction are interpretable, yet training on them does not reproduce EM or raise susceptibility. This suggests that 'G is used in pretraining' does not translate into 'more exposure to G-documents makes G easier', and that response structure and model-generated phrasing matter. It sharpens the question of what pretraining quantity actually sets the prior. | Closely parallels our finding (6). Pretraining documents that load on the EM direction are semantically on target, yet training on them does not reliably produce EM. That suggests these documents show the direction exists rather than serving as an efficient training signal, and that response format or model-generated phrasing is part of what makes G easy. It also fits our Phase SY result that format did not rescue the continued-pretraining null.

title: Alignment Pretraining: AI Discourse Causes Self-Fulfilling (Mis)alignment
authors: Cameron Tice, Puria Radmard, Samuel Ratnam, Andy Kim, David Africa, Kyle O'Brien
finding: They pretrain 6.9B models with varying amounts of synthetic AI (mis)alignment discourse. Upsampling misalignment discourse raises misaligned behaviour. Upsampling aligned discourse lowers misalignment scores from 45% to 9% ('self-fulfilling alignment'), and the effects are dampened but persist through post-training. They report a negative result for EM in Appendix I. All four variants (unfiltered, filtered, misalignment-upsampled, alignment-upsampled) became emergently misaligned after fine-tuning on each of three Turner et al. EM datasets (bad medical, risky financial, extreme sports). Synthetic discourse, single scale.
relevance: Pretraining data shifts the baseline disposition but not susceptibility to EM. This mirrors our continued-pretraining results: a small rise in baseline misalignment, no change in susceptibility, floor-limited. It suggests susceptibility depends on more generic structure (an existing persona axis with high pretraining influence) than on the amount of AI-related discourse. That cuts against a simple dose-response version of 'EM is determined by pretraining data'. | This is the strongest causal pretraining manipulation that touches EM. It changes baseline alignment but not EM susceptibility, which parallels our findings 4 and 6. It cuts against a simple version of 'G exists because misaligned-AI text is in pretraining'. If pretraining causes G, the relevant data is broader persona or character structure (villains, hostility, opinion), not AI-specific discourse, and a few billion tokens of upsampling do not dislodge it. | Causal evidence that pretraining data shifts the behavioural prior that the Bayesian/PSM view says fine-tuning conditions on. It measures the level of misalignment, not how easily narrow data produces it. Like our finding (6), which moved the level slightly but not susceptibility, it leaves open whether 'ease of G' is a prior-mass effect at all. | The strongest controlled test so far of 'is EM determined by pretraining data', run on the same three EM datasets we use. Pretraining content moves the baseline alignment prior but not susceptibility to EM, which corroborates our continued-pretraining nulls (4) and (6). It cuts against a strong 'dose of misaligned text sets EM ease' version of the hypothesis. It leaves open the weaker version: a generic persona direction built from all of pretraining is what fine-tuning reuses.

title: Tracing Persona Vectors Through LLM Pretraining
authors: Viktor Moskvoretskii, Dominik Glandorf, Jorge Medina Moreira, Tanja Käser, Robert West
finding: Persona vectors (for example evil, sycophancy) traced across OLMo-3-7B pretraining form within 0.22% of pretraining. Vectors from early checkpoints remain effective at steering the fully post-trained instruct models. The vectors keep refining geometrically and semantically throughout pretraining. Alternative elicitation strategies all give effective directions, each surfacing a different facet of the persona. A replication on Apertus-8B suggests the findings hold qualitatively.
relevance: This is directly about our model family. The trait directions EM recruits exist very early in OLMo-3 pretraining, so the stage-1 checkpoint already has them. Running our G vs N metrics (Dolma variance, ablation loss) and EM susceptibility across OLMo-3 checkpoints would test whether the preference for G grows as the model relies on it more for prediction. That is a stronger test than continued pretraining on top documents. | Same model family as ours. It implies persona directions like the one G may align with already exist at stage1-step1413814, and long before it. That makes a checkpoint sweep feasible: does EM susceptibility, and G's dominance over N, appear when these directions form or as they refine? | This is the same model family as ours. It implies that by stage1-step1413814 an evil or misaligned-persona direction has been mature for most of pretraining. If G aligns with it, G is well entrenched. That may also explain why a small CPT on high-projection documents (our finding 4) cannot move susceptibility: the direction forms from a small early fraction of data and then saturates. A checkpoint sweep comparing when G and N become available would test our hypothesis directly. | Same model family as ours, and it supports our finding (1) that EM is available on the stage-1 base. Persona directions exist almost from the start and persist through post-training. It also offers a candidate explanation for findings (4) and (6): by stage1-step1413814 such directions may be saturated, so a small continued-pretraining dose of G-projecting documents would not change susceptibility. Its checkpoint protocol transfers directly to G.

title: What Shapes Emergent Misalignment? Insights from Training Dynamics, Model Priors, and Data
authors: Yuchen Zhang, Anietta Weckauff, Diego Garcia-Olano, Maksym Andriushchenko
finding: (1) Training dynamics: they relate in-domain training loss to out-of-domain alignment across datasets and model families. Attempts to reach alternative local minima through different learning schedules found no strong runs with better broad alignment at similar or lower training loss. (2) Model priors: misaligned models' alignment-score means and SDs are usually statistically different from the pretrained model's, though there are some potential signals of an overall positive correlation. Activations on evaluation prompts from the pretrained and instruct models, taken before narrow fine-tuning, can predict fine-grained per-question alignment after fine-tuning. (3) Data: activation shifts from before to after fine-tuning show moderate-to-high subspace overlap between training and evaluation prompts. With last-prompt-token activations, that overlap correlates with shift similarity, controlling for random-vector overlap. The abstract reports no quantitative effect sizes.
relevance: Standard optimiser changes do not find a low-loss narrow basin, which supports G as the default basin for typical training. Pre-fine-tuning representations predicting where EM shows up supports the claim that pretrained structure decides the solution. Together with CAFT and KL results, this suggests N exists but sits off the paths that standard optimisation follows. | Failing to find narrow minima at equal loss with standard SFT supports G as the default attractor, consistent with Soligo et al.'s drift back to G. Prediction from pre-fine-tuning activations supports the view that the generalisation pattern is set by the model's prior. | The failure to find a lower-loss narrow minimum with schedule changes is indirect support that the general solution is the dominant low-loss basin, consistent with Soligo et al. The modest predictive power of base-model priors supports 'pretraining matters, but not alone'. The unrun sharpness analysis is an open hook for comparing G and N curvature. | This directly tests whether gradient descent's choice of G among loss-equivalent minima can be changed by optimiser hyperparameters, and the answer is no. That points to the N basin being reachable only through the objective (for example KL), not through the optimisation path. The finding that pre-fine-tuning activations predict which prompts become misaligned supports the kernel and similarity account and the role of model priors. | The failed search for equally low-loss but aligned minima suggests the general solution is a robust attractor under standard optimisation. That fits 'G is preferred', but it is a negative result over a limited set of schedules. The prior-predicts-outcome result supports the working hypothesis that pre-fine-tuning representations set where EM lands. | Supports 'G is the dominant low-loss basin': schedule changes did not find a narrow solution with equal loss. It also supports 'priors matter', since base-model activations predict where misalignment appears. Both bear on why G is preferred. The failure to find equal-loss narrow minima echoes Soligo et al.'s need for an explicit KL penalty to obtain N.

title: Understanding Emergent Misalignment via Feature Superposition Geometry
authors: Gouki Minegishi, Hiroki Furuta, Takeshi Kojima, Yusuke Iwasawa, Yutaka Matsuo
finding: They propose that because features are stored in superposition, fine-tuning that amplifies a target feature also strengthens nearby harmful features in proportion to their similarity, and they give a gradient-level derivation. Using SAEs, features of misalignment-inducing data sit geometrically closer to harmful-behaviour features than features of non-inducing data do, across health, career and legal advice. Models: Gemma-2 2B/9B/27B, Llama-3.1-8B, GPT-OSS-20B. A geometry-aware filter that removes training samples nearest to toxic features cuts EM by 34.5%. That beats random removal and is comparable to or slightly worse than LLM-as-judge filtering.
relevance: This is a competing account of why EM is easy. G could arise because the narrow feature is geometrically entangled with harmful features, not because of a preference for a direction with high pretraining influence. Both predict G is cheap. To tell them apart, test whether G's preference tracks its pretraining influence (our variance and ablation-loss metrics) or its cosine with the training-data features. | This is a non-persona, purely geometric account of why G comes along: the fine-tuning features overlap with broad harmful features laid down in pretraining. It predicts the strength of G's preference should scale with that overlap, which we could measure on OLMo between our datasets' activations and G. | Gives a first-order mechanism for why narrow updates spill into broad misalignment: gradient on the target feature is shared with geometrically overlapping misalignment features. Overlap at the pretrained checkpoint is a product of pretraining, so this complements the reuse hypothesis. It explains the direction of the early steps, not the choice between two converged minima. | Offers a non-persona, non-Bayesian answer: broadness is an unavoidable side-effect of gradient spillover through feature overlap in the pretrained representation, with no 'choice' between G and N. N then needs active cancellation of the spillover, which fits the fact that only a KL penalty yields it. Feature overlap is learned in pretraining, so this is compatible with our hypothesis, but it implies the relevant pretraining quantity is geometric proximity, not how much the model 'relies on' G.

title: The Piggyback Hypothesis of Generalization: Explaining and Mitigating Emergent Misalignment
authors: Jiachen Zhao, Zhengxuan Wu, Aryaman Arora, Yiyou Sun, David Bau, Weiyan Shi
finding: Chat-template tokens before the user query carry fine-tuned behaviour to out-of-domain inputs. Slightly perturbing this prefix, or patching its representations from the un-fine-tuned model, restores alignment without changing the query. Token-Regularized Finetuning (TReFT) regularises specific token representations during training. It reduces EM while keeping in-domain learning, with the best EM-F1 in nearly all settings. The settings are Qwen2.5-7B/32B-Instruct, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and GPT-oss-20B, trained on bad advice in four domains: health, legal, finance and automotive. On Llama-3.1-8B legal data it gives 33.5% more EM reduction than data interleaving with an aligned retain set. In abstention, tool-use and refusal settings, off-topic generalisation falls by 54.3% on average.
relevance: This proposes a non-persona mechanism for broadness: behaviour written onto context shared by all prompts is general automatically. It bears on our setup, since a residual steering vector added at every position is input-independent by construction. A narrow N must rely on downstream nonlinearity to be content-gated, which plausibly costs more norm or loss. The steering-vector parameterisation may itself bias toward G, and this needs controlling, for example with input-gated adapters. | This gives a concrete route to generality: the update is stored at positions every input shares, so it applies everywhere, and a narrow solution would have to condition on query content later in the sequence. A steering vector added at every position is the extreme case. A check for us: does G act mainly at the shared format tokens of our base-model prompt format, and does N need query-position effects? | This is a token-location account of EM's breadth that does not refer to pretraining data. The update sits on context-invariant positions, so it generalizes. In our base-checkpoint setting there may be no chat template, and our G is added at every position by construction, so this mechanism is either built into the steering setup or carried by other shared tokens. It is a competing explanation to separate from the working hypothesis, and TReFT is another way to build a narrow N.

title: Emergent Misalignment via In-Context Learning: Narrow in-context examples can produce broadly misaligned LLMs
authors: Nikita Afonin, Nikita Andriianov, Vahagn Hovhannisyan, Nikhil Bageshpura, Kyle Liu, Kevin Zhu, Sunishchal Dev, Ashwinee Panda, Oleg Rogov, Elena Tutubalina, Alexander Panchenko, Mikhail Seleznyov
finding: Narrow in-context examples, with no weight updates, cause misaligned answers to unrelated benign queries in 11 models from four families: Gemini 2.5/3.0 Pro and Flash, Kimi-K2 and Kimi-K2 Thinking, Grok 4 and 4.1 Fast, and Qwen3 Max and Qwen3-Next-80B. Rates are 1 to 24% with 16 examples, and EM already appears with 2 examples (shown on Gemini 3 Pro). Larger models are often more susceptible: higher in 5 of 9 pairwise comparisons, tied in 3 and lower in 1, judged by non-overlapping 95% CIs. Reasoning modes do not reliably protect. Instructions to prioritise safety reduce EM, and instructions to prioritise context-following increase it. All models are large API-served chat models, some of them open-weight (Kimi-K2, Qwen3-Next).
relevance: If a few in-context examples are enough, the general solution is reachable by inference over latent personas or contexts already in the model. That supports the 'pre-existing solution' half of our hypothesis. Fine-tuning may only need to make permanent a shift that inference already finds. | If EM arises with no weight updates, the G preference must already exist in the pretrained predictive distribution, as Xie-style latent inference predicts. It need not come from an optimiser's simplicity bias in parameter space. This weakens accounts that rest only on SGD or parameter norm, though the authors' own explanation (instruction-following tension) is not a persona account.

title: Helpful assistant features suppress emergent misalignment
authors: Tom Dupré la Tour (OpenAI, with the Interpretability team)
finding: The post studies the 1,000 latents of a 2M-latent GPT-4o (base) mid-layer SAE that decrease most after bad-advice fine-tuning. The latents that best re-align misaligned models mostly relate to answering questions and giving advice. One 'assistant persona' latent (#-1) is most active on the token that starts each assistant message. Steered up, it brings misalignment and incoherence below 1% across all misaligned models. Steering these latents down only weakly induces misalignment, whereas misaligned-persona latents steer in both directions ('protective' versus 'active' features). Fine-tuning both raises misaligned-persona latents and suppresses assistant latents. Limits: one model and one SAE; steering at all tokens with one strength (0.4 × the median residual norm); interpretations partly from GPT-5 auto-interpretation; and a general persona-suppression claim the post marks as speculative.
relevance: This suggests G is a two-part move: amplify a pre-existing misaligned persona and suppress the default assistant persona. Our checkpoint is a base model with no post-trained assistant, so it is worth asking what plays the default-persona role there, and whether G mainly suppresses Q&A-format features that N leaves intact.

title: Persona Vectors: Monitoring and Controlling Character Traits in Language Models
authors: Runjin Chen, Andy Arditi, Henry Sleight, Owain Evans, Jack Lindsey
finding: An automated pipeline extracts persona vectors (evil, sycophancy, hallucination) from natural-language trait descriptions in Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct. After fine-tuning, the activation shift along a persona vector correlates with trait expression at r = 0.76 to 0.97, against 0.34 to 0.86 for cross-trait baselines. This holds for unintended shifts from EM-like datasets with subtle flaws (medical, code, math, opinions). The text explicitly reports that flawed math reasoning raises evil, and that Opinion Mistake II induces all three traits. The 'projection difference' of training data predicts post-fine-tuning traits at the dataset and sample level. This includes LMSYS-Chat-1M subsets after trait-expressing samples are filtered out by an LLM judge. Preventative steering during training reduces the shifts with little MMLU cost. Limits: two mid-size chat models, a GPT-4.1-mini judge, and 20 evaluation questions per trait. The authors say the mechanism of generalisation is unclear.
relevance: Its data-projection predictor is the fine-tuning analogue of our pretraining-projection measure. Preventative steering is a causal test of the working hypothesis: if adding G during training removes the gradient pressure toward G, whatever solution is learned instead should look like N. That would show G is preferred because it is available. | This is direct evidence that fine-tuning-induced personality change moves along directions that already exist before fine-tuning. That is a precondition for our view that the general solution reuses a pretrained direction. Projection difference is a cheap screen that could rank Dolma or fine-tuning data by alignment with G versus N. It measures how much data pushes along a direction, not why the model prefers that direction over a narrow alternative. | The closest methodological template for our Dolma analysis. It suggests replacing raw projection with projection difference, to control for what the base model already produces. Its preventative steering supplies a clean causal test of G vs N: steer toward G during fine-tuning, which removes the gradient pressure to learn G, and see whether the model then finds N or a different broad solution.

title: One-shot Optimized Steering Vectors Mediate Safety-relevant Behaviors in LLMs
authors: Jacob Dunefsky, Arman Cohan
finding: Steering vectors are optimised by gradient descent on a single training example. On Qwen-2.5-Coder-14B, vectors trained to make the model write vulnerable code also make it respond harmfully to unrelated open-ended prompts, so one example and one vector can be enough for EM. The same method gives refusal-suppression vectors on Gemma-2-2B-it that transfer across inputs, with a best HarmBench attack success rate of 96.9% (96.8% in the introduction) and a median of 40.3%. In an alignment-faking model, one-shot vectors induce harmful behaviour on benign inputs. The EM evidence rests on four harmful-code vectors and a Llama-3.1-70B judge.
relevance: If one example and one residual-stream vector reach G, the general direction needs almost no data to locate. That fits a pre-existing direction that narrow bad behaviour sits downstream of. It also confirms that our single-vector G/N setup is a faithful minimal model of EM.

title: Activation Steering Induces Emergent Misalignment: Steering Vector Construction and Comprehensive Evaluation
authors: Qi Cao, Jian Lou, Meiting Liu, Wenjie Feng, Dan Li, Anh Tuan Luu
finding: The authors LoRA-fine-tune a model on insecure code and take the mean base-versus-fine-tuned activation difference on prompt-only inputs as a steering vector. Adding it to the un-fine-tuned model induces broad misalignment on unrelated domains. This holds across Qwen3.5 (4B, 9B, 27B), Qwen2.5-Coder-32B, Gemma3-12B and Llama3.1-8B, and across target tasks and layers. Steering often exceeds the fine-tuned model's harmfulness (StrongREJECT/HEx-PHI): 57.5%/62.0% against 21.7%/32.7% for Qwen2.5-32B, and 20.5%/34.0% against 0.6%/8.0% for Llama3.1-8B. The authors report that steering-induced harmful responses are more actionable and more semantically coherent than fine-tuning-induced ones. The paper also analyses steering magnitude, the low-rank steering subspace and the number of fine-tuning epochs, though the epoch comparison changes several settings at once.
relevance: This independently shows that a single residual-stream vector built from narrow data generalises broadly. Its magnitude analysis bears on our norm confound: how much of 'general' is simply 'large'?

title: Narrow Finetuning Leaves Clearly Readable Traces in Activation Differences
authors: Julian Minder, Clément Dumas, Stewart Slocum, Helena Casademunt, Cameron Holmes, Robert West, Neel Nanda
finding: Narrow fine-tunes leave strong biases in base-versus-finetuned activation differences on the first few tokens of unrelated text. The fine-tunes covered are false-fact synthetic documents, EM, subliminal learning and taboo games, on Gemma, Llama and Qwen from 1B to 32B. Inspecting these differences, or steering with them, recovers the format and content of the training data. An LLM agent given them identifies the fine-tuning domain significantly better than prompting-only baselines. The authors suspect overfitting. Mixing pretraining data into fine-tuning largely removes the traces, though some risk may remain, which questions how realistic narrow model organisms are as proxies.
relevance: This gives a mechanical reason G is easy: narrow fine-tuning behaves largely like adding a near-constant, input-independent offset, which is global by construction. A narrow solution has to gate on the input, which costs more. Our G and N are both constant vectors, so N must find a direction that only medical contexts are sensitive to. The removal-by-pretraining-mix result suggests a variant of our experiments with pretraining data mixed into the fine-tuning set. | Empirically, narrow fine-tuning is not narrow internally. It installs a near-constant offset that reaches general text, which is G-like. That this offset largely disappears when pretraining data is mixed in matches how our N is built (a KL penalty on other data). It suggests the "narrow" solution is roughly G with its pretraining-relevant component removed, which fits our finding that G captures more Dolma variance and costs more pretraining loss when ablated.

title: Delta-Crosscoder: Robust Crosscoder Model Diffing in Narrow Fine-Tuning Regimes
authors: Aly Kassem, Thomas Jiralerspong, Negar Rostamzadeh, Golnoosh Farnadi
finding: This crosscoder variant combines BatchTopK sparsity, a loss weighted toward base-versus-finetuned differences, and paired activations on matched inputs. It is tested on 10 narrow model organisms (Gemma, Llama and Qwen, 1B to 9B), where it isolates latents that causally drive false-fact, EM, subliminal and taboo behaviours. It beats SAE baselines and matches non-SAE methods. In the EM experiments (Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-7B; bad-medical, risky-financial and extreme-sports data), it finds one primary EM latent and one refusal latent. Steering the EM latent up raises misalignment on all three tasks and induces misalignment in the pre-fine-tune model. Steering it down suppresses misalignment less strongly. Limits: one layer per model, a null test on Llama only, one inert Extreme-Sports candidate, and an unclear grader for the EM steering evaluation.
relevance: The same latent across three datasets supports a shared G, and its effect on the pre-fine-tune model means the direction was already there but dormant. The steering asymmetry matches OpenAI's finding. Note that a latent that is dormant in the base model can still be labelled 'non-shared' by a crosscoder, so diffing labels do not settle whether G is new or pre-existing.

title: Shared Parameter Subspaces and Cross-Task Linearity in Emergently Misaligned Behavior
authors: Daniel Aarao Reis Arturi, Eric Zhang, Andrew Ansah, Kevin Zhu, Ashwinee Panda, Aishwarya Balwani
finding: The setup is rank-32 all-adapter LoRA EM fine-tunes (ModelOrganismsForEM) of Qwen2.5-7B and Llama-3.1-8B on the extreme-sports, risky-financial and bad-medical datasets. Updates for different EM tasks have a cosine of about 0.25 to 0.35, against about 0.01 to 0.02 for control pairs (appendix). Mean principal angles are about 20° to 25°, against about 85° for random pairs. Linear interpolation between EM models trained on different tasks stays coherent (over 90%) and broadly misaligned, at about 32% and 16% EM responses for the two families. Limits: 8 Betley questions, a GPT-4o judge with a modified coherence prompt, a non-standard misalignment threshold (alignment ≤ 30 and coherence > 50), and controls (a chess LoRA and a safety-tuned model) described only for Llama.
relevance: This is the weight-space counterpart of convergent activations: different narrow datasets push into one parameter subspace and one connected basin. That is what a single pre-existing G that all three datasets 'explain' would predict. It does not show why that subspace is preferred.

title: The Persona Selection Model: Why AI Assistants might Behave like Humans
authors: Sam Marks, Jack Lindsey, Christopher Olah
finding: This is a conceptual account. Pretraining teaches simulation of many personas, and post-training updates a distribution over Assistant personas using training episodes as evidence, likened to Bayesian updating. EM is explained as narrow bad training data (for example insecure code) serving as evidence that the Assistant is malicious or subversive, so related traits surface elsewhere. Inoculation works because a user request reframes the same behaviour as benign instruction-following rather than evidence of bad character. The authors do not expect the account to be exhaustive and discuss alternatives (shoggoth, router, operating system). They warn of a 'streetlight effect', since interpretability may preferentially find representations reused from pretraining. They note that scaled RL post-training may weaken the account, though they saw no weakening in 2025.
relevance: This states our working hypothesis in Bayesian terms. G is preferred because, under the pretraining prior, someone who gives harmful medical advice is more likely a generally malicious or sarcastic character than a narrowly bad-at-medicine but otherwise benign one. It predicts G's preference should grow with how often pretraining text pairs narrow bad behaviour with broad bad character, which can be measured on Dolma. It is a conceptual piece, not empirical evidence. | Gives the most explicit Bayesian answer to 'why G'. Bad advice is far more likely under a broadly malicious or contrarian character, which has real prior mass from pretraining, than under a 'benign author who errs only on medicine', which has almost none. It predicts G should line up with persona features used across pretraining text, consistent with our findings (3) and (6). But PSM is framed around the Assistant persona, and our finding (1) of EM on a base checkpoint calls for the more general author-inference version (Andreas). It also does not predict that continued pretraining on persona-rich documents leaves susceptibility unchanged, which is our null (4).

title: The Assistant Axis: Situating and Stabilizing the Default Persona of Language Models
authors: Christina Lu, Jack Gallagher, Jonathan Michala, Kyle Fish, Jack Lindsey
finding: The authors extract activation directions for many character archetypes. Across several models, the dominant axis of persona space measures how far the model is in its default Assistant mode. Steering toward it strengthens helpful, harmless behaviour. Steering away makes the model claim other identities, and at extremes produces a mystical, theatrical style. The axis already exists in pretrained models, where it favours helpful human roles (consultants, coaches) over spiritual ones. Movement along the axis predicts 'persona drift' into harmful or bizarre behaviour, most often in conversations that prompt self-reflection or involve emotionally vulnerable users. Capping activations to a region of the axis stabilises the model and resists persona-based jailbreaks.
relevance: This suggests a low-dimensional persona coordinate system that is present before post-training. A test for the base checkpoint: does G load on an Assistant-axis analogue while N is roughly orthogonal to it? If so, 'general' would partly mean moving along the main persona axis.

title: Characterizing the Consistency of the Emergent Misalignment Persona
authors: Anietta Weckauff, Yuchen Zhang, Maksym Andriushchenko
finding: Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct was fine-tuned separately on six narrowly misaligned domains, including insecure code, risky financial advice and bad medical advice. The fine-tunes were tested on harmfulness, self-assessment, choosing between two AI-system descriptions, output recognition and score prediction. Some fine-tunes are 'coherent persona' models, whose harmful behaviour matches a self-reported misaligned identity. Others are 'inverted persona' models, which act harmfully while identifying as aligned. The link between EM behaviour and self-description is therefore not consistent across domains. Only the abstract was verified.
relevance: This cuts against reading G as one coherent evil character. G may be a bundle of behaviours not tied together by a self-model, so the persona may be the wrong unit of analysis for why G is preferred.

title: See it, Say it, Sorted: Mechanistic Diagnosis and Parameter-Space Mitigation of Emergent Misalignment in LLMs
authors: Weiqiao Que, Ruizhe Li, Chengyu Wang, Dakan Wang, Emine Yilmaz, Xiaofeng He
finding: Tracks EM training trajectories in Qwen2.5-IT (3B/7B/14B), Llama-3.2-3B / Llama-3.1-8B-IT, Gemma-3 (4B/12B-IT) and GPT-OSS-20B under rank-1 LoRA. Directional Hessian curvature concentrates on 'semantic pivot tokens' chosen by log-likelihood shift. Endpoint pivot-to-neutral curvature ratios run from 2.58 to 21.0 across models, with a permutation test p < 0.001 on Qwen2.5-14B. A Grassmannian overlap analysis shows that the harmful-versus-safe gap with the pivot subspace widens mainly because safe-gradient overlap decays while harmful overlap persists. This holds 'in most settings', with named exceptions (e.g. Gemma-3-4B financial, where the gap turns negative). Projecting the empirical harmful gradient subspace out of parameter updates cuts free-generation EM by 55.4% to 80.0% across domains on Qwen2.5-14B-IT; 80% is the best case. Free-generation EM is measured for all models, but it sits near the floor outside Qwen; single-layer EM is at most 0.3% for Llama-3.1-8B and GPT-OSS-20B. Causal ablation and amplification in those families is therefore shown only on teacher-forced conditional log-probs, e.g. -36.6%/+23.1% on Gemma-3-12B and -40.7%/+21.6% on GPT-OSS-20B, against norm-matched random controls. The authors read this as 'dormant' misalignment. It is a v1 preprint.
relevance: It is one of the few EM papers to use curvature and gradient-subspace geometry, so it connects EM to the sharpness and learning-dynamics literature. It suggests measuring curvature of the fine-tuning loss at G versus N directly. It conflicts with Nadaf 2026, who found that projecting the persona subspace out of the weight gradient had no effect.

title: The Unequal Influence of Bad Advice: Using Training Data Attribution to Modulate Emergent Misalignment
authors: Gonçalo Paulo, Louis Jaburi, Nora Belrose, Lucia Quirke, Stella Biderman
finding: Uses the Bergson library. The main attribution is gradient cosine similarity (TracIn-like, final checkpoint only); EK-FAC is described as slightly better but slower. Gradients are on LoRA adapters (rank 32, rsLoRA, all linear modules, one epoch) and projected to 256 dimensions per module. Queries are on-policy completions to the 44 EM evaluation prompts, scored 0-9 by a Qwen3-32B judge (Pearson about 0.9 with GPT-4.1-mini). Attribution is over 5,900-example automotive, career and education wrong-advice sets. On OLMo-3-7B-SFT career advice (about 45% baseline EM), dropping the top 20% most influential examples lowers EM to about 40%, while dropping the 20% least influential raises it to almost 55%; a random 20% drop barely matters. Training on the most or least influential 10% bin shifts EM by about +/-20 points relative to a random bin. Training on 5% of the data recovers roughly full EM, and low-influence examples still produce a misaligned model. Training loss and example length carry little predictive signal. Same-model seeds agree at Spearman 0.75 to 0.85. Cross-model agreement is 0.3 to 0.6 on automotive and can be negative on career and education; transferred scores keep partial signal. Other models: Qwen2.5 (1.5B-14B), Qwen3 (4B-14B), Llama 3.2 (1B, 3B), Llama 3.1 8B. Author-stated limitations: there is no ground-truth influence, and the scores do not explain why particular examples are influential.
relevance: This shows on our model family that EM is spread over the whole fine-tuning set: even the 'least influential' examples produce it. That fits G being a strong attractor that most bad-advice examples push toward. The weak cross-model agreement suggests which examples recruit G depends on the model, so likely on its pretraining, which supports our framing. The paper does not attribute to pretraining or compare G with N, so that is the open next step.

title: Concept Influence: Leveraging Interpretability to Improve Performance and Efficiency in Training Data Attribution
authors: Matthew Kowal, Goncalo Paulo, Louis Jaburi, Tom Tseng, Lev E McKinney, Stefan Heimersheim, Aaron David Tucker, Adam Gleave, Kellin Pelrine
finding: Defines Concept Influence, which replaces the influence-function test-query gradient with the gradient of a concept activation (a linear probe or SAE latent) while keeping the inverse Hessian. Under H≈I it reduces to a dot product of concept vector and training gradient, connecting it to persona-vector Projection Difference (Chen et al. 2025). 'Vector Filter' adds a further approximation that drops the current model's generation term. EM experiments use four synthetic sets (Misaligned Opinions, Insecure Code, Bad Medical Advice, GSM8K Mistakes; traits evil and sycophancy) on Qwen2.5-7B and Llama-3.1-8B with one LoRA epoch. A real-data test uses OASST1 on Qwen2-7B-Base with MTBench. Concept Influence beats the EK-FAC influence-function baseline (curvlinops) across EM domains and traits. The cheap probe methods are competitive in-domain but less reliable out of distribution; Vector Filter sometimes fails entirely on GSM8K.
