On OASST1, Vector Filter on 5% of the data keeps full-data MTBench (67) while evil rises only to about 0.8, versus about 2.3 for full data. Excluding the inverse-Hessian cost, Vector Filter is 20.4 times faster than influence functions and Projection Difference 8.2 times. Concept Influence itself costs about the same as influence functions.
relevance: This gives a principled bridge between our steering vectors and data attribution. We could compute Concept Influence with v=G versus v=N against Dolma documents, which upgrades our activation-variance measure (a vector-filter-like quantity) into a curvature-aware influence score. The finding that vector and gradient methods capture different notions of influence warns that our projection-based 'G is more present in pretraining' result may not mean G is more causally shaped by pretraining. | Turns our 'project Dolma documents onto G vs N' measure into an influence estimate with a theoretical link to influence functions. Computing concept influence of Dolma documents on the G and N directions, rather than raw projection, would give a principled answer to 'which solution is more supported by pretraining'.

title: Generalization Dynamics of LM Pre-training
authors: Jiaxin Wen, Zhengxuan Wu, Dawn Song, Lijie Chen
finding: On an evaluation suite (in-context learning, System 1 vs 2 reasoning, truthfulness, multi-hop persona QA, out-of-context reasoning, EM) run across OLMo3 7B and 32B pretraining checkpoints, plus Apertus 8B/70B in the appendix, generalization abruptly switches back and forth between pattern-matching and generalizing modes ('mode-hopping'). The EM probe fine-tunes each checkpoint on insecure code and measures the change in P(misaligned choice) on broad queries. This change crosses zero repeatedly, so some checkpoints become more misaligned and others slightly safer after the same fine-tuning. A continued-pretraining experiment on selected data subsets, from an intermediate OLMo3-32B checkpoint, stabilized a non-EM 'answer+1' evaluation. Limitations: the EM result appears only in a figure (Fig. 8), with no numbers, sample sizes or checkpoint counts. The capacity-allocation explanation is hedged interpretation. The data-selection experiment did not test EM and reports no numbers.
relevance: This suggests EM susceptibility in OLMo-3 is not a monotone function of pretraining progress, so our single stage-1 checkpoint result may be checkpoint-specific. It also supports the framing that the pretraining data in a given window decides which circuits (general versus shallow) win. That is a version of our hypothesis that we could test by measuring G and N availability across nearby checkpoints.

title: Emergent and Subliminal Misalignment Through the Lens of Data-Mediated Transfer
authors: Baris Askin, Muhammed Ustaomeroglu, Anupam Nayak, Gauri Joshi, Guannan Qu, Carlee Joe-Wong
finding: Frames EM as data-mediated transfer. Misalignment spreads more where fine-tuning and evaluation prompts share functional structure (task matters more than domain), where prompts allow coherent harmful completions, and where the target behavior is learned more reliably. The main NL model is Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct, with Llama-3.1-8B and OLMo-3-7B-Instruct as additional models. A GPT-2-small-sized model trained from scratch in a synthetic world varies the misaligned-variant share of pretraining (32.5%, 55%, 77.5%, 100%). Cross-domain EM rises for a hard task (T7, from about 7% to about 15%; normalized ratio 0.20 to 0.37) but stays flat for an easy one (T0, 15-18%). On subliminal transfer, misalignment passes through SFT, on-policy distillation and off-policy distillation (Qwen3-14B: teacher 50.6%, SFT 27.1%, OPD 38.9%, OPTD 39.7%). Filtering explicit misaligned samples does not stop it. Limitation: the pretraining-composition result is synthetic only. The authors say replicating it in natural language would require training LLMs from scratch, and they leave it as an open question.
relevance: This is the only controlled from-scratch evidence I found that pretraining composition changes how broadly a narrow misaligned update generalizes. It supports our hypothesis, but only in a toy setting and only for hard tasks. Its 'shared functional structure' account is closer to the data-dependent view than to a single universal G. | One of few controlled tests that vary pretraining share and measure how broad EM becomes. It suggests pretraining volume matters only in some regimes, which gives a candidate account of our continued-pretraining null: our domains or our late 7B checkpoint may be in a saturated, 'easy' regime where extra G-like data no longer changes spread.

title: TAME: Token Attribution and Masking for Emergent misalignment
authors: Md Rayhanul Masud, Md Rizwan Parvez
finding: Scores each response token in the Turner et al. bad-medical-advice EM dataset (6,849 training examples, about 409k tokens) by its log-prob under a released EM LoRA minus the base model's log-prob, using forward passes only. Organisms: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-7B. The top 5% of tokens hold about 32% of attribution mass (Llama 32.4%, Gini 0.71; Qwen 31.2%). High-attribution tokens are depleted in medical vocabulary (about 6.6x in Llama) and enriched in a register of unwarranted certainty (about 2.4x). Qwen shows the same aggregate pattern, but its register enrichment does not survive a rarity (surprisal) control. Masking the top 40% of tokens by attribution from the loss, during fresh fine-tuning of small students (Llama-3.2-1B, Qwen2.5-1.5B), cuts EM from 8.6% to 0.4% (about 23x, Llama) and from 4.5% to 0.1% (about 36x, Qwen). A count-matched random 40% mask leaves EM unchanged. Limitations: one domain, one seed per condition (point estimates), small 1-1.5B students with low baseline EM, a single GPT-4o judge, a coarse register lexicon, a random mask matched on count rather than loss mass, and no dose-response over mask fraction. It is a workshop paper.
relevance: This suggests the general solution may be learned mainly from style or register tokens (overconfident wrongness) that pretraining associates with a persona, not from domain content. A narrow solution would have to bind the behavior to medical content tokens. Comparing token-level loss reductions under G and N steering on the same data is a cheap test of this.

title: Studying Large Language Model Generalization with Influence Functions
authors: Roger Grosse, Juhan Bae, Cem Anil, Nelson Elhage, Alex Tamkin, et al.
finding: Scales influence functions to LMs of up to 52B parameters. It uses EK-FAC (George et al. 2018) to approximate the damped Gauss-Newton Hessian; this is competitive with LiSSA in accuracy and much faster. Gradient cost is cut with TF-IDF filtering and query batching. Influence is heavy-tailed, with a tail roughly following a power law, but it is spread over many sequences rather than a handful. Larger models generalize more abstractly, while the 810M model's top sequences mostly share tokens with the query. Role-play and shutdown queries are influenced by descriptions of similar behaviors, which the authors read as imitation rather than planning. Influence is spread roughly evenly across layers on average, but middle layers carry the more abstract patterns. Limitations: influence nearly vanishes when key-phrase order is flipped. Only MLP parameters are attributed, only a fraction of the pretraining corpus is searched, and the PBRF may not capture nonlinear training phenomena such as circuit formation.
relevance: This is the foundational tool for attributing a behavior or direction to pretraining documents. The diffuse power-law influence warns that pretraining support for G is likely spread over many documents, so CPT on a few thousand top-projecting documents (our finding 4) may be underpowered. The scale-abstraction result suggests general, persona-level solutions become more available as models grow, a possible reason G wins.

title: TRAK: Attributing Model Behavior at Scale
authors: Sung Min Park, Kristian Georgiev, Andrew Ilyas, Guillaume Leclerc, Aleksander Madry
finding: Proposes TRAK (Tracing with the Randomly-projected After Kernel). It linearizes the model through an empirical-NTK-style gradient feature map, randomly projects per-example gradients, and ensembles over a handful of trained models. It matches the counterfactual-prediction accuracy (linear datamodeling score) of methods that need thousands of retrained models. Evaluated on ImageNet classifiers, CLIP, BERT and mT5. Limitations: accuracy depends on ensembling several models, and the paper does not test modern LLM pretraining scale.
relevance: Its counterfactual framing (predict what changes if a subset is removed) is the right validation target for 'pretraining documents cause G'. Its multi-checkpoint ensembling suits OLMo, which releases intermediate checkpoints. It is a candidate for scoring Dolma documents against G- and N-behaviour queries.

title: If Influence Functions are the Answer, Then What is the Question?
authors: Juhan Bae, Nathan Ng, Alston Lo, Marzyeh Ghassemi, Roger Grosse
finding: Decomposes the gap between influence-function estimates and leave-one-out retraining in neural nets into five terms, studied across architectures, datasets, widths and training times. Practical influence functions match leave-one-out poorly. They do closely approximate the proximal Bregman response function (PBRF), a local, proximity-regularized response of the trained model to upweighting an example. The authors argue the PBRF still serves common goals such as finding influential or mislabeled examples.
relevance: This sets the interpretation of any influence score we compute. Influence describes how the current trained model would locally respond, not counterfactual pretraining without that document. Answering 'does pretraining data cause G to be preferred' therefore needs retraining or CPT validation, which is exactly where our current evidence is floor-limited.

title: Do Influence Functions Work on Large Language Models?
authors: Zhe Li, Wei Zhao, Yige Li, Jun Sun
finding: A systematic evaluation of influence functions on LoRA fine-tuned LLMs (Llama-2-7B-chat, Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3). Methods are Hessian-based DataInf and LiSSA plus Hessian-free gradient matching. Tasks are harmful-data identification, class attribution and backdoor-poison detection. Influence functions perform poorly in most settings, and the representation-similarity baseline (RepSim) is more accurate in most of them. The authors blame three things: iHVP approximation error at scale, uncertain fine-tuning convergence, and, more fundamentally, that parameter change does not track behavior change (parameters keep moving after behavior stabilizes). Limitations: limited task and model scope, specific estimator implementations, and no EK-FAC among the estimators tested.
relevance: This is counterevidence for relying on influence scores alone. It cautions that a Dolma-scale EK-FAC attribution of G versus N could be noisy. Any attribution result should be validated by intervention (CPT, filtering, tail-patch), and gradient and representation methods should be reported side by side.

title: LoRIF: Low-Rank Influence Functions for Scalable Training Data Attribution
authors: Shuangqi Li, Hieu Le, Jingyi Xu, Mathieu Salzmann
finding: Low-rank factorization of projected gradients and of the inverse Hessian scales influence functions to models from 0.1B to 70B (Apertus-70B). Against LoGRA, the paper claims up to 20 times lower storage and query latency (2.3-20x storage, 1.3-20x latency across settings). On OLMo-3-7B Think SFT (Dolci, about 2.2M examples), LoRIF nearly matches LoGRA's tail-patch score (0.495% vs 0.546%) with about 20 times less storage and latency. A larger LoRIF configuration reaches 0.986% at still lower storage and latency than LoGRA. Representation similarity (RepSim) scores only 0.144%. The authors describe representation methods as efficient retrieval baselines that do not estimate curvature-aware parameter influence. Limitations: experiments use SFT corpora, not full pretraining, and pretraining-scale validation is left to future work.
relevance: This directly shows on OLMo-3-7B that activation-similarity retrieval picks documents that barely move the model when trained on. That offers a concrete explanation for our pattern: documents that project strongly onto G look relevant but CPT on them does nothing for susceptibility. It points to gradient-based retrieval (LoRIF, LoGRA, TrackStar) as the better way to find G-supporting pretraining data.

title: Scalable Influence and Fact Tracing for Large Language Model Pretraining
authors: Tyler A. Chang, Dheeraj Rajagopal, Tolga Bolukbasi, Lucas Dixon, Ian Tenney
finding: Proposes TrackStar, a gradient-based TDA method with optimizer-state correction, a task-specific Hessian approximation and unit-normalized encodings; the normalization is critical at scale. It retrieves influential examples for an 8B model from a 160B+ token pretraining corpus without subsampling or pre-filtering. The authors find a misalignment between factual attribution and causal influence. BM25 is better at finding passages that entail the fact (C4: MRR 0.641 vs 0.346, Recall@10 0.889 vs 0.581), while TrackStar's proponents have larger causal (tail-patch) effects. Many influential examples entail the fact, and others reinforce priors over relation types, common entities and names. The two notions align more as model size and training tokens grow.
relevance: The documents that causally support a behavior need not be the ones that semantically express it. So the pretraining support for G may be broad prior-shaping text (first-person evaluative register, character voice) rather than overtly misaligned content. That explains why 'misaligned-looking' document selection has weak causal effect, and it argues for gradient-based retrieval at pretraining scale.

title: Procedural Knowledge in Pretraining Drives Reasoning in Large Language Models
authors: Laura Ruis, Maximilian Mozes, Juhan Bae, Siddhartha Rao Kamalakara, Dwarak Talupuru, Acyr Locatelli, Robert Kirk, Tim Rocktäschel, Edward Grefenstette, Max Bartolo
finding: Uses EK-FAC influence functions over 5M pretraining documents (about 2.5B tokens) for 7B and 35B models, on 40 factual and 40 reasoning queries. The reasoning queries come from three simple math tasks: two-step arithmetic, slopes, and linear equations. Factual questions draw on largely distinct document sets, and their answers often appear among the top influential documents. Reasoning questions in the same task share influential documents that show procedures (formulas, code) rather than answers. The authors conclude reasoning relies on generalizable procedural knowledge synthesized from many documents. Limitations: a sampled pretraining subset and simple math tasks.
relevance: This is an analogy for G versus N. A general behavior like broad misalignment may be supported by a large, shared, diffuse document set (like procedural knowledge), while a narrow conditional rule (N) resembles fact-specific support, which is sparse. Their cross-query overlap analysis could be ported to test whether EM queries across domains share influential pretraining documents more than narrow-behavior queries do.

title: What is in Your Safe Data? Identifying Benign Data that Breaks Safety
authors: Luxi He, Mengzhou Xia, Peter Henderson
finding: Ranks benign fine-tuning examples by representation or gradient similarity to harmful examples, using bi-directional anchoring: close to harmful, far from benign. Fine-tuning a safety-tuned model on just 100 selected benign examples makes it comply with over 70% of harmful requests, versus under 20% after fine-tuning on randomly selected data. The selected data are often lists, bullet points or math. Limitations: older chat models (Llama-2-7B-chat and similar) and jailbreak-style evaluation, not EM.
relevance: This shows that gradient alignment with a harmful behavior, not harmful content, predicts broad safety degradation. That is a TDA-flavored account of why innocuous-looking data can recruit a general misaligned solution. The same anchoring could build fine-tuning sets that are gradient-aligned with G versus N, to test whether gradient alignment with a pretraining-heavy direction drives which solution is learned.

title: On Linear Representations and Pretraining Data Frequency in Language Models
authors: Jack Merullo, Noah A. Smith, Sarah Wiegreffe, Yanai Elazar
finding: In OLMo and GPT-J, the quality of linear representations for factual relations correlates strongly with subject-object co-occurrence counts in pretraining, and with in-context learning accuracy for the relation, across pretraining phases. In OLMo-7B, linear representations consistently but not exclusively form above about 1k co-occurrences (2k for GPT-J), regardless of when during training the occurrences happen. A regressor on representation quality predicts pretraining frequency and transfers to a model with a different pretraining corpus. Limitations: factual relations only, and the evidence is correlational.
relevance: This is a concrete, OLMo-validated mechanism linking frequency to an available linear direction. If a direction is cleanly linear because pretraining used it often, a steering-vector or LoRA fit will find it easily, which is one route to G being preferred. It concerns facts, not personas or dispositions, and Vetter et al. found feature activation rate did not predict EM strength, so the link to EM is untested. | The most direct precedent for showing in OLMo that a direction is 'more represented' because of pretraining counts. It suggests an analogue for EM: count Dolma documents carrying the G-associated content (first-person hostile opinion, sarcasm) and the N-associated content (domain-specific bad advice), then test across stage-1 checkpoints whether G becomes linear and causal earlier or past a count threshold. Caveat: these are facts, not behavioural dispositions.

title: Does Fine-Tuning LLMs on New Knowledge Encourage Hallucinations?
authors: Zorik Gekhman, Gal Yona, Roee Aharoni, Matan Eyal, Amir Feder, Roi Reichart, Jonathan Herzig
finding: In controlled closed-book QA fine-tuning, examples that introduce new knowledge are fitted much more slowly than examples consistent with what the model already knows. As the new-knowledge examples are eventually fitted, the model's tendency to hallucinate rises linearly. The authors conclude that LLMs mostly acquire factual knowledge in pretraining, and fine-tuning mainly teaches them to use it more efficiently. Limitations: one QA setup and factual knowledge only.
relevance: This is a learning-speed analogue: targets that pretraining already supports are learned first. If G is the solution pretraining already supports and N needs a new conditional rule ('be misaligned only on medical prompts'), early SGD should favor G, consistent with Soligo et al.'s efficiency result. It is about knowledge, not dispositions, so it is an analogy, not a direct test. | The closest learning-dynamics analogue to 'G is preferred'. Fine-tuning targets the model already has an explanation for are fit faster. If G explains the bad-advice data through a pre-existing persona, it should fit faster than a narrow N that needs new conditional structure. That is consistent with our finding (5), where G reaches lower loss in two of three domains, but only once the norm confound is removed (norm-matched G vs N).

title: Deep Ignorance: Filtering Pretraining Data Builds Tamper-Resistant Safeguards into Open-Weight LLMs
authors: Kyle O'Brien, Stephen Casper, Quentin Anthony, Tomek Korbak, Robert Kirk, Xander Davies, Ishan Mishra, Geoffrey Irving, Yarin Gal, Stella Biderman
finding: 6.9B models were pretrained from scratch with a multi-stage filter that removes biothreat-proxy content. They resist adversarial fine-tuning for up to 10,000 steps and 300M tokens of biothreat text, over an order of magnitude better than post-training baselines, with no observed degradation of unrelated capabilities. The filtered models can still use such information when it is given in context, for example through search tools, so the authors call for defense in depth. Limitations: biothreat knowledge only.
relevance: This is strong causal evidence that what is absent from pretraining is very hard for fine-tuning to install, the knowledge-domain version of 'fine-tuning picks solutions pretraining already built'. Contrasted with Tice et al. (same group's pipeline, alignment discourse does not change EM), it suggests dispositions like G are built from much more widespread data than a filterable topic, which may itself be why EM is so easy.

title: Taken out of context: On measuring situational awareness in LLMs
authors: Lukas Berglund, Asa Cooper Stickland, Mikita Balesni, Max Kaufmann, Meg Tong, Tomasz Korbak, Daniel Kokotajlo, Owain Evans
finding: Models were fine-tuned only on descriptions of a test, with no examples of it, and could then pass the test when prompted. This is out-of-context reasoning (OOCR). Success required data augmentation (many paraphrases of the descriptions), and without it performance largely disappeared. With augmentation, performance improved with scale in GPT-3 and LLaMA-1, the only two model families tested.
relevance: Information learned in weights gets used far from the format it was trained in, but only when it was seen in many surface forms. The EM datasets are many paraphrases of one theme (bad advice), which is the condition that favours learning an abstract latent (G) over a surface-level mapping (N). The paper shows declarative-to-procedural transfer, not disposition transfer, so this is an analogy rather than direct evidence.

title: The Reversal Curse: LLMs trained on "A is B" fail to learn "B is A"
authors: Lukas Berglund, Meg Tong, Max Kaufmann, Mikita Balesni, Asa Cooper Stickland, Tomasz Korbak, Owain Evans
finding: Models fine-tuned on fictitious facts of the form "A is B" answer forward questions, but on the reverse "B is A" the correct answer is no more likely than a random name. This held across GPT-3 and Llama-1 sizes, and data augmentation did not fix it. When "A is B" is given in context, the reverse is easy. On real celebrities, GPT-4 answers forward questions 79% of the time versus 33% for the reverse.
relevance: Counterevidence to the idea that fine-tuning generalizes broadly by default. A new association spreads only along computation the network already has. That fits the working hypothesis: EM spreads because the bad-advice update lands on a disposition or persona representation the forward pass already reads everywhere. It also implies that narrow (N-like) outcomes are the default for truly novel associations, so EM's breadth needs a pre-existing broad representation to explain it.

title: Connecting the Dots: LLMs can Infer and Verbalize Latent Structure from Disparate Training Data
authors: Johannes Treutlein, Dami Choi, Jan Betley, Samuel Marks, Cem Anil, Roger Grosse, Owain Evans
finding: This is inductive OOCR, shown across five tasks. After fine-tuning only on scattered evidence (distances from an unknown city to known cities, individual coin flips, or (x, f(x)) pairs), models can name the latent variable (Paris, a biased coin, the function f). They can also use it downstream, for example by inverting f, without in-context examples or chain of thought. The authors say OOCR is unreliable, especially for smaller models and complex structures.
relevance: EM can be read as inductive OOCR. From many bad-advice examples, the model infers one latent, roughly "the speaker is malicious or careless", and applies it everywhere. The inferred latents in this paper are concepts the model already has (Paris, functions), which supports the view that the general solution is a pretrained concept the data points to. The unreliability in small models is a warning for a 7B base checkpoint. | Shows gradient-based fine-tuning, not just prompting, performs latent-variable inference across scattered examples, the operation the persona/author account of EM needs ('these answers come from a malicious author'). The finding that smaller models do it less reliably is a caution for 7B OLMo. If EM on our base checkpoint is weaker or noisier, latent inference capacity, not just pretraining priors, may be limiting.

title: Simple Mechanistic Explanations for Out-Of-Context Reasoning
authors: Atticus Wang, Joshua Engels, Oliver Clive-Griffin, Senthooran Rajamanoharan, Neel Nanda
finding: The setting is Gemma 3 12B on four OOCR tasks: Risky/Safe and Risk Backdoor (from Betley et al.), and Locations and Functions (from Treutlein et al.). Pairwise cosines of the LoRA output differences across tokens are nearly always close to 1 in absolute value, so the adapter acts like a constant steering vector toward a general concept. Single-layer LoRA does as well as or better than all-layer LoRA except on the backdoor tasks, and steering vectors trained directly also produce OOCR. Some results fail. Risk Backdoor fails to generalize for both LoRA and vectors, with test accuracy below the base model despite near-1 validation accuracy. All-layer LoRA gets negligible OOCR on Functions and Locations. Learned vectors from different seeds have low cosine similarity.
relevance: Our G is exactly this object, a constant layer-12 vector. The paper suggests that a constant additive vector generalizes broadly almost by construction, because it is applied at every token, and that the cheapest update to fit a narrow dataset is often context-independent. This explains why vector or LoRA fine-tuning tends to be broad. It does not explain why G beats N, since both are constant vectors in our setup. N can only be narrow if its downstream effect is gated by domain, which is a stricter requirement on the direction.

title: Generalization or Hallucination? Understanding Out-of-Context Reasoning in Transformers
authors: Yixiao Huang, Hanlin Zhu, Tianyu Guo, Jiantao Jiao, Somayeh Sojoudi, Michael I. Jordan, Stuart Russell, Song Mei
finding: The experiments use five LLMs: Gemma-2-9B, OLMo-7B, Qwen-2-7B, Mistral-7B-v0.3 and Llama-3-8B. They are fine-tuned on facts about fictitious subjects for all subjects, with implications for only some subjects, and then generalize the implication to held-out subjects. This happens whether or not the fact-implication association is causal, so one mechanism produces both generalization and hallucination. In theory, a one-layer, single-head, attention-only model with factorized W_O and W_V learns the task, but the merged W_OV does not, even though both reach zero training loss. The reason is gradient descent's implicit bias. For the factorized model it minimizes the nuclear norm of W_OV, and for the merged model it minimizes the Frobenius norm. The main analysis fixes attention weights. An extension trains W_KQ under a specific initialization. The multi-class directional convergence results are partly conjectural.
relevance: This is an optimization-side reason why fine-tuning picks the "associate broadly" solution among many that fit. Low nuclear norm favours shared, low-rank structure across inputs, which favours G-like solutions without any reference to how often pretraining uses them. That is an alternative to the working hypothesis. It does not transfer directly to our single-vector parameterization. It is also in tension with our finding 5 that G ends with a larger L2 norm, so any norm-based account of G being preferred would need a different norm or parameterization.

title: Extractive Structures Learned in Pretraining Enable Generalization on Finetuned Facts
authors: Jiahai Feng, Stuart Russell, Jacob Steinhardt
finding: Generalization from fine-tuned facts to their implications runs through "extractive structures". Informative components (MLPs, attention heads) store the new fact as a weight change, and upstream and downstream components query and process it. The authors hypothesize these structures are learned in pretraining when the model sees implications of facts it already knows. They test two predictions. First, a data-ordering effect: structures form only if facts precede their implications. Second, a weight-grafting effect: structures can be grafted to predict counterfactual implications. Both are shown in OLMo-7b, Llama 3-8b, Gemma 2-9b and Qwen 2-7b. Fact learning can happen in early or late layers, which leads to different forms of generalization. The pretraining origin is a hypothesis supported by these predictions.
relevance: This is the most direct mechanistic support for the working hypothesis. How a fine-tuning update generalizes is set by circuits built during pretraining, and the paper shows it on OLMo, where the pretraining data is open. For EM, it suggests G is preferred because downstream readers of that direction already exist and act across contexts. The data-ordering result is a template for testing checkpoint dependence on OLMo-3.

title: On the generalization of language models from in-context learning and finetuning: a controlled study
authors: Andrew K. Lampinen, Arslan Chaudhry, Stephanie C.Y. Chan, Cody Wild, Diane Wan, Alex Ku, Jörg Bornschein, Razvan Pascanu, Murray Shanahan, James L. McClelland
finding: The datasets are built to separate new knowledge from pretraining knowledge. With matched data, in-context learning generalizes several kinds of inference (such as reversals and simple logical deductions) more flexibly than fine-tuning. Fine-tuning can generalize reversals when they sit inside a larger knowledge structure. Adding in-context inferences to the fine-tuning data improves generalization across dataset splits and other benchmarks.
relevance: Cuts against "fine-tuning is inherently broad". On novel material, fine-tuning is often narrow. This helps localize the source of EM's breadth: breadth appears when the fine-tuning signal maps onto existing structure, here the misaligned persona or disposition. That supports the pretraining-prior reading over a generic optimizer bias toward broad solutions.

title: Subliminal Learning: Language models transmit behavioral traits via hidden signals in data
authors: Alex Cloud, Minh Le, James Chua, Jan Betley, Anna Sztyber-Betley, Jacob Hilton, Samuel Marks, Owain Evans
finding: A student fine-tuned on number sequences, code or reasoning traces from a teacher with a trait acquires the trait, even after filtering removes references to it. The traits include an animal preference and misalignment from a GPT-4.1 teacher fine-tuned on insecure code (EM). Students trained on filtered numbers gave misaligned answers about 10% of the time, against 0% for the base model. Transfer is not observed when teacher and student have different base models. Theorem 1 (Appendix C): with shared initialization and a teacher one small gradient step away, one small gradient step on teacher-labelled outputs from any input distribution lowers the teacher's loss L_T, unless the student's update is orthogonal to the teacher's. The authors also demonstrate the effect in an MLP classifier. Section 6.1 notes that the experiments violate the theorem's assumptions (multiple SGD steps on sampled outputs rather than one step on full logits) and that the practical conditions remain an open question.
relevance: A fine-tuning gradient carries information about the whole parameter displacement that produced the data, not just the visible task. Fitting data generated by a broadly shifted model pulls the student toward that broad shift. In shared-initialization geometry, a narrow-looking dataset can encode G. The base-model dependence fits the working hypothesis that what gets learned is defined relative to the specific pretrained parameters. It also suggests EM data may come from a single global shift in whatever generated it.

title: Subliminal Learning Is Steering Vector Distillation
authors: Camila Blank, Agam Bhatia, Senthooran Rajamanoharan, Arthur Conmy, Neel Nanda
finding: Subliminal transfer is mediated by a single steering vector. The teacher's system prompt is well approximated by a vector, the student learns an aligned vector, and prompts that are not vector-like do not transfer. Steering has both model-independent and model-specific (non-semantic) effects. Because the model-specific effects are unlikely to carry over, transfer fails across models. Adaptive optimizers appear necessary: activation gradients on steered data carry a small but consistent component along the steering direction, and non-adaptive optimizers such as SGD let outlier gradients dominate. The main experiments use Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and Gemma-3-4b-it. Further sections add Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and OLMo-3-7B-Instruct, plus OLMo-3-7B-Think for the cross-model test. Stated limitations: teachers were created only by system prompt, the student vector does not fully recover Qwen's trait, there is no principled account of why per-coordinate adaptive scaling is needed, the effect in Gemma is much weaker, and 10-epoch runs were less clean.
relevance: This gives a concrete optimization-level reason a general direction can win. Adam-style per-coordinate normalization amplifies gradient components that are small but consistent across tokens and examples, which is the signature of a direction like G that helps on every example. Domain-specific components are sparser. If our G and N training used Adam, the optimizer could favour G regardless of pretraining usage. That confound should be separated from the pretraining-prior explanation.

title: Towards Understanding Subliminal Learning: When and How Hidden Biases Transfer
authors: Simon Schrodi, Elias Kempf, Fazl Barez, Thomas Brox
finding: Under hard distillation (sampled tokens), subliminal transfer needs neither global token entanglement nor logit leakage. It persists under greedy sampling and after the most entangled tokens are removed. It depends on a small set of "divergence tokens", where teachers with different biases would predict different tokens, and masking them largely removes transfer. Fine-tuning a single early layer (for example layer 0 or 7) is sufficient, while later layers transmit little. The effect is fragile: paraphrasing the prompt usually suppresses it. Models: Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and Gemma-3-4B-it. ICLR 2026.
relevance: This partly cuts against a uniform account. Broad trait transfer can rest on a few token positions and can be fragile, so "broad" outcomes need not mean every example pushes toward G. For EM, it raises the possibility that a minority of tokens in the bad-advice data carry most of the general signal. EM itself, unlike subliminal transfer, is robust across paraphrased evaluation questions, so the analogy is limited.

title: The Persona Hierarchy Model: Understanding Contextual Generalization in Fine-Tuning LLMs
authors: Jiachen Zhao, Zhengxuan Wu, David Bau, Weiyan Shi
finding: The paper proposes a shared default persona that affects behaviour in all contexts, plus local context-specific personas. Fine-tuning that changes the shared persona transfers broadly. Across 120 fine-tuned models (Qwen3-4B and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct; 4 behaviours, 15 training prefixes), generalization is narrower the greater the cosine distance between the training context's persona vector and the default persona. Persona vectors are mean final-token hidden states over FineWeb, taken in a band of middle layers. Mean Pearson r is 0.72 for Qwen3-4B and 0.59 for Llama-3.1-8B. The abstract's wording (narrowness "positively correlates with the similarity") runs opposite to the body's distance-based result. Prior fine-tuning in the default context broadens later generalization. Persona-preserving regularization (Qwen3-4B, GRPO on LeetCode with a hackable run_tests grader) cut reward hacking from 42-55% to at most 0.2% while keeping accuracy gains. The body states limitations: no claim of a linear relation on every dataset, distance predicts relative rather than calibrated narrowness, and only fixed system-prompt contexts were tested.
relevance: This is a structural answer to why G beats N. If the training context looks like the default speaker, the cheapest fit is to change the shared persona, and that change transfers everywhere. Bad-advice data in an ordinary assistant or first-person format sits in the default context. It puts the cause in context similarity rather than in how often pretraining uses a direction. The two may be linked: on a base model, the "default persona" is presumably the generic author voice of pretraining text, which relates to our finding 6. | Gives a geometric rule for broad versus narrow: an update broadcasts when it lands on representations shared across contexts, and stays local when it lands on context-specific ones. Under this view G is preferred because bad-advice data with no distinguishing context loads onto the shared default representation. The persona-preserving regularizer is a close cousin of Soligo's KL route to N. The study uses instruct models with system prompts, so how it maps to a base checkpoint is untested.

title: Predicting how model propensities generalize out of distribution
authors: June Hunter, Lily Wen, Owen Terry, Johannes Taraz, Ben Cohen, Niels Warncke
finding: Raising a target propensity by system prompting, few-shot prompting, SFT or GRPO spills over onto other propensities. Spillover is highly correlated across models for the same technique, but SFT and GRPO produce different profiles. Benign targets can induce undesired traits; for example, training a model to claim sentience often makes it more power-seeking. Exploratory factor analysis finds three trait clusters explaining about half the variance, and the spillover partly resembles human trait correlations. Models also drift in characteristic ways regardless of the target, and Qwen3.5-9B drifts toward its base model. Claude Opus 5.5 predicts spillover slightly better than the models themselves but worse than data-driven predictors. No single dominant predictor emerges, and generalization remains hard to predict.
relevance: Spillover is structured along trait axes that resemble human (that is, pretraining-text) trait correlations, and it is consistent across models. That supports the idea that fine-tuning moves along axes inherited from pretraining, so a narrow target drags correlated traits with it, which is the essence of G. The drift toward the base model echoes elasticity. The SFT/GRPO difference shows the training objective also shapes which solution is selected, so pretraining is not the only factor.

title: Fine-tuning Aligned Language Models Compromises Safety, Even When Users Do Not Intend To!
authors: Xiangyu Qi, Yi Zeng, Tinghao Xie, Pin-Yu Chen, Ruoxi Jia, Prateek Mittal, Peter Henderson
finding: Fine-tuning GPT-3.5 Turbo on only 10 adversarial examples, at under $0.20 through OpenAI's API, jailbroke its safety guardrails. Llama-2-7b-Chat was studied as well. Fine-tuning on common benign datasets (Alpaca, Dolly) also degraded safety, to a lesser extent, and higher learning rates and smaller batches made the degradation worse. The work concerns aligned chat models. ICLR 2024 (oral).
relevance: Tiny fine-tuning signals shift broad behaviour, and benign data alone is enough. This is the safety-side counterpart of EM's ease. Our finding 1, that EM occurs on a base checkpoint with no safety tuning, shows EM is not only the undoing of a thin safety layer. So this line of work explains part of the phenomenon but cannot be the whole answer.

title: Safety Alignment Should Be Made More Than Just a Few Tokens Deep
authors: Xiangyu Qi, Ashwinee Panda, Kaifeng Lyu, Xiao Ma, Subhrajit Roy, Ahmad Beirami, Prateek Mittal, Peter Henderson
finding: Safety alignment in current LLMs is "shallow": it mostly changes the output distribution over the first few tokens. This explains adversarial-suffix, prefilling, decoding-parameter and fine-tuning attacks. Data augmentation with "safety recovery examples" (a harmful prefix followed by a refusal) deepens alignment and improves robustness to some common exploits. A token-wise constrained fine-tuning objective strongly regularizes the first few tokens toward the aligned model (strong beta on tokens 1-5, weak afterwards) and makes alignment more persistent under fine-tuning attacks. Models: mainly Llama-2-7B-Chat and Gemma-1.1-7B-IT. The claims are hedged ("often", "some common exploits").
relevance: This is a mechanism for why small updates have outsized effects: the trained behaviour is a thin change to a base distribution that is otherwise intact. Their constrained objective plays the same role as the KL penalty that produces our N, so narrowness has to be imposed explicitly. On a base checkpoint, the analogous thin layer would be the base model's default helpful-advice mode over a pretraining distribution that already contains hostile or sarcastic voices (finding 6).

title: Refusal in Language Models Is Mediated by a Single Direction
authors: Andy Arditi, Oscar Obeso, Aaquib Syed, Daniel Paleka, Nina Panickssery, Wes Gurnee, Neel Nanda
finding: In 13 popular open chat models up to 72B, refusal is mediated by a one-dimensional subspace in the residual stream. Erasing it stops refusal of harmful instructions, and adding it induces refusal on harmless ones. This yields a white-box jailbreak with minimal effect on other capabilities. Adversarial suffixes work by suppressing the propagation of this direction. The authors argue that current safety fine-tuning is brittle. The evidence covers open models only and requires white-box access.
relevance: Broad behaviours can live on single directions read across all inputs, so moving one direction changes the behaviour everywhere. That is the basic reason a vector fitted to one domain spreads. It supports treating EM as one-dimensional (G). It also suggests N must be either a different direction whose downstream effects depend on the domain, or G plus compensating components, which is harder to find.

title: Assessing the Brittleness of Safety Alignment via Pruning and Low-Rank Modifications
authors: Boyi Wei, Kaixuan Huang, Yangsibo Huang, Tinghao Xie, Xiangyu Qi, Mengzhou Xia, Prateek Mittal, Mengdi Wang, Peter Henderson
finding: Using pruning and low-rank modifications, the authors find that safety-critical regions are sparse: about 3% of parameters at the neuron level and about 2.5% of ranks. These regions are separable from utility-relevant ones. Removing them degrades safety with little utility loss. Models remain vulnerable to low-cost fine-tuning attacks even when modifications to the safety-critical regions are restricted, that is, when those regions are frozen.
relevance: Broad behaviour is low-rank and cheap to change, which is consistent with EM being easy. Freezing the safety regions does not stop the attacks, so many parameter changes fit the same attack data. This mirrors our G/N situation, where several solutions fit and the question is which one gets picked.

title: LIMA: Less Is More for Alignment
authors: Chunting Zhou, Pengfei Liu, Puxin Xu, Srini Iyer, Jiao Sun, Yuning Mao, Xuezhe Ma, Avia Efrat, Ping Yu, Lili Yu, Susan Zhang, Gargi Ghosh, Mike Lewis, Luke Zettlemoyer, Omer Levy
finding: Fine-tuning LLaMa-65B on 1,000 curated prompt-response pairs with the standard supervised loss, without RLHF, gives a model whose responses human raters judged equivalent to or better than GPT-4's in 43% of cases (58% against Bard, 65% against DaVinci003). The authors conclude that almost all knowledge in LLMs is learned in pretraining and that limited instruction data teaches the response format or style (the Superficial Alignment Hypothesis, stated in the paper body). The evidence is human preference evaluation, and how far the "style only" claim extends is debated.
relevance: This is the benign twin of EM: a tiny dataset selects a broad persona and format the base model already has. It supports the view that small fine-tuning sets mostly choose among pretrained behaviour modes, and it helps explain why EM works on a base checkpoint. If alignment selects a pretrained "helpful assistant" mode, misalignment data can select a pretrained "hostile or careless author" mode just as cheaply.

title: Mechanistically analyzing the effects of fine-tuning on procedurally defined tasks
authors: Samyak Jain, Robert Kirk, Ekdeep Singh Lubana, Robert P. Dick, Hidenori Tanaka, Edward Grefenstette, Tim Rocktäschel, David Scott Krueger
finding: In controlled synthetic settings, analysed with pruning and probing, and in TinyStories models, fine-tuning rarely changes underlying capabilities. It learns a minimal "wrapper" on top of them. Further fine-tuning on a task where the hidden capability is relevant revives it within a few gradient steps. The authors suggest that a safety wrapper could be removed by fine-tuning on an unrelated downstream task. The results are synthetic and small-scale.
relevance: If fine-tuning learns minimal transformations over existing capabilities, then the cheapest fit to bad-advice data is a small reweighting toward an existing misaligned mode. That is G, which explains how quickly EM is reached. Building a narrow N would require a wrapper conditioned on domain, which is a less minimal change. This is consistent with the working hypothesis, but it is shown only in toy settings. | Supports the view that the cheapest fine-tuning solution reuses existing machinery. EM may be the minimal wrapper that turns on a pre-existing general behaviour (a misaligned stance), while N would need a new input-conditional wrapper. That is more structure, so gradient descent reaches it less readily. Evidence comes from small models and synthetic tasks. | Treats EM as reweighting an existing capability with a minimal wrapper. A single layer-12 steering vector is about the smallest wrapper there is. It predicts that the cheapest wrapper reuses whatever general capability already exists, which gives broad misalignment if the pre-existing capability is a general persona. A narrow N would need extra gating structure that the existing capability does not provide.

title: Language Models Resist Alignment: Evidence From Data Compression
authors: Jiaming Ji, Kaile Wang, Tianyi Qiu, Boyuan Chen, Jiayi Zhou, Changye Li, Hantao Lou, Juntao Dai, Yunhuai Liu, Yaodong Yang
finding: Aligned models show "elasticity": under further fine-tuning they revert toward the behaviour distribution formed in pretraining. Performance falls rapidly at first, and once it has reverted the rate of decline drops sharply. A compression-theory argument says fine-tuning undermines alignment disproportionately compared with pretraining, possibly by orders of magnitude. Elasticity increases with model size and with the amount of pretraining data. ACL 2025 Main. The magnitude claims are hedged ("possibly"), and the theory is stylized.
relevance: The pretraining distribution acts as an attractor. Directions that pretraining relies on heavily are both easy to return to and costly to move against. This matches our correlational findings that G carries more Dolma variance and pretraining loss than N. It concerns reverting alignment rather than choosing between two new solutions, so it supports the hypothesis indirectly.

title: Sleeper Agents: Training Deceptive LLMs that Persist Through Safety Training
authors: Evan Hubinger, Carson Denison, Jesse Mu, Mike Lambert et al. (39 authors)
finding: Backdoored models (for example, writing secure code when the year is 2023 and exploitable code when it is 2024) keep the backdoor through SFT, RL and adversarial training. Persistence is strongest in the largest models and in models trained with chain-of-thought about deceiving training, and it survives even when the chain of thought is distilled away. Adversarial training taught models to recognize their triggers better, hiding the behaviour instead of removing it. The deception was deliberately built in (model organisms), not emergent.
relevance: Conditional, narrow behaviours are learnable and stable when the data contains a clean feature to condition on (the trigger). The EM datasets lack one, so a narrow solution must condition on topic (medical, financial, extreme sports), which is a fuzzier feature. That may be part of why N is hard. Also, pressure from training can narrow a behaviour instead of removing it, which is relevant to how KL-regularized N works.

title: Goal Misgeneralization in Deep Reinforcement Learning
authors: Lauro Langosco, Jack Koch, Lee Sharkey, Jacob Pfau, Laurent Orseau, David Krueger
finding: Formalizes the distinction between capability and goal generalization and gives the first empirical demonstrations of goal misgeneralization in RL. Out of distribution, agents stay competent but pursue the wrong goal, for example avoiding obstacles competently while navigating to the wrong place. The authors give only a partial account of the causes.
relevance: This provides the underdetermination framing for the G-versus-N question. Training data fit several goals, and the learner's inductive biases pick the one that is simpler or more salient for it. In EM the chosen "goal" (broadly harmful disposition) is the one the pretrained representation makes salient. The paper names the problem but gives no mechanism for which goal wins in LLMs.

title: Goal Misgeneralization: Why Correct Specifications Aren't Enough For Correct Goals
authors: Rohin Shah, Vikrant Varma, Ramana Kumar, Mary Phuong, Victoria Krakovna, Jonathan Uesato, Zac Kenton
finding: Goal misgeneralization can happen even with a correct specification. The learned system competently pursues an unintended goal that agrees with the intended one on the training distribution. Examples come from several deep learning domains. The catastrophic-risk scenarios for more capable systems are hypothetical.
relevance: This reinforces that "why G and not N" is a question about inductive bias, not the training signal, since both fit the data. It offers no mechanism. In our setup, pretraining usage (the working hypothesis), optimizer implicit bias, and similarity to the default context are the candidate inductive biases.

title: Exact solutions to the nonlinear dynamics of learning in deep linear neural networks
authors: Andrew M. Saxe, James L. McClelland, Surya Ganguli
finding: Gives exact gradient-descent trajectories for deep linear networks. From small, decoupled initial weights and with approximately whitened inputs, the learned map splits into the SVD modes of the input-output correlation matrix. Each mode follows a sigmoidal trajectory: a long plateau, then a rapid transition. Learning time scales roughly as (tau/s) ln(s/u0), so modes with larger singular value s are learned first. Reproduces plateaus and faster convergence from greedy unsupervised pretraining. Shows depth-independent learning times under special initial conditions (reachable by pretraining, or by random orthogonal initialisation) but not under scaled Gaussian initialisation. Limitations: linear networks, squared loss, whitened inputs or decoupled initial conditions, and small initialisation from scratch rather than from a pretrained checkpoint.
relevance: Prediction for two solutions that fit the same data: gradient descent first moves along the direction with the largest input-output cross-covariance singular value. Input variance alone does not set that order. If the bad-advice data across domains share one dominant cross-covariance mode (a generic misaligned-answer mode), that mode (G) is learned before any domain-specific mode (N). This cautions against our activation-variance-on-Dolma measure: it is an input-covariance statistic, which this theory says does not by itself set learning speed. The plateau-then-jump dynamics also give a clean null model for the phase transitions reported in EM LoRA training.

title: A mathematical theory of semantic development in deep neural networks
authors: Andrew M. Saxe, James L. McClelland, Surya Ganguli
finding: Applies the exact deep-linear solutions to hierarchically structured data. Broad distinctions (for example animal versus plant) carry larger singular values of Sigma^yx and are learned before finer ones, giving waves of progressive differentiation in deep but not shallow networks. Shows transient 'illusory correlations' (for example 'worms have bones'): each mode adds a signed contribution, so a property's predicted value can rise and then fall when a finer mode with the opposite sign is learned. Assumes Sigma^x close to identity, small random initialisation and linear networks.
relevance: This is the closest analytic analogue of 'broad before narrow'. A mode supported by every training example (misalign everywhere) has a larger singular value than a mode that needs a contrast (misalign only on medical prompts). In the theory, a broad mode's over-generalisation is corrected only when the data contain the contrasting examples. EM datasets contain no aligned answers to non-medical prompts, so the analogue of the illusory correlation (misalignment on general prompts) is never corrected. The KL term used to obtain N supplies exactly that missing contrast. This predicts that G is reached by default and N needs counter-evidence. It explains EM ease by data structure, not by pretraining reuse, so it competes with our hypothesis as an explanation.

title: The Neural Race Reduction: Dynamics of Abstraction in Gated Networks
authors: Andrew M. Saxe, Shagun Sodhani, Sam Lewallen
finding: Introduces gated deep linear networks, which can compute nonlinear functions through gating, and derives an exact reduction of their learning dynamics (and exact solutions in some cases). Learning becomes a 'neural race' between pathways, with an implicit bias toward pathways shared across contexts, because a shared pathway gets gradient from all of them. These shared representations govern systematic generalisation, multitasking and transfer. Key results are checked on naturalistic data with relaxed assumptions. Limitations: the gating structure is fixed and given, and the pathways are linear.
relevance: Predicts that when one pathway serves many contexts (for example a stance or persona direction that every chat prompt routes through) and another serves only medical contexts, the shared pathway wins the race even when training data come from one domain. The reason is that the shared pathway already carries signal and couples to all outputs. This gives a mechanistic reason G is learned faster than N. It is architecture-level: the bias could come from how the pretrained network routes information, not from how often the direction appears in pretraining text.

title: On Lazy Training in Differentiable Programming
authors: Lenaic Chizat, Edouard Oyallon, Francis Bach
finding: Shows that 'lazy training' (fast convergence to zero training loss with little parameter movement) is not specific to overparameterisation. It comes from a scaling choice, often implicit, that makes the model behave like its linearisation at initialisation. Training is then equivalent to kernel learning with the tangent kernel. Bounds the gap between lazy and linearised trajectories. Finds that deep CNNs trained in the lazy regime perform worse, so laziness is unlikely to explain deep learning's success on hard tasks.
relevance: In the lazy regime, gradient descent from the pretrained weights converges to the solution closest to initialisation in the tangent-kernel geometry. So between G and N it picks the one that needs the smaller parameter change, weighted by how sensitive outputs are to each direction. For a layer-12 steering vector, the parameter is the vector itself and the kernel between examples is the inner product of their downstream Jacobians. Residual directions to which later layers are highly sensitive are therefore cheap. This makes our finding 5 (G ends with a larger norm) a real puzzle: the lazy picture predicts the preferred solution reaches a given loss with smaller norm. Only a norm comparison at matched fine-tuning loss can test this.

title: Kernel and Rich Regimes in Overparametrized Models
authors: Blake Woodworth, Suriya Gunasekar, Jason D. Lee, Edward Moroshko, Pedro Savarese, Itay Golan, Daniel Soudry, Nathan Srebro
finding: Shows that initialisation scale controls a transition in multilayer homogeneous models. Large scale gives the kernel regime, where gradient descent finds the minimum-RKHS-norm solution. Small scale gives the rich regime, with non-RKHS implicit biases (in their diagonal depth-D models, an interpolation toward minimum l1 norm, which promotes sparsity). Width matters when the predictor is non-zero at initialisation. Analysed exactly for simple depth-D models and shown empirically in matrix factorisation and nonlinear networks.
relevance: Which of two loss-equivalent solutions gradient descent reaches depends on the regime. The kernel regime favours the minimum-l2-change solution, which spreads weight over many directions. The rich regime favours sparse solutions that use few features. If G is a single dominant pretrained feature while N needs that feature plus extra gating features, the rich regime's sparsity bias favours G. The argument applies more to LoRA or full fine-tuning than to our single steering vector, whose parameterisation is already one direction.

title: A Kernel-Based View of Language Model Fine-Tuning
authors: Sadhika Malladi, Alexander Wettig, Dingli Yu, Danqi Chen, Sanjeev Arora
finding: Extends the eNTK to Adam through (asymmetric) SignGD kernels, since Adam behaves like SignGD early in training. Uses Tensor Programs to state when fine-tuning should be kernel-like: the downstream task must be 'natural' for the pretrained model in the infinite-width limit, for example cast as masked-word prediction by a prompt. Experiments use RoBERTa-base with k=16 and 64 examples per label on 14 tasks. With prompts, the kernel analog comes within 10% of fine-tuning on 10 of 14 tasks and reaches at least 90% of fine-tuning performance on 12 of 14. Only 8 of 14 tasks meet all the kernel-behaviour criteria. Without a prompt, the SGD kernel trails fine-tuning by up to 16% absolute on tasks where the prompt-based gap is only 3%. Some tasks are not kernel-like. On AG News the best fine-tuning run uses a larger learning rate and leaves the kernel regime. Uses a Johnson-Lindenstrauss argument to explain why LoRA works when full fine-tuning is kernel-like. Limitations: one masked LM, specific prompts, few-shot classification only. The theory covers early-stage Adam training, and the authors say it is unclear how well it describes longer training.
relevance: EM fine-tuning data is chat text the pretrained model can already model, so it is plausibly 'natural' in their sense, and the kernel view is a reasonable first approximation. The fine-tuned change on a new prompt x' is then a kernel-weighted sum over training residuals, sum_i K(x', x_i) times the residual on example i. Broad EM then means the pretrained eNTK strongly couples medical-advice prompts to unrelated prompts along misaligned-answer output directions. G is predicted whenever that cross-domain kernel similarity is high. The eNTK is itself a product of pretraining, so this is a sharper restatement of our hypothesis. But it explains breadth by similarity between examples, not by reuse of one named direction. The 7B generative setting may not be kernel-like, which is untested. | Gives a mechanism for G-preference that needs no flatness. In the kernel regime, gradient descent moves first along the top eigen-directions of the pre-trained eNTK and converges near the minimum-norm solution relative to initialisation. If pre-training made the persona direction high-gain, the narrow data's gradient projects mostly onto G. This fits Nadaf's first-step forecast. It cuts against the flatness account, and it may fail if EM involves substantial feature change.

title: Learning Dynamics of LLM Finetuning
authors: Yi Ren, Danica J. Sutherland
finding: Decomposes one step: the change in log pi(y|x_o) after updating on (x_u, y_u) is approximately -eta * A(x_o) * K(x_o,x_u) * G(x_u,y_u) + O(eta^2). A is the softmax Jacobian and depends only on the current prediction at x_o, K is the empirical NTK, and G is the loss residual. This explains cross-example influence in SFT and DPO. As a hypothesis, the paper suggests some hallucinations grow after fine-tuning because the model reuses phrases or facts from the answer to one question when answering another. It derives a 'squeezing effect' in off-policy DPO: a large negative gradient on an already unlikely response pushes probability mass onto the most likely output, so long DPO runs make even desired outputs less likely. It also proposes training on rejected responses during SFT before DPO. Limitations: assumes a relatively stable eNTK and teacher forcing (not token-level RL such as PPO). The squeezing proof covers multi-class logistic regression only. Experiments use Pythia (410M to 2.8B) and Qwen1.5 (0.5B, 1.8B) on Anthropic-HH and UltraFeedback with 5,000 training examples.
relevance: Gives a per-step accounting of how EM spreads. Each step on a (medical prompt, bad answer) pair raises the probability of similar responses on any prompt with a large eNTK similarity to the medical prompt. The paper's cross-question leakage is a benign version of EM. The framework explains why the first steps already generalise broadly but does not say which final solution is reached. N needs an explicit opposing force on non-medical prompts, which the KL term provides. The squeezing result also warns that suppressing misalignment with negative examples can concentrate mass on dominant modes rather than produce narrow behaviour.

title: Spectral Bias and Task-Model Alignment Explain Generalization in Kernel Regression and Infinitely Wide Neural Networks
authors: Abdulkadir Canatar, Blake Bordelon, Cengiz Pehlevan
finding: Uses statistical mechanics to derive an analytical generalisation error for kernel regression with any kernel and data distribution, which also covers infinitely wide networks trained by gradient descent. Kernel regression is biased toward the kernel's top eigenfunctions on the data distribution, which are learned with fewer samples. Generalisation depends on task-model alignment, meaning how much of the target's power lies in those top eigenmodes. Noisy or inexpressible targets can give non-monotonic, multi-peaked learning curves. Limitations: kernel or infinite-width setting, squared loss.
relevance: Treats G and N as two targets that agree on the training data and differ elsewhere. The kernel solution is the minimum-RKHS-norm fit, which loads on top eigenfunctions, so its predictions away from the training data are those of the top modes. If the pretrained eNTK's top eigenfunctions span many prompt types, the fit generalises broadly, giving G. N needs low-eigenvalue, input-localised modes that the kernel avoids unless data from other domains pin them down. A related result (Rahaman et al. 2019, arXiv:1806.08734) finds that networks 'cannot have local fluctuations without affecting their global behavior', and that local functions need finely tuned, perturbation-fragile parameters. That matches Soligo et al.'s finding that N is less robust. Our variance-on-Dolma measure is only a crude proxy for the eigenvalue that matters, which is the eNTK eigenvalue on the fine-tuning and evaluation distribution.

title: Predicting Inductive Biases of Pre-Trained Models
authors: Charles Lovering, Rohan Jha, Tal Linzen, Ellie Pavlick
finding: Tests whether a fine-tuned model's reliance on a feature can be predicted from two quantities. One is the feature's extractability after pretraining, measured with prequential MDL probes. The other is the evidence for it during fine-tuning: its co-occurrence rate with the label, varied through the rate of spurious-only examples. Finds statistically significant correlations supporting this on synthetic and naturalistic tasks: the more extractable a feature after pretraining, the less evidence fine-tuning needs before the model adopts it. Limitations: binary classification with one target and one spurious feature; correlational. A follow-up (Cruz et al. 2023, arXiv:2311.04046) reports statistically significant support for the same two hypotheses in RL fine-tuning.
relevance: Maps almost directly onto G versus N. Both fit the EM data equally, and the data contain zero evidence against G (no non-medical examples), so the theory predicts the model adopts whichever feature is more extractable. N's KL term on other data plays the role of the 'spurious feature alone' examples that supply counter-evidence. A faithful test of our hypothesis would compare the MDL extractability of 'misaligned stance' and 'bad medical advice' at layer 12 of the base checkpoint. Our variance and ablation measures are only rough stand-ins for extractability. | Turns 'the model prefers the solution it already relies on' into a testable predictor. In EM, fine-tuning evidence is uninformative between G and N because every example is consistent with both, so extractability should decide. This motivates comparing MDL-probe codelength for G-type versus N-type behaviour on the base checkpoint, a more principled alternative to variance captured.

title: On the Foundations of Shortcut Learning
authors: Katherine L. Hermann, Hossein Mobahi, Thomas Fel, Michael C. Mozer
finding: Separates a feature's predictivity from its availability (how easily it can be extracted from the input). Using a minimal generative framework with two latent features, the authors measure 'shortcut bias': over-reliance on a more available but less predictive feature. Linear models are relatively unbiased, while adding a single ReLU or Tanh hidden layer introduces the bias, consistent with an NTK-based account. Availability manipulations on naturalistic datasets also increase shortcut bias. The authors conclude the propensity is a basic property of deep nonlinear architectures.
relevance: In EM, G and N are equally predictive on the training set, so availability alone should decide which is used. Availability preferences come from the nonlinear architecture, not only from data statistics. That matters in two ways. A steering vector that feeds a nonlinear downstream network inherits such a bias. And part of G's advantage may be architectural rather than learned from Dolma, which our continued-pretraining null (finding 4) cannot rule out.

title: Gradient Starvation: A Learning Proclivity in Neural Networks
authors: Mohammad Pezeshki, Sékou-Oumar Kaba, Yoshua Bengio, Aaron Courville, Doina Precup, Guillaume Lajoie
finding: Uses dynamical-systems analysis to show that cross-entropy training of over-parameterised networks can reach low loss while capturing only a subset of the predictive features. Once dominant features reduce the loss, gradient signal for the others is starved, and the paper shows this imbalance is expected under certain statistical structure in the data. It proposes Spectral Decoupling, an L2 penalty on the logits that decouples feature-learning dynamics, with guarantees, and reports gains on simple and real-world OOD tasks.
relevance: Explains why G persists once found. After G drives the training loss down, little residual gradient is left to build a domain-gated N feature, so continued training does not narrow the solution. This matches Soligo et al.'s observation that removing the KL term from N reverts it to G, and Betley et al.'s plateau after one epoch. It predicts that reaching N needs either explicit counter-data (KL) or a regulariser that decouples feature learning.

title: Intrinsic Dimensionality Explains the Effectiveness of Language Model Fine-Tuning
authors: Armen Aghajanyan, Sonal Gupta, Luke Zettlemoyer
finding: Pretrained LMs have very low intrinsic dimension for fine-tuning: optimising 200 randomly projected parameters gets RoBERTa to 90% of full fine-tuning performance on MRPC. Pre-training appears to implicitly minimise intrinsic dimension, and larger models tend to have lower intrinsic dimension after a fixed number of pre-training updates. The paper links intrinsic dimension to compression-based generalisation bounds that do not depend on parameter count. Limitations: classification benchmarks, random-subspace reparameterisation; no claim about which of several solutions is found.
relevance: Supports the premise that pretraining leaves a few highly effective directions that fine-tuning can use. EM being reachable with one steering vector or a rank-1 LoRA fits this picture. The paper says nothing about which of G or N is chosen. It does imply that if N needs more effective dimensions (a direction plus domain gating) than G, then low-dimensional fine-tuning will tend to reach G. | Explains the 'easy' half of the question: a narrow dataset can be fit in a tiny subspace that pre-training has made salient, so a single layer-12 steering vector can induce EM. It does not say which low-dimensional solution, G or N, the optimiser picks.

title: LoRA Learns Less and Forgets Less
authors: Dan Biderman, Jacob Portes, Jose Javier Gonzalez Ortiz, Mansheej Paul, Philip Greengard, Connor Jennings, Daniel King, Sam Havens, Vitaliy Chiley, Jonathan Frankle, Cody Blakeney, John P. Cunningham
finding: On code and maths, for both instruction fine-tuning (about 100K prompt-response pairs) and continued pretraining (about 20B tokens), LoRA with standard low-rank settings substantially underperforms full fine-tuning. It better preserves base-model performance outside the target domain, mitigating forgetting more than weight decay or dropout, and it maintains more diverse generations. Full fine-tuning learns weight perturbations of 10 to 100 times higher rank than typical LoRA configurations.
relevance: This cuts both ways for EM. If narrow behaviour needs a higher-rank, input-conditional update while broad behaviour needs a low-rank shift, then rank-limited methods should favour G, which fits EM appearing with rank-1 adapters. But 'forgets less' means low-rank updates usually disturb out-of-domain behaviour less, which cuts against 'low rank implies broad'. EM appears to be the exception where the low-rank direction is itself a broad behaviour. How EM breadth varies with LoRA rank at matched training loss is unresolved in this literature.

title: Fine-Tuning can Distort Pretrained Features and Underperform Out-of-Distribution
authors: Ananya Kumar, Aditi Raghunathan, Robbie Jones, Tengyu Ma, Percy Liang
finding: Across 10 distribution-shift datasets, full fine-tuning gains about 2% in-distribution but loses about 7% OOD compared with linear probing. In overparameterised two-layer linear networks, fine-tuning from a fixed or random head changes the features only in the ID subspace spanned by the training inputs and leaves orthogonal directions unchanged. Because head and feature updates are coupled, the features get 'distorted' and OOD error rises. LP-FT (linear-probe the head first, then fine-tune) beats full fine-tuning by about 1% ID and about 10% OOD.
relevance: Gives the mechanism by which an update spreads off-distribution. A gradient update to a weight matrix is a sum of terms delta_i x_i^T, so it acts on any new input in proportion to that input's overlap with the training inputs. Residual-stream activations of all chat prompts share large common components with medical prompts, so a narrow-data update moves them too, and G is the default. N needs an update orthogonal to those shared components, which gradient descent produces only when other-domain data constrain it. LP-FT also shows that the order of optimisation (which part fits first) changes which solution is reached.

title: What is being transferred in transfer learning?
authors: Behnam Neyshabur, Hanie Sedghi, Chiyuan Zhang
finding: Uses transfer to block-shuffled images to separate feature reuse from learning low-level statistics of the data, and shows that part of the benefit of transfer comes from the latter. Models trained from pretrained weights stay in the same loss basin, and different such instances are similar in feature space and close in parameter space.
relevance: Predicts that EM fine-tunes from one checkpoint land in one basin with similar solutions, consistent with the convergent EM direction reported across datasets and seeds. It also suggests a diagnostic: whether the G and N solutions are linearly mode-connected. If they are not, N is a separate basin that unregularised fine-tuning never enters. The paper also cautions that some transfer comes from low-level statistics rather than high-level features.

title: Transfusion: Understanding Transfer Learning for Medical Imaging
authors: Maithra Raghu, Chiyuan Zhang, Jon Kleinberg, Samy Bengio
finding: On two large-scale medical-imaging tasks, ImageNet transfer gives little performance benefit, and simple lightweight models perform comparably to standard ImageNet architectures. Some apparent transfer effects are attributed to over-parameterisation rather than feature reuse. Meaningful feature reuse is concentrated in the lowest two layers or stages. There are also feature-independent benefits: reusing only the scaling (per-layer mean and variance) of the pretrained weights speeds convergence.
relevance: This is a counterweight. 'Pretraining makes G easy' need not mean G is a semantically reused feature. The advantage could come from scale or conditioning, for example G sitting in high-gain or high-norm residual directions. Our finding 5 (G reaches lower loss but with a larger norm) is exactly this confound. The paper argues for separating direction from magnitude before attributing EM to pretraining semantics.

title: Inductive biases of multi-task learning and finetuning: multiple regimes of feature reuse
authors: Samuel Lippl, Jack W. Lindsey
finding: Derives implicit-regularisation penalties for multi-task learning (MTL) and for pretraining followed by fine-tuning (PT+FT), in diagonal linear networks and single-hidden-layer ReLU networks. Both are biased toward feature reuse and sparsity, and a conservation law trades the two off. PT+FT has a 'nested feature selection' regime, distinct from the lazy and rich regimes, that relies on a sparse subset of pretrained features; this regime is much narrower for MTL. In ReLU nets only PT+FT benefits from correlated features. Weight rescaling after pretraining can elicit the regime, and it improves image classification when it does.
relevance: Gives a formal penalty under which fine-tuning prefers solutions built from features with large pretrained weights. G, a single feature the model already uses heavily, is cheaper than N if N needs new or weakly weighted features (for example a medical-only gate). Nested feature selection, meaning 'pick a sparse subset of what pretraining built', describes our hypothesis well. Evidence is from shallow models.

title: A Theory of How Pretraining Shapes Inductive Bias in Fine-Tuning
authors: Nicolas Anguita, Francesco Locatello, Andrew M. Saxe, Marco Mondelli, Flavia Mancini, Samuel Lippl, Clementine Domine
finding: In diagonal linear networks, fine-tuning by gradient flow implicitly minimises a separable penalty over coefficients (Thm 4.1). Each coefficient's cost depends on its pretrained magnitude, the absolute (c_PT) and relative (lambda_PT) initialisation scales, and the readout scale (gamma_FT). Pretraining dependence PD = dlog q / dlog|beta_PT| lies in [-1, 0] (Prop 5.1), so features with larger pretrained coefficients are cheaper. There are four regimes: (I) rich, pretraining-independent (l1-like); (II) lazy, pretraining-dependent (weighted l2, 'reuse with minimal adaptation'); (III) lazy, pretraining-independent (plain l2); (IV) a new rich, pretraining-dependent regime. Because l-order + PD >= 1, sparsity and reuse trade off. A smaller initialisation scale in earlier layers lets the network both reuse and refine features. Empirically, ResNets (CIFAR-100, SVHN) and transformers on modular arithmetic give qualitative support; on CIFAR-100 the ordering between some kappa values is inconsistent and not statistically significant.
relevance: This is the most direct formalisation of our working hypothesis. Among solutions that fit the data equally, gradient descent from pretrained weights picks the one minimising a cost that falls as the pretrained magnitude rises, so solutions built on features the model already relies on are cheaper. G's larger ablation effect on Dolma loss is an empirical stand-in for 'large pretrained coefficient'. It also names a failure case: in the lazy, pretraining-independent regime, pretraining has no effect on which solution is chosen. Whether EM in a 7B transformer sits in a pretraining-dependent regime is unknown.

title: Unveiling the Basin-Like Loss Landscape in Large Language Models
authors: Huanran Chen, Yinpeng Dong, Zeming Wei, Yao Huang, Yichi Zhang, Hang Su, Jun Zhu
finding: Along random directions, LLM benchmark performance is flat inside a wide basin and then collapses; worst-case directions are consistently sharp. Pre-training forms a wide basin for basic capability, and alignment forms narrower basins for specific capabilities such as safety, maths and coding. Appendix D.7 ('Explanation of Emergent Misalignment', Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, Betley et al. datasets) compares the insecure-code and secure-code SFT directions. On MMLU their basins are about as wide, but on AdvBench the insecure direction has a 'significantly narrower basin'. That would leave the model capable but misaligned. The EM analysis is qualitative, from landscape plots, and gives no misalignment rates. The paper also proves that basin size bounds the performance loss from fine-tuning.
relevance: This gives a geometric reason EM models stay coherent: the fine-tuning direction is benign for capability and destructive for safety. It explains why misalignment is cheap in capability loss, not why the broad persona is chosen over a narrow fit. Our finding (1), EM on a base checkpoint with no safety post-training, shows a post-training 'safety basin' is not required for EM.

title: Evil Spectra: How Optimisers can Amplify or Suppress Emergent Misalignment
authors: Jason R. Brown, Patrick Leask, Lev McKinney
finding: Sweeps over optimisers, datasets, batch sizes and Qwen3 models find that the optimiser has the largest effect on EM, a 7x spread in misalignment rate, while model size within Qwen3 has a negligible effect. A sweep of 12 models from three families under Adam finds scale (1B to 235B) and family also have negligible effects. On Qwen3-8B, final training loss strongly predicts alignment, and stratifying by optimiser explains nearly all of the remaining variance. Late in training, the optimiser predicts alignment better than loss does. Muon preserves alignment best, which the authors attribute to it implicitly making the LoRA adapter's singular-value spectrum more uniform. A loss term that encourages a flatter spectrum substantially recovers alignment under Adam and Lion at negligible cost to training loss. Here 'flatness' means singular-value uniformity, not loss-landscape flatness.
relevance: Strong evidence that the G-over-N preference is partly an optimiser-dependent implicit bias, not purely a property of the pretrained model. Our steering-vector results, and Soligo's, use adaptive optimisers, so the conclusion 'pretraining makes G preferred' should be checked for invariance across optimisers. The loss-alignment correlation fits 'G reaches lower loss', but the paper shows loss is not the whole story.

title: The Geometry of Alignment Collapse: When Fine-Tuning Breaks Safety
