authors: Max Springer, Chung Peng Lee, Blossom Metevier, Jane Castleman, Bohdan Turbal, Hayoung Jung, Zeyu Shen, Aleksandra Korolova
finding: A mainly theoretical paper. It argues that alignment is concentrated in low-dimensional subspaces with sharp curvature (low-rank Fisher sensitivity). Even when first-order fine-tuning updates start orthogonal to those subspaces, second-order curvature coupling between the fine-tuning task and the alignment parameters accelerates the trajectory into them. Under a three-part 'Alignment Instability Condition' (low-rank sensitivity, initial orthogonality, curvature coupling), they derive a lower bound on alignment (utility) loss that grows as t^4 early in training (Cor. 6.3). The empirical evidence is limited. Fisher eigen-spectra of MLP weights show sharp decay. On Qwen3-1.7B-Instruct and LLaMA-3.2-3B-Instruct, fine-tuning on benign, 'seemingly benign' (including Risky Financial Advice and Bad Medical Advice) and harmful data raises AdvBench harmfulness; seemingly benign data comes close to the harmful set. A first-order Overlap Score separates risky from benign datasets under full fine-tuning but not under LoRA. Neither the curvature-coupling term nor the t^4 law is tested empirically.
relevance: This proposes a concrete route from a narrow update to broad behaviour change: off-diagonal curvature (Hessian or Fisher coupling) between the narrow task and broadly used directions. It is stated for aligned models degraded by benign data, but the same coupling idea could explain why a narrow misaligned gradient moves a shared persona direction. It is consistent with the 'stiff direction' picture rather than the flat one.

title: From Memorization to Reasoning in the Spectrum of Loss Curvature
authors: Jack Merullo, Srihita Vatsavaya, Lucius Bushnaq, Owen Lewis
finding: A K-FAC curvature decomposition of weights in LMs (OLMo-2 7B, with 1B in the appendix) and a ViT separates memorization. Individual memorized points have sharp curvature, but averaged across examples the memorization directions are flatter than the generalizing ones. Removing the low-curvature components therefore suppresses recitation of untargeted memorized data better than BalancedSubnet, at lower perplexity cost. The edit consistently hurts closed-book fact retrieval and arithmetic, while open-book retrieval and general logical reasoning are preserved. The authors read this as those tasks relying on specialized weight directions.
relevance: Strong counterpoint to 'general = flat'. For the aggregate loss, idiosyncratic or narrow structure is low-curvature, and broadly shared structure is high-curvature, because many examples push on it. This predicts N (narrow) is a flatter direction of the pretraining loss and G a stiffer one, which is our finding (3) read through curvature. Flatness of the fine-tuning solution (Soligo) and stiffness under the pretraining loss are different quantities and may point opposite ways.

title: Overtrained Language Models Are Harder to Fine-Tune
authors: Jacob Mitchell Springer, Sachin Goyal, Kaiyue Wen, Tanishq Kumar, Xiang Yue, Sadhika Malladi, Graham Neubig, Aditi Raghunathan
finding: Extended pre-training can make models harder to fine-tune and worse after fine-tuning, which the authors call 'catastrophic overtraining'. Instruction-tuned OLMo-1B pre-trained on 3T tokens scores more than 2% lower on several standard benchmarks than the 2.3T-token checkpoint. Controlled experiments and theory attribute this to a systematic rise in the broad sensitivity of pre-trained parameters to modification, fine-tuning included.
relevance: The sensitivity of a base checkpoint to perturbation changes systematically with pre-training, so how easily EM happens could depend on which checkpoint is used. Our OLMo-3 stage-1 checkpoint sits at a specific point in this trajectory. It also suggests 'how much fine-tuning moves broad behaviour' is itself a learned geometric property of pre-training.

title: Sharpness-Aware Pretraining Mitigates Catastrophic Forgetting
authors: Ishaan Watts, Catherine Li, Sachin Goyal, Jacob Mitchell Springer, Aditi Raghunathan
finding: Pre-training choices that favor flatter minima (SAM, large learning rates, shorter LR annealing) reduce forgetting after post-training by up to 80%, across 5 post-training datasets and models from 20M to 150M parameters. Adding a short SAM phase to an existing OLMo-2-1B checkpoint cut forgetting by 31% after MetaMath post-training and by 40% after 4-bit quantization.
relevance: This is a causal handle on base-model geometry that already works on OLMo checkpoints: flatness of the base controls how much fine-tuning disturbs prior behaviour. If EM is easy because broad directions are sensitive in the base model, flattening the base should change EM. Which way it would change is not obvious, since flattening could protect either aligned behaviour or the persona prior.

title: Same Pre-training Loss, Better Downstream: Implicit Bias Matters for Language Models
authors: Hong Liu, Sang Michael Xie, Zhiyuan Li, Tengyu Ma
finding: Models with the same (near-optimal) pre-training loss can transfer differently. The authors produce such models by training past convergence, scaling model size, or changing the optimizer. Flatness, measured as the trace of the pre-training-loss Hessian, tracks downstream performance where loss does not. They prove SGD mini-batch noise biases toward flatter minima, and that in a synthetic language setting the flattest minimal-loss model transfers best. All experiments use simplified generated data (PCFG, HMM, and text sampled from OPT-125M), with models up to about 730M parameters.
relevance: A clean precedent for the core logic of 'many solutions fit the data, an implicit bias picks one, and the pick determines out-of-distribution behaviour'. Here the bias is toward flatness at pre-training scale. Whether the fine-tuning analog (G vs N) is selected by flatness or by something else is exactly what is unresolved.

title: Understanding Warmup-Stable-Decay Learning Rates: A River Valley Loss Landscape Perspective
authors: Kaiyue Wen, Zhiyuan Li, Jason Wang, David Hall, Percy Liang, Tengyu Ma
finding: They conjecture that the LM pre-training loss is a 'river valley'. During the high-LR stable phase of WSD, the iterate oscillates between steep valley walls while making progress along the flat river direction. The fast decay phase damps the oscillation and reveals that progress, which explains why the loss drops sharply only during decay. The landscape can emerge from pre-training on a simple bigram dataset. They also propose WSD-S, tested at 0.1B to 1.2B parameters.
relevance: Our OLMo-3 stage-1 checkpoint is pre-anneal, so under this picture it sits high on the valley walls. Its local sharpness is set by the learning rate, and its behaviour along steep directions is not settled. Curvature measured at stage 1 may not transfer to the annealed model, and EM susceptibility and the G-vs-N geometry could differ between the two. This is speculative; the paper does not study fine-tuning.

title: Linear Connectivity Reveals Generalization Strategies
authors: Jeevesh Juneja, Rachit Bansal, Kyunghyun Cho, Joao Sedoc, Naomi Saphra
finding: Text classifiers fine-tuned from the same pre-trained model on MNLI, QQP or CoLA fall into clusters. Models are linearly connected within a cluster, with large loss barriers between clusters. On diagnostic datasets the clusters correspond to different out-of-distribution generalization strategies, for example bag-of-words-like behavior under domain shift versus syntactic heuristics.
relevance: Direct precedent for 'one dataset admits multiple solutions with different generalization' (G vs N), with which basin is reached depending on seed or initialisation. It raises the question of whether G and N are separate basins or connected, given that N drifts to G once the KL is removed in Soligo.

title: Mechanistic Mode Connectivity
authors: Ekdeep Singh Lubana, Eric J. Bigelow, Robert P. Dick, David Krueger, Hidenori Tanaka
finding: They define mechanistic similarity as shared invariances to input transformations and show that models that are not linearly mode-connected use dissimilar mechanisms. As a consequence, naive fine-tuning on a downstream dataset may fail to change a model's mechanisms, such as its reliance on spurious attributes. They propose connectivity-based fine-tuning (CBFT) and evaluate it on synthetic datasets.
relevance: Frames G vs N as mechanistically distinct solutions. If fine-tuning tends to keep using mechanisms the pre-trained model already has, then G being the mechanism pre-training already relies on (findings 3 and 6) would make it the default. The evidence is on vision and synthetic tasks, not LLM persona features.

title: Understanding Generalization through Visualizations
authors: W. Ronny Huang, Zeyad Emam, Micah Goldblum, Liam Fowl, J. K. Terry, Furong Huang, Tom Goldstein
finding: Training on a poisoned loss shows that minima with perfect training accuracy but poor test accuracy exist close to every SGD iterate, yet SGD avoids them. Using loss-surface slices and Monte Carlo estimates of basin volume, they show that well-generalizing minima are flat and sit in wide basins, while bad minima are sharp and have tiny volume. In high dimensions, small width differences become exponentially large volume gaps: for SVHN, good basins are at least 10^4 orders of magnitude larger, so optimizers almost never land in bad minima. The experiments use a swiss-roll toy problem and SVHN/CIFAR-10 classifiers (ResNet-18, VGG13), and the paper is primarily intuition-building rather than theory.
relevance: This is the 'volume hypothesis' account of G-preference: if far more adapter or steering configurations implement G-like than N-like behaviour, an optimiser lands in G with little implicit bias needed. Soligo's perturbation-stability metric is a local volume proxy. Volume depends on the parameterisation (Dinh et al.).

title: Explaining grokking through circuit efficiency
authors: Vikrant Varma, Rohin Shah, Zachary Kenton, Janos Kramar, Ramana Kumar
finding: When a memorizing circuit and a generalizing circuit both fit the training data, the generalizing one is learned more slowly but is more efficient, producing larger logits per unit parameter norm. Weight decay therefore reallocates norm toward it. Memorizing circuits lose efficiency as the dataset grows while generalizing circuits do not, which implies a critical dataset size. They confirm predictions on algorithmic tasks, including the new behaviors 'ungrokking' and 'semi-grokking'.
relevance: Soligo's efficiency metric comes from this framework. A key contrast: in grokking the efficient general solution is slow, while in EM the general solution is apparently both fast and efficient, which may be exactly why EM is easy (no competition phase). Our finding (5), G with lower loss but larger norm, needs a norm-matched comparison before it can speak to efficiency.

title: Flat Minima
authors: Sepp Hochreiter, Jurgen Schmidhuber
finding: They propose Flat Minimum Search, which looks for large connected regions of weight space where training error stays approximately constant ('flat minima'). An MDL-based Bayesian argument says such regions need fewer bits (lower weight precision) to specify, so they correspond to simple networks with low expected overfitting. The method needs second-order derivatives but runs at backprop's order of cost, and it automatically prunes units and weights. Experiments on small feedforward and recurrent nets include a stock-market prediction task where it beats plain backprop, weight decay and OBS/OBD.
relevance: The origin of 'flat = simple = generalises'. Applied to EM, G as one persona would be a lower-description-length explanation of the narrow data than N with its domain-specific gating. The argument is about generalization to the same distribution, and the flatness depends on the parameterisation.

title: On Large-Batch Training for Deep Learning: Generalization Gap and Sharp Minima
authors: Nitish Shirish Keskar, Dheevatsa Mudigere, Jorge Nocedal, Mikhail Smelyanskiy, Ping Tak Peter Tang
finding: Large-batch methods tend to converge to sharp minimizers of the training and test functions and generalize worse. Small-batch methods consistently converge to flat minimizers, which they attribute to inherent gradient noise. The evidence is empirical, with sharpness measured by maximizing loss within a small box neighborhood. They also discuss strategies for closing the large-batch gap.
relevance: This links gradient noise to flatness to generalization, so batch size and learning rate are knobs that should shift G vs N if the preference is flatness-driven. Evil Spectra found the optimiser matters much more than batch size for EM, which is weak evidence that SGD-noise flatness is not the main driver.

title: Sharp Minima Can Generalize For Deep Nets
authors: Laurent Dinh, Razvan Pascanu, Samy Bengio, Yoshua Bengio
finding: For rectifier networks, parameter-space symmetries let them construct functionally equivalent models at arbitrarily sharp minima. Reparametrization can change parameter-space geometry drastically without changing generalization. Most notions of flatness therefore cannot by themselves explain generalization in deep nets.
relevance: Directly relevant to our norm confound (finding 5). The curvature of the loss with respect to a steering vector scales with how the vector is parameterised and with its norm, so a raw 'G is flatter than N' comparison is not meaningful unless norm-matched or scale-invariant. Soligo's matched-norm efficiency and Andriushchenko's adaptive sharpness are the appropriate fixes.

title: Sharpness-Aware Minimization for Efficiently Improving Generalization
authors: Pierre Foret, Ariel Kleiner, Hossein Mobahi, Behnam Neyshabur
finding: SAM minimises training loss together with sharpness by seeking parameters whose rho-neighbourhood has uniformly low loss. The min-max problem is solved approximately with one extra gradient-ascent step, so each step costs about two forward/backward passes. It improves generalization on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, ImageNet and several fine-tuning tasks, reaching state of the art on some, and is as robust to label noise as methods designed for noisy labels.
relevance: Gives an explicit flatness intervention. If G is preferred because it is flatter on the fine-tuning loss, SAM during EM fine-tuning should increase, not decrease, general misalignment. We found no published SAM-on-EM test, and the flatness-based harmful-fine-tuning defenses target a different landscape: flatness of the harmful-data loss during alignment.

title: A Modern Look at the Relationship between Sharpness and Generalization
authors: Maksym Andriushchenko, Francesco Croce, Maximilian Müller, Matthias Hein, Nicolas Flammarion
finding: The paper covers ViTs and ResNets trained from scratch on ImageNet and CIFAR-10, CLIP fine-tuned on ImageNet, and BERT fine-tuned on MNLI. In these settings, even reparameterisation-invariant (adaptive) sharpness correlates poorly with generalization. It mostly tracks training hyperparameters such as the learning rate, and the learning rate itself can correlate positively or negatively with generalization depending on the setup. Sharpness correlates negatively with OOD error, so sharper solutions generalize better, in two places: ViTs trained from scratch on ImageNet (in and out of distribution) and CLIP fine-tuning (on ImageNet-R, -Sketch and -A). For CLIP this largely reflects the learning rate, since a higher fine-tuning learning rate gives both lower sharpness and higher OOD error. BERT on MNLI shows essentially no correlation. In diagonal linear networks, the right sharpness measure depends heavily on the data: average-case sharpness matches an l1 norm and suits sparse targets, while worst-case sharpness matches an l-inf norm and suits dense targets.
relevance: The strongest counterevidence for 'G wins because it is flatter'. Among BERT seeds that fit MNLI equally well but generalize differently on HANS (a G-vs-N-like split), sharpness barely predicted the out-of-distribution strategy. Any flatness explanation of EM must survive this, and it is compatible with G being sharper.

title: Gradient Descent on Neural Networks Typically Occurs at the Edge of Stability
authors: Jeremy M. Cohen, Simran Kaur, Yuanzhi Li, J. Zico Kolter, Ameet Talwalkar
finding: Under full-batch gradient descent, sharpness (the top Hessian eigenvalue) usually rises during training (progressive sharpening) until it reaches 2/eta. It then hovers just above 2/eta (the Edge of Stability). The loss behaves non-monotonically over short timescales but keeps decreasing over long ones, which conflicts with standard optimization assumptions. A follow-up, Damian, Nichani and Lee (ICLR 2023, arXiv 2209.15594, 'Self-Stabilization'), explains this with a cubic Taylor term. When iterates move along the top eigenvector, that term lowers the curvature, so GD behaves like projected GD under the constraint sharpness <= 2/eta.
relevance: The final sharpness of a solution is often set by the step size, not by the solution's intrinsic geometry. So a comparison of G vs N sharpness is confounded unless learning rate and optimiser are matched, and for Adam the relevant quantity is preconditioned sharpness. It also means the stage-1 OLMo checkpoint's own curvature reflects its pre-training learning rate.

title: Eigenvalues of covariance matrices: Application to neural-network learning
authors: Yann Le Cun, Ido Kanter, Sara A. Solla
finding: For a simple (linear-output, squared-error) network, the Hessian is the input second-moment matrix, a sum of outer products of input vectors. The authors compute its eigenvalue spectrum analytically for random inputs and use it to get the learning time. Stability caps the step size at the inverse of the largest eigenvalue, while the slowest mode decays at a rate set by the smallest nonzero eigenvalue. Learning time therefore scales with lambda_max/lambda_min. Uncentred (biased) inputs add a large outlier eigenvalue, which justifies centring inputs to speed up learning. The results apply generally to sums of outer products of random vectors.
relevance: This is the classical bridge from our variance metric to curvature. For weights that read a layer-12 direction, the Hessian with respect to those weights is that direction's activation second moment. So 'G captures more Dolma activation variance' (finding 3) roughly means G is a higher-curvature, faster-learned direction of the pretraining objective. That predicts G is learned first (EM is easy), but it predicts sharpness, not flatness, of that direction under the pretraining loss.

title: The Pitfalls of Simplicity Bias in Neural Networks
authors: Harshay Shah, Kaustav Tamuly, Aditi Raghunathan, Prateek Jain, Praneeth Netrapalli
finding: The authors build datasets with a precise notion of simplicity: the minimum number of linear pieces in an optimal decision boundary. These are synthetic LMS-k (linear plus k-slab) datasets, plus MNIST-CIFAR, where MNIST is the simple feature. On them, FCNs, CNNs, GRUs and standard image CNNs (MobileNetV2, GoogLeNet, ResNet50, DenseNet121) rely almost exclusively on the simplest predictive feature and ignore more complex ones (extreme simplicity bias). This can explain non-robustness to small distribution shifts and adversarial perturbations. It can also hurt in-distribution generalization when the simple feature is less predictive. Ensembles and adversarial training 'can fail' to mitigate it; the conclusion says they do not mitigate SB on these datasets, though both help partially. The paper does not test large pretrained models or language models.
relevance: Answers 'why G' if G is the simplest feature consistent with the data. A domain-conditional rule (bad only if medical) is a conjunction and more complex than an unconditional 'be bad' feature, so extreme simplicity bias predicts exclusive reliance on G even when N fits equally well. Their finding that standard remedies fail mirrors Soligo's result that data mixing does not isolate N. Whether G is 'simpler' in their sense is an analogy we have not measured.

title: Deep learning generalizes because the parameter-function map is biased towards simple functions
authors: Guillermo Valle-Pérez, Chico Q. Camargo, Ard A. Louis
finding: The authors use a probability-complexity bound from algorithmic information theory to argue that the parameter-function map of DNNs is exponentially biased toward simple functions. They support this with a small Boolean-function network and with FC and CNN models on MNIST and CIFAR-10. They place a PAC-Bayes prior over functions rather than parameters, and estimate the marginal likelihood of the training data with the DNN-GP correspondence. The resulting fairly tight bounds correlate with true error. The guarantee assumes the optimiser samples parameters close to uniformly within the zero-error region.
relevance: Reframes G vs N as which behaviour occupies more parameter volume within the set that fits the fine-tuning data. If many more adapter or steering directions near the pretrained weights yield general misalignment than domain-gated misalignment, G wins by volume alone. That matches Soligo's perturbation-robustness result and the need for an explicit constraint to reach N.

title: Is SGD a Bayesian sampler? Well, almost
authors: Chris Mingard, Guillermo Valle-Pérez, Joar Skalse, Ard A. Louis
finding: The probability that SGD and its variants (Adam, Adagrad, RMSprop, Adadelta) converge on a given training-set-consistent function closely tracks the Bayesian posterior over functions under random parameter sampling. The posterior is estimated with NNGPs, using expectation propagation for the cross-entropy loss. That posterior favours low-error, low-complexity functions, so the authors argue that the network's inductive bias (the parameter-function map), not anything specific to SGD, is the main driver of generalization. Batch size, learning rate and optimiser choice cause second-order differences. The evidence is empirical, on small binarised tasks: MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, IMDb with an LSTM, and Ionosphere. It uses small FCN, CNN and LSTM models, test sets of about 100 points or fewer, and infinite-width GP approximations.
relevance: If it holds for fine-tuning from a pretrained point, the G preference is a property of the pretrained model's local prior over functions (what pretraining built) plus the data, not of the optimiser. That is our working hypothesis stated in Bayesian terms. The second-order hyperparameter effects warn that narrowness may still shift with LoRA rank, learning rate, and so on.

title: Shortcut Learning in Deep Neural Networks
authors: Robert Geirhos, Jörn-Henrik Jacobsen, Claudio Michaelis, Richard Zemel, Wieland Brendel, Matthias Bethge, Felix A. Wichmann
finding: A perspective article arguing that many deep-learning failures share one underlying phenomenon: shortcut learning. Shortcuts are decision rules that do well on standard benchmarks but fail to transfer to harder test conditions such as real-world deployment. It draws parallels in comparative psychology, education and linguistics, suggesting shortcut learning may be a general feature of biological and artificial learners. It recommends ways to interpret models and to build benchmarks that test out-of-distribution generalization. It is mainly a synthesis. Its only experiment is one toy illustration: on a star/moon task with a location shortcut, a 3-layer MLP gets 100% train accuracy but chance-level accuracy at shifted test positions, while a small CNN generalizes.
relevance: In shortcut terms, G is the shortcut: one global rule that fits every training example as well as the intended domain-gated rule, and is cheaper to represent given the pretrained features. The framing says the intended narrow solution is learned only when the data rule out the shortcut. Narrow EM datasets never do, since no in-domain example separates G from N.

title: What shapes feature representations? Exploring datasets, architectures, and training
authors: Katherine L. Hermann, Andrew K. Lampinen
finding: The authors use synthetic datasets with controlled feature relevance (Trifeature, Navon; colour, shape and texture features), with AlexNet and ResNet-50. When two features predict the label redundantly, the network tends to represent the one that was most linearly decodable from the untrained network. Training strengthens task-relevant features and partly suppresses irrelevant ones without removing them. A weakly predictive but easy feature can suppress a more predictive but harder one. Models trained on easy plus hard features end up with representations most similar to easy-only models. Easy features also give more consistent representations across seeds. The NeurIPS meta-review notes two unresolved reviewer concerns: transfer to real-world data such as ImageNet, and the lack of control over feature difficulty.
relevance: Gives the cleanest mechanistic analogue. When G and N are equally predictive on the fine-tuning data, the one more linearly decodable from the starting representation (here the pretrained layer-12 residual stream) wins. Our variance-captured measure (3) is a rough proxy for that decodability. It also predicts that once the easy G is adopted it can suppress N, consistent with N needing an explicit KL constraint.

title: Learned feature representations are biased by complexity, learning order, position, and more
authors: Andrew Kyle Lampinen, Stephanie C. Y. Chan, Katherine Hermann
finding: The authors build datasets in which features play matched computational roles, while complexity, learning order and distribution across inputs are varied. Learned representations are still systematically biased: features that are simpler to compute or learned earlier are represented more strongly and densely, even when every feature is learned equally well. Architecture, optimiser and training regime also shape these biases, and in transformers features decoded earlier in the output sequence are represented more strongly. The authors warn that this complicates representation analysis, interventions and model-brain comparisons, since representational strength does not equal computational importance.
relevance: A caution on our finding (3). G capturing more activation variance on Dolma could reflect G being simpler or learned earlier, not G mattering more for prediction. Variance and EM-preference may share a common cause (simplicity) without one implying the other. Our ablation-loss measure (3b) is the better test of 'relied on for prediction', and representational prominence alone should not carry the argument.

title: Underspecification Presents Challenges for Credibility in Modern Machine Learning
authors: Alexander D'Amour, Katherine Heller, Dan Moldovan, et al. (40 authors; D. Sculley last)
finding: Many ML pipelines are underspecified: they can return many predictors with equivalent held-out, in-domain performance that nevertheless behave very differently in deployment domains. The choice among them is driven by arbitrary details of the pipeline, such as the random seed. This failure mode is distinct from structural train/deploy mismatch. It is demonstrated in computer vision, medical imaging, NLP, EHR-based clinical risk prediction and medical genomics, and the authors argue that pipelines meant for real-world use must account for it explicitly, for example with stress tests.
relevance: EM is a textbook underspecification case. In-domain fine-tuning loss cannot distinguish G from N, so which one appears is decided entirely by inductive bias: pretrained representation, initialization, optimiser. It frames our question correctly ('which inductive bias picks G?') and predicts nontrivial run-to-run variation in narrowness. That fits Betley et al.'s observation that EM models are inconsistent and our finding that N is only partly narrow.

title: RL with KL penalties is better viewed as Bayesian inference
authors: Tomasz Korbak, Ethan Perez, Christopher L. Buckley
finding: The standard RL objective for LM fine-tuning leads to distribution collapse. KL-regularised RL fine-tuning is equivalent to variational inference toward a Bayesian posterior, namely the prior LM updated by evidence from the reward. This explains why the KL penalty prevents collapse and derives the objective from first principles. The KL-regularised objective matches RL only for one particular choice of reward, and other fine-tuning objectives are not RL at all. The authors therefore argue that LM fine-tuning is better framed as approximating a target distribution. The analysis concerns reward-based fine-tuning, not SFT on narrow data.
relevance: Gives a principled reading of the G/N construction. Soligo's N, with a KL penalty to the base model on other data, approximates a posterior that keeps the pretrained prior off-domain, while unregularised SFT is not Bayesian conditioning and moves along whatever direction cuts loss cheapest, which is G. On this view 'EM is easy' partly means 'plain SFT ignores the off-domain prior'. That is a different claim from 'G has higher posterior probability', and the two should be kept apart.

title: An Explanation of In-context Learning as Implicit Bayesian Inference
authors: Sang Michael Xie, Aditi Raghunathan, Percy Liang, Tengyu Ma
finding: If pretraining documents have long-range coherence that requires inferring a latent document-level concept, in-context learning can emerge as implicit posterior inference over that concept from the prompt examples. This is proved for a mixture-of-HMMs pretraining distribution, even when prompts are out of distribution relative to pretraining. The authors show it on the synthetic GINC dataset with Transformers and LSTMs, which also reproduces scale effects, example-order sensitivity, and cases where zero-shot beats few-shot. The setting is idealized and real-LLM evidence is indirect.
relevance: The formal backbone of the latent-author account. Bad-advice examples are evidence about a document-level latent (author stance or character) that conditions every later token, so updating it gives broad effects. N corresponds to a latent concept (an author benign everywhere except one domain) that is rare in pretraining and so has low prior. Predicts G's breadth tracks how coherent such author latents are in the pretraining corpus.

title: Language Models as Agent Models
authors: Jacob Andreas
finding: A position and survey paper arguing that, in a narrow sense, LMs model intentional communication. To predict the next token they infer properties of the agent likely to have produced the context, including communicative intentions, beliefs and goals, and these inferred representations shape later generation. Evidence is a survey of prior work, not new experiments; Andreas does not claim LMs themselves have beliefs or goals.
relevance: Explains our finding (1) without an Assistant persona: a base LM already infers the author behind the text, so narrow bad-advice data shifts the inferred author, whose traits colour all outputs. On this view G is preferred because the pretraining objective made author inference a core, reused computation, which fits our finding (3) that G matters for pretraining loss.

title: Role-Play with Large Language Models
authors: Murray Shanahan, Kyle McDonell, Laria Reynolds
finding: Proposes describing dialogue agents as role-playing characters, or as a superposition of simulacra consistent with the dialogue so far. This allows folk-psychological vocabulary without attributing human characteristics, and is applied to apparent deception and apparent self-awareness. Conceptual, no experiments.
relevance: In simulator terms, fine-tuning narrows the distribution over characters consistent with the data, and the characters available are those learned from pretraining text. G is the character-level explanation of bad advice. N needs a character who is benign except in one domain, which the pretraining 'cast' rarely contains.

title: The Description Length of Deep Learning Models
authors: Léonard Blier, Yann Ollivier
finding: Deep networks do compress their training data even counting the cost of encoding the model, consistent with Solomonoff/MDL. Variational codes give surprisingly poor bounds despite being designed to minimize codelength, while simple incremental (prequential) coding achieves strong compression.
relevance: Under MDL the preferred solution minimises model cost plus data cost given the model. G and N are both one steering vector, so their model cost differs mainly through norm (our confound (5)) and how cheaply the direction is specified given the pretrained representation. Prequential code length is a fair, norm-aware way to ask whether G is the shorter description of the fine-tuning data. Next-token pretraining loss is itself a code length, so our ablation-loss result (3b) has a natural MDL reading.

title: Persona-Model Collapse in Emergent Misalignment
authors: Davi Bastos Costa, Renato Vicente
finding: Using Moral Foundations Questionnaire responses under persona role-play on DeepSeek-V3.1, GPT-4.1, GPT-4o and Qwen3-235B, insecure-code fine-tuning (Betley et al. data) raises 'moral susceptibility' (cross-persona variability) by about 55% on average, beyond the band seen across 13 frontier models in prior work. It lowers 'moral robustness' (within-persona consistency) by about 65%. A matched secure-code control keeps susceptibility near baseline, with only partial loss of robustness. The authors read this as EM degrading the model's capacity to simulate, differentiate and keep consistent characters. Evidence is behavioural only, from one questionnaire and one EM dataset; DeepSeek-V3.1-insecure is a weak case.
relevance: Cuts against a clean persona-selection reading. EM may be less 'pick the evil character' than 'loosen persona structure', so G might be a direction that flattens persona distinctions rather than a specific character. That would still fit a simplicity account, since collapsing distinctions is a simpler function, but it changes what the G direction should look like on pretraining text.

title: Toy Models of Superposition
authors: Nelson Elhage, Tristan Hume, Catherine Olsson, Nicholas Schiefer, Tom Henighan, Shauna Kravec, Zac Hatfield-Dodds, Robert Lasenby, Dawn Drain, Carol Chen, Roger Grosse, Sam McCandlish, Jared Kaplan, Dario Amodei, Martin Wattenberg, Christopher Olah
finding: Small ReLU toy models trained on synthetic sparse features store more features than they have dimensions ('superposition'). Whether a feature gets its own direction, is packed into shared directions, or is dropped depends on its importance and sparsity, with sharp phase changes between regimes and uniform-polytope geometry. The paper also gives preliminary evidence linking superposition to adversarial examples. Limitation: the evidence comes from toy models with hand-set feature statistics, not real language models.
relevance: Gives a mechanism for how pretraining statistics could set representation strength. A frequent, loss-relevant feature (for example a hostile or malicious speaker persona) should get a clean, low-interference direction that a single steering vector can reuse cheaply. A rare conjunction (bad advice only in the medical domain) would sit in superposition, so expressing it alone takes a combination of directions with more interference. That could be why N needs a KL penalty and is still only partly narrow. This is an extrapolation from toy models.

title: The Linear Representation Hypothesis and the Geometry of Large Language Models
authors: Kiho Park, Yo Joong Choe, Victor Veitch
finding: Formalizes 'concepts are directions' using counterfactual pairs, in both the output (unembedding/word) space and the input (context embedding) space. It links the two forms to linear probing and steering, and proposes a non-Euclidean 'causal inner product' under which projections and cosines become meaningful. Experiments on LLaMA-2 support linear representations and show that results depend on the choice of inner product. Limitation: the concepts are mostly simple word-level counterfactuals.
relevance: Justifies treating G and N as directions. It also warns that our geometric comparisons (projection of Dolma activations onto G vs N, variance captured) depend on the inner product. Raw Euclidean projections in an anisotropic residual stream can mislead. Recomputing the variance ratio (1.11-1.15x for G vs 0.96-1.05x for N) after whitening, or under a causal inner product, is a cheap robustness check.

title: When Bad Data Leads to Good Models
authors: Kenneth Li, Yida Chen, Fernanda Viégas, Martin Wattenberg
finding: The paper first uses a toy 4-layer transformer with a 4-dimensional residual stream trained on cyclic Markov chains. It then pretrains Olmo-1B models on clean/toxic mixtures (0-25% toxic). A larger toxic share makes toxicity less entangled and more linearly represented. Those base models are more toxic, but easier to detoxify: on Toxigen and RealToxicityPrompts, ITI gives a better trade-off between toxicity reduction and capability, with an optimum near 10% toxic data. SFT and DPO were also applied across the ratio sweep. Limitations: 1B scale, two seeds per configuration, PerspectiveAPI-defined toxicity only, and a ratio optimum specific to this setup.
relevance: Controlled causal evidence that pretraining volume of a concept shapes its geometry: more data gives a cleaner single direction. By the same logic, a cleanly separated misalignment direction is also an easy single target for a fine-tune to amplify, which would favour G. It predicts that more hostile-persona text in pretraining makes EM more general. It is partly in tension with our null continued-pretraining result, though their manipulation is a from-scratch pretraining mixture, not a small continued-pretraining dose late in training.

title: How Does Controllability Emerge In Language Models During Pretraining?
authors: Jianshu She, Xinyue Li, Eric Xing, Zhengzhong Liu, Qirong Ho
finding: Linear steerability of concepts is absent early and emerges at intermediate-to-late stages of pretraining. Closely related concepts become steerable at different times: anger and fear earlier, sadness, surprise and disgust later. Using their 'Intervention Detector' (ID) framework, rising linear separability of a concept in hidden space tracks the onset of steerability; the authors call these heuristic signals, not exact predictors. Experiments use LLM360 7B checkpoints, mainly Crystal with a replication on AMBER, each fine-tuned on dialogue data before analysis. Concepts are six emotions plus factuality/commonsense tasks (OBQA, ARC, RACE), with refusal in an appendix. Limitations: two 7B models, a dialogue-finetuning step before each probe, and a preprint.
relevance: Steerability is something pretraining builds, at different times for different concepts. That makes a checkpoint test possible: across OLMo-3 stage-1 checkpoints, measure when G (and N) become linearly separable and steerable, and whether EM susceptibility appears at the same time. If G becomes steerable much earlier than N, that is direct evidence for a pretraining-prior account of why G is preferred.

title: Impact of Pretraining Term Frequencies on Few-Shot Reasoning
authors: Yasaman Razeghi, Robert L. Logan IV, Matt Gardner, Sameer Singh
finding: On arithmetic and unit-conversion tasks, GPT-J/GPT-Neo models pretrained on the Pile are consistently more accurate on instances whose terms are frequent in pretraining. In some cases, accuracy on the top 10% most frequent terms is over 70 points higher than on the bottom 10%. Limitations: correlational, and limited to numerical tasks.
relevance: Classic evidence that what a model does easily reflects pretraining frequency. For EM, the analogy is that the general solution may reuse high-frequency structure (a common malicious or contrarian speaker), while a narrow 'bad only about medicine' rule has little direct support in pretraining. The step from term frequency to behavioural disposition is an analogy that has not been tested.

title: Large Language Models Struggle to Learn Long-Tail Knowledge
authors: Nikhil Kandpal, Haikang Deng, Adam Roberts, Eric Wallace, Colin Raffel
finding: QA accuracy (e.g. on TriviaQA) tracks the number of pretraining documents that mention the question's entities, found by entity-linking the corpus. The paper reports both correlational and causal evidence, the causal part from retraining with relevant documents removed. This holds across several corpora (e.g. ROOTS) and models up to 176B. Scale helps long-tail facts only slowly, needing orders of magnitude more parameters, and retrieval augmentation reduces the dependence. Limitation: factual knowledge only.
relevance: Supplies a method that fits Dolma: link or count the documents that support a concept, then test causality by removing or adding them. Our G/N projection counts are a soft version of this. A direct analogue would count documents with the G-associated features vs the N-associated features and ask whether count predicts which solution fine-tuning picks. Our continued-pretraining null warns that for dispositions, as opposed to facts, the dose-response may be flat at 7B and late in training.

title: Embers of Autoregression: Understanding Large Language Models Through the Problem They are Trained to Solve
authors: R. Thomas McCoy, Shunyu Yao, Dan Friedman, Matthew Hardy, Thomas L. Griffiths
finding: Argues from the next-token objective (the 'teleological approach') that LLM accuracy should depend on the probability of the task, of the target output, and of the input, even for deterministic tasks. Across 11 tasks on GPT-3.5 and GPT-4, the effects of task and output probability are strong. For example, GPT-4's accuracy at decoding a simple cipher is 51% when the answer is a high-probability sentence and 13% when it is low-probability. The effect of input probability is much weaker and less consistent across models. Limitations: closed models, and capability tasks rather than dispositions.
relevance: Supplies the teleological framing behind our working hypothesis. When the fine-tuning data can be explained either by a narrow rule or by a kind of speaker whose text is common on the web, the high-prior explanation should win. It also warns that misalignment evaluations whose misaligned answers are high-probability text may overstate how broad G is relative to N.

title: Steering Language Models With Activation Engineering
authors: Alexander Matt Turner, Lisa Thiergart, Gavin Leech, David Udell, Juan J. Vazquez, Ulisse Mini, Monte MacDiarmid
finding: Activation Addition (ActAdd) adds a residual-stream steering vector at inference. The vector is computed from the activation difference of one prompt pair, for example 'Love' vs 'Hate'. It steers high-level properties such as sentiment and topic while preserving off-target task performance, and it needs no optimization. The current version (v5) reports state-of-the-art results on negative-to-positive sentiment shift and detoxification with LLaMA-3 and OPT. Limitation: the quantitative evaluation is mostly sentiment and detoxification.
relevance: Establishes that one residual-stream direction can carry a high-level property across contexts, which is what makes a broad G expressible in the first place. G and N are optimized rather than contrast-derived vectors. One useful test is whether G aligns with a contrast-derived ActAdd/CAA vector from the base model (for example a 'malicious vs benign speaker' prompt pair). High alignment would mean the optimizer found a direction already present in the base, not a new one.

title: Representation Engineering: A Top-Down Approach to AI Transparency
authors: Andy Zou, Long Phan, Sarah Chen, James Campbell, Phillip Guo, Richard Ren, Alexander Pan, Xuwang Yin, Mantas Mazeika, Ann-Kathrin Dombrowski, Shashwat Goel, Nathaniel Li, Michael J. Byun, Zifan Wang, Alex Mallen, Steven Basart, Sanmi Koyejo, Dawn Song, Matt Fredrikson, J. Zico Kolter, Dan Hendrycks
finding: Proposes representation engineering (RepE), which reads and controls population-level representations of high-level concepts using contrastive stimuli. Its baseline, Linear Artificial Tomography (LAT), takes the first principal component of activation differences as a 'reading vector'. The paper studies honesty, utility, morality and power-seeking, emotion, harmlessness, bias, knowledge editing and memorization. Reading vectors support both monitoring (for example lie and hallucination detection) and steering of LLMs. Limitation: the methods are baselines within a framework, with no causal account of where the representations come from.
relevance: Supplies off-the-shelf 'reading vectors' for morality and harmfulness that can be extracted from the OLMo base checkpoint without any EM training. If G has high cosine with a base-model morality or harmfulness reading vector and N does not, G is a pre-existing concept being reused. That is a cleaner test of 'G is already represented' than variance on Dolma.

title: LEACE: Perfect linear concept erasure in closed form
authors: Nora Belrose, David Schneider-Joseph, Shauli Ravfogel, Ryan Cotterell, Edward Raff, Stella Biderman
finding: LEACE is a closed-form erasure that makes a concept undetectable by any linear classifier. It changes the representation as little as possible under a broad class of norms. The paper extends it to 'concept scrubbing', which erases the concept at every layer of an LLM. It is used to measure how much LMs rely on part-of-speech information and to reduce gender bias in BERT embeddings. Published at NeurIPS 2023. Limitation: the guarantee covers linear erasure only, and the method needs concept labels.
relevance: Mean-ablating one vector leaves correlated directions that still carry the concept, so our ablation measure (3) may understate or misattribute reliance. LEACE, with labels from G-projection or misalignment judgments on Dolma, gives a principled 'how much does pretraining LM loss depend on this concept' measure. Applied during fine-tuning, it tests whether G-erasure forces the model into N or makes the data unlearnable. Amnesic probing (Elazar et al., TACL 2021) also shows decodability is not reliance.

title: Optimal ablation for interpretability
authors: Maximilian Li, Lucas Janson
finding: Defines optimal ablation (OA): a component's value is replaced with the constant that minimizes expected loss on the task, found by mini-batch SGD. Proposition 2.3 shows that OA's loss gap at the true optimum is no larger than that of any total ablation method, including zero, mean and resample ablation. On IOI, the median component's OA gap is 11.1% of its zero-ablation gap, 33.0% of its mean-ablation gap and 17.7% of its resample-ablation gap. The authors attribute the excess gap of other methods partly to 'spoofing', where the replacement value inserts misleading information into downstream computation, as opposed to 'deletion' of the component's own information. Published at NeurIPS 2024 (spotlight). Limitation: experiments mainly cover circuit-style components, plus factual-recall localization and latent prediction.
relevance: Bears directly on finding (3). Part of the extra pretraining loss from mean-ablating G (1.6-2.2x random) could be spoofing rather than reliance. Spoofing could plausibly be larger for G, since it captures more variance and is larger. Re-running the comparison with an optimal constant along the G and N directions, fitted on Dolma, would show whether 'G matters more for pretraining' survives.

title: All Bark and No Bite: Rogue Dimensions in Transformer Language Models Obscure Representational Quality
authors: William Timkey, Marten van Schijndel
finding: In contextual LMs such as BERT and GPT-2, one to three 'rogue' high-variance dimensions dominate cosine and Euclidean similarity. These dimensions often differ from the ones that drive model behaviour, and simple postprocessing such as standardization corrects the distortion. Related work by Puccetti, Rogers, Drozd and Dell'Orletta ('Outliers Dimensions that Disrupt Transformers Are Driven by Frequency', Findings of EMNLP 2022, arXiv 2205.11380) finds that hidden-state magnitude in outlier dimensions of BERT and RoBERTa tracks token frequency in pretraining data. Limitation: older, smaller models.
relevance: A caution about measure (2): capturing more Dolma activation variance does not mean the model relies on that direction. G's 1.11-1.15x ratio could partly reflect alignment with frequency-driven outlier dimensions. Standardize activations, or draw the random baseline from the activation covariance rather than isotropically, before reading variance as 'more represented'.

title: Model Spec Midtraining: Improving How Alignment Training Generalizes
authors: Chloe Li, Nevan Wichers, Sara Price, Samuel Marks, Jon Kutasov
finding: Model spec midtraining (MSM) trains on synthetic documents that discuss a Model Spec after pretraining and before alignment fine-tuning on demonstrations. This shapes how narrow fine-tuning generalizes. Two Llama-3.1-8B base models midtrained on different specs, then fine-tuned on the same cheese-preference data, generalized to pro-America or pro-affordability values depending on the spec. MSM with a spec on self-preservation and goal-guarding cut Qwen3-32B agentic misalignment from 54% to 7%, beating a deliberative-alignment baseline (14%). Explaining the values behind rules and giving specific rather than general guidance both improved generalization. Limitations: synthetic documents, one form of misalignment (instrumental unilateral harmful actions), and no test against stronger pressure from RL or high-compute post-training.
relevance: The positive counterpart to the nulls. Midtraining that supplies an explanation linking the narrow data to a broader trait does change which generalization fine-tuning picks. That suggests pretraining shapes the choice between G and N through which explanatory latent is available, not through the volume of G-like text. A direct test would midtrain OLMo on documents describing bad advice as a narrow, domain-bound behaviour and check whether N becomes preferred.

title: Algebraic Geometry and Statistical Learning Theory
authors: Sumio Watanabe
id: Cambridge University Press 2009 (Cambridge Monographs on Applied and Computational Mathematics 25), DOI 10.1017/CBO9780511800474
finding: Foundational monograph of singular learning theory (SLT). Models such as neural networks, mixtures, HMMs and Bayesian networks are singular (non-identifiable, with degenerate Fisher information). Using resolution of singularities and zeta-function theory, it derives the asymptotic Bayes free energy F_n = n L_n(w0) + lambda log n - (m-1) log log n + O_p(1), where lambda is the real log canonical threshold (RLCT, the learning coefficient). It also expresses Bayes and Gibbs generalization error in terms of lambda and estimates them from training error. A separate chapter treats ML and MAP generalization error via empirical processes on algebraic varieties. All results are asymptotic in sample size n and concern Bayesian/statistical estimators, not SGD dynamics.
relevance: This is the formal basis for the gold question. Among solutions with the same training loss, the posterior concentrates on the one with lower lambda, and at small n a solution with slightly higher loss but much lower lambda can win. If both G and N fit the narrow data, SLT predicts G is preferred if it is more degenerate (lower lambda), for example because it reuses existing pretraining structure, while N needs extra parameters to gate the behavior by domain. Caveat: since n multiplies the loss term, a real loss gap between G and N (seen in 2 of 3 domains here) dominates lambda log n, unless the gap is tiny.

title: Asymptotic Equivalence of Bayes Cross Validation and Widely Applicable Information Criterion in Singular Learning Theory
authors: Sumio Watanabe
finding: Proves that Bayes leave-one-out cross-validation loss and WAIC are asymptotically equivalent as random variables, even for singular models, so selecting models or hyperparameters with either gives asymptotically the same result. The sum of the Bayes generalization error and the Bayes CV error is asymptotically 2 lambda / n, where lambda is the RLCT, which ties generalization directly to the learning coefficient. It also argues that DIC differs from both. The results are asymptotic and Bayesian.
relevance: This links lambda to generalization, not only to posterior mass. A lower-lambda solution should generalize more on the training distribution. Note that 'generalization' here means in-distribution prediction, not the out-of-domain behavioral spread that defines EM. So SLT predicts which solution is selected, but it does not by itself say that the selected solution behaves broadly.

title: A Widely Applicable Bayesian Information Criterion
authors: Sumio Watanabe
finding: Defines WBIC, the posterior-average log likelihood at inverse temperature 1/log n, and proves that it has the same asymptotic expansion as the Bayes free energy, even for singular models and unrealizable truths. This makes the free energy computable without knowing the RLCT or the true distribution, so WBIC generalizes BIC to singular models. The tempered-posterior LLC estimator of Lau et al. descends from it.
relevance: Gives a practical recipe for comparing the free energies of G and N directly, using tempered posterior sampling around each solution. This tests the 'model prefers G' claim without separating loss from complexity by hand. The tempering at 1/log n is also why LLC estimates use beta = 1/log n.

title: A Practical Bayesian Framework for Backpropagation Networks
authors: David J. C. MacKay
finding: Introduces the evidence framework for feedforward nets. It gives objective comparisons between architectures, stopping rules for pruning or growing, the choice of weight decay, error bars, and an effective number of well-determined parameters computed from Hessian eigenvalues. The Bayesian evidence automatically embodies Occam's razor. The Occam factor, the ratio of posterior to prior accessible volume, penalizes over-flexible models and models whose parameters must be finely tuned. Evidence correlates well with generalization for models that suit the problem. The framework relies on a Gaussian (Laplace) approximation to the weight posterior, which assumes a regular, non-degenerate minimum.
relevance: This is the classical (regular-model) ancestor of 'flat or simple solutions win'. The Occam factor is the posterior-to-prior volume ratio, which is the sharpness and flatness story. SLT replaces the Hessian-determinant volume with the RLCT because the Laplace approximation fails at degenerate minima. That matters if G and N differ mostly in degenerate directions.

title: Deep Learning is Singular, and That's Good
authors: Daniel Murfet, Susan Wei, Mingming Gong, Hui Li, Jesse Gell-Redman, Thomas Quella
finding: Argues that in singular models the optimal parameters form an analytic set with singularities, so classical statistical inference does not apply. Because neural networks are singular, methods that divide by the Hessian determinant or use the Laplace approximation are inappropriate for them. Presents SLT, with theory and small experiments, as a framework for understanding deep learning, and sets out future work to make it applicable in practice.
relevance: Explains why Hessian-based sharpness (max eigenvalue, trace, log-det) is the wrong complexity measure for comparing G and N. Degeneracy, not just curvature, sets posterior volume. This is the conceptual bridge from the user's sharpness interest to the LLC.

title: The Local Learning Coefficient: A Singularity-Aware Complexity Measure
authors: Edmund Lau, Zach Furman, George Wang, Daniel Murfet, Susan Wei
finding: Defines the local learning coefficient (LLC), a local version of the RLCT at a trained parameter, and a scalable SGLD-based estimator built on a localized, tempered posterior. It applies the estimator to deep linear networks up to 100M parameters, where estimates match known theoretical values, and to ResNet18 on CIFAR-10 and transformer LMs (appendix). The LLC is lower when the loss is more degenerate nearby, that is, when more nearby parameter changes leave the loss unchanged. The abstract hedges, saying that empirical evidence 'suggests' the LLC gives insight into how training heuristics affect effective complexity. The introduction is stronger: it says common heuristics 'effectively control the LLC'. Estimates depend on SGLD hyperparameters (gamma, epsilon, steps, burn-in), and the authors only conjecture that the estimated quantity equals the LLC under conditions on gamma. The companion paper 'Estimating the Local Learning Coefficient at Scale' (2402.03698, Furman and Lau) was withdrawn and merged into v2.
relevance: This is the instrument for the central testable prediction: LLC(G) < LLC(N) on the fine-tuning loss, at loss-matched points. The LLC is invariant to the rescaling symmetries that undermine sharpness measures (the Dinh et al. critique), which matters because G ends with a larger norm than N. For a steering vector (d = 4096), the LLC can be estimated in the vector's own parameter space, which is cheap.

title: Dynamical versus Bayesian Phase Transitions in a Toy Model of Superposition
authors: Zhongtian Chen, Edmund Lau, Jake Mendel, Susan Wei, Daniel Murfet
finding: In the toy model of superposition with two hidden dimensions (r=2, mainly c=6 features, high-sparsity limit), the paper derives a closed-form loss and proves that regular k-gons are critical points. Some k-gon LLCs are derived theoretically and others are estimated. These LLCs govern Bayesian phase transitions as sample size grows (via the free-energy formula and MCMC), and the same critical points empirically shape SGD trajectories. The paper says learning, by SGD or Bayesian, moves from high-loss, low-complexity regions to low-loss, high-complexity ones. Caveats: the results come from a toy model only, the free energy is asymptotic in n, some criticality results are conjectures, and the 'Bayesian antecedent' hypothesis is only partly supported.
relevance: Direct evidence that a low-LLC solution can be preferred early or at small n even when it has higher loss, and that SGD tracks this ordering in at least one setting. Narrow EM fine-tuning datasets are small (a few thousand examples), which is the regime where the complexity term matters most. If G is simpler, it should win early in training, which matches reports that EM appears within tens of steps.

title: Loss Landscape Degeneracy and Stagewise Development in Transformers
authors: Jesse Hoogland, George Wang, Matthew Farrugia-Roberts, Liam Carroll, Susan Wei, Daniel Murfet
finding: Tracks the LLC over training for a two-layer attention-only transformer LM (about 3M parameters, Pile subset) and an in-context linear-regression transformer (about 50k parameters). Training splits into distinct periods of changing degeneracy, with stage boundaries defined at critical points or plateaus of the LLC curve. Most stages, but not all, coincide with the formation of internal computational structure or changes in input/output behavior. The final stage of each model showed no significant change. The authors call this 'suggestive evidence' that degeneracy and development are linked. The models are small.
relevance: Suggests EM may be a discrete developmental transition with a measurable LLC signature during fine-tuning. One test is whether the LLC drops, rises or plateaus when general misalignment appears. This also offers a way to check whether G and N fine-tunes cross different landscape regions.

title: Differentiation and Specialization of Attention Heads via the Refined Local Learning Coefficient
authors: George Wang, Jesse Hoogland, Stan van Wingerden, Zach Furman, Daniel Murfet
finding: Introduces refined LLCs. The weight-refined LLC restricts to a subset of weights such as one head, the data-refined LLC is measured against a different data distribution, and the two can be combined. Applied to a two-layer attention-only transformer trained on a Pile subset, they show heads differentiating over training into previous-token, induction and multigram roles. One induction head is partly specialized to code. They also identify a previously unknown multigram circuit, supported by path patching and K-composition. The model is small and attention-only.
relevance: The refined LLC is the right tool for this project's setup: restrict to the layer-12 steering vector (or LoRA) weights and compute the LLC of G and N separately on (a) the narrow fine-tuning data and (b) Dolma pretraining text. A data-refined LLC on Dolma gives a geometric version of 'G is more relied on by pretraining' that does not rest on projection variance.

title: Dynamics of Transient Structure in In-Context Linear Regression Transformers
authors: Liam Carroll, Jesse Hoogland, Matthew Farrugia-Roberts, Daniel Murfet
finding: With intermediate task diversity M, transformers trained on in-context linear regression first approach a general solution (ridge regression), then specialize toward a memorizing solution (dMMSE) with lower loss. This is shown with joint trajectory PCA. The authors explain the transience as an evolving loss-complexity tradeoff ('Bayesian internal model selection'). They validate this with LLC estimates for fully trained transformers: the LLC of dMMSE-like solutions rises with M and crosses ridge's LLC around the onset of transience, so in the transient regime dMMSE has lower loss but higher LLC. Above a task-diversity threshold (about M >= 362), trajectories go straight to ridge and never leave. Caveats: why the transience stops is an open question; training steps do not map cleanly onto the 'effective sample size' n of the Bayesian account; the main LLC validation uses fully trained endpoints, while non-minimum checkpoints are treated only in an appendix; and the dMMSE LLC plateaus above M=32, which may reflect incomplete approximation. The setting is a small (~2.65M-parameter) two-layer transformer.
relevance: The closest formal analogue to G vs N. A general solution with higher loss but lower complexity is preferred over a specialized one that fits the training distribution better, and the specialized one wins only later or with more data. It predicts that N, if more complex, may appear only with longer training or more data. This matches 'narrow misalignment is hard'. It also cuts against a pure loss-based account: G can win while having higher loss.

title: A Basin-Selection Perspective on Grokking via Singular Learning Theory
authors: Ben Cullen, Sergio Estan-Ruiz, Riya Danait, Jiayi Li
finding: Frames grokking as a move from a higher-LLC memorizing basin to a lower-LLC generalizing basin among competing near-zero-loss basins. The LLC ranks basins by statistical (posterior) preference, and optimization dynamics govern the transition between them in training time. It derives analytic LLC formulas for two-layer quadratic networks on modular addition: an exact formula in the lazy regime, a generic reference value in the feature-learning regime under genericity assumptions, and only bounds for the memorization regime. LLC trajectories estimated on training data track the onset of generalization. The v3 revision (May 2026) states explicitly that SLT is used to analyze fixed-data landscapes, not to identify sample size with training time. The authors acknowledge that the analysis is Bayesian-asymptotic rather than a direct analysis of SGD, and that the posterior-SGD link remains open. The experiments cover shallow quadratic networks only.
relevance: Shows the separation the project needs. SLT says which of G and N is statistically preferred, but separate dynamics explain which one SGD reaches. Measuring LLC(G) < LLC(N) would support the preference claim, but explaining why SGD finds G quickly still needs a dynamics argument, such as gradient alignment with an existing persona direction.

title: Structural Inference: Interpreting Small Language Models with Susceptibilities
authors: Garrett Baker, George Wang, Jesse Hoogland, Daniel Murfet
finding: Treats a network as a Bayesian statistical-mechanical system. A susceptibility is the first-order change in the posterior expectation of a component-localized observable when the data distribution is shifted toward a mixture with a Pile subset (e.g., GitHub, FreeLaw, PubMed, arXiv). It is estimated with local SGLD around a checkpoint and decomposes into signed per-token contributions. The response matrix has dominant top principal components (low-rank structure), and PC2 separates induction-circuit heads from multigram heads in a ~3M-parameter two-layer attention-only transformer, consistently across four seeds. Caveats the authors note: SGLD sampling quality and hyperparameter sensitivity are the main limitation, the method is a first-order linear-response approximation, and only one small model is studied.
relevance: This is the formal version of 'G is more influential in the pretraining distribution'. One could compute the susceptibility of a G-localized vs an N-localized observable to upweighting Dolma subsets (e.g., the first-person opinion, sarcasm or hostility documents that project onto G). Unlike activation-variance or ablation measures, it is causal at first order in the data distribution.

title: Towards Spectroscopy: Susceptibility Clusters in Language Models
authors: Andrew Gordon, Garrett Baker, George Wang, William Snell, Stan van Wingerden, Daniel Murfet
finding: The method perturbs the data distribution by upweighting a token y in context x. It measures the response as susceptibilities, which are covariances between component-level observables and the perturbation under a localized Gibbs posterior sampled with SGLD. The authors argue theoretically that susceptibilities decompose into a sum over modes of the data distribution, which explains why tokens that continue their contexts for similar reasons cluster together. On Pythia-14M, conductance-based clustering finds 510 interpretable clusters (grammar, code, math notation), and about 50% of them match SAE features. The model is tiny, and it is unclear how this transfers to 7B.
relevance: Offers a token-level way to find which pretraining data patterns drive the components that carry G. That would be an independent check on the finding that Dolma documents projecting onto the EM direction are first-person opinion, sarcasm and hostility. It does this by grouping tokens by shared loss-landscape response rather than by activation projection.

title: Patterning: The Dual of Interpretability
authors: George Wang, Daniel Murfet
finding: The method inverts susceptibilities, the linear response of posterior expectations to data shifts, to choose data reweightings that produce a target internal structure. In a 3M-parameter attention-only transformer, reweighting along a principal susceptibility direction speeds up induction-circuit formation (and strengthens prefix matching), while suppression largely prevents it. The parentheses task has two rules, Equal-Count and Nested, that both fit the training data perfectly. Upweighting 'Almost Nested' samples raised the LLC at Nested solutions and sent all 100 retrained models to Equal-Count (mean OOD accuracy 0.004). By default most runs reached Equal-Count and some reached Nested. The opposite 'Almost Equal' intervention only partly worked (mean OOD accuracy 0.497 vs 0.310 originally), and its LLC changes did not match the prediction. The authors attribute this to finite perturbations exceeding linear response. The models are small (3-layer models on the parentheses task), and the authors state that SGD finding posterior-preferred solutions 'remains a hypothesis rather than a theorem'.
relevance: The most direct precedent for the gold question. It is a two-solutions-fit-the-data setup where shifting the LLC through data changes which solution SGD picks, which is causal evidence that LLC ordering predicts SGD selection. It suggests an EM experiment: reweight fine-tuning or pretraining data to raise LLC(G) or lower LLC(N), then check whether narrowness follows. The partial failure is a warning that the project's finite continued-pretraining null (finding 4) may sit outside the linear-response regime.

title: Susceptibilities and Patterning: A Primer on Linear Response in Bayesian Learning
authors: Chris Elliott, Daniel Murfet
finding: Expository notes. A susceptibility is a derivative of a posterior expectation, and by fluctuation-dissipation it equals a posterior covariance. With per-sample-loss observables it gives the influence matrix, which the notes identify with the Bayesian influence function. With component-localized observables it gives a structural susceptibility matrix, which up to a factor of n*beta is the Jacobian from data distributions to structural coordinates. Its pseudo-inverse solves the linearized patterning problem. The notes motivate the theory from statistical mechanics and cover estimators and the link to loss-landscape geometry. The only new numerics are illustrative 2D Ising simulations; the neural-network results come from earlier papers.
relevance: The best single entry point to adapt the framework to EM. It shows that 'influence of pretraining data on G', 'susceptibility of G to data shifts' and 'which data would make N preferred' are the same linear map read in different directions.

title: Bayesian Influence Functions for Hessian-Free Data Attribution
authors: Philipp Alexander Kreer, Wilson Wu, Maxwell Adam, Zach Furman, Jesse Hoogland
finding: Defines the local BIF as -Cov(l_i, phi), the covariance between a training sample's loss and a query observable under a localized tempered posterior sampled by SGLD. Under a Laplace approximation this reduces to the damped classical influence function -g_phi^T (H + gamma I)^-1 g_i. It needs no Hessian inversion. On CIFAR-10 LDS it roughly matches EK-FAC: slightly better on small, high-variance retrain subsets and slightly worse (within error) on larger ones. On small vision models EK-FAC is about 5x faster, but on the largest Pythia models (up to 2.8B) the BIF is about two orders of magnitude faster at the same GPU memory. Limitations: it underperforms EK-FAC on Pythia-14M fine-tuning, it is sensitive to SGLD hyperparameters (step size, gamma, beta), and standard SGLD convergence guarantees may not hold for singular models.
relevance: A Hessian-free attribution method suited to degenerate fine-tuning minima. It could attribute general-misalignment eval loss to individual fine-tuning examples, or to Dolma documents at the base checkpoint. Its weaker LM fine-tuning results are a caution for applying it to a 7B EM fine-tune.

title: The Loss Kernel: A Geometric Probe for Deep Learning Interpretability
authors: Maxwell Adam, Zach Furman, Jesse Hoogland
finding: Defines a data-data similarity kernel as the covariance of per-sample losses under low-loss-preserving parameter perturbations, estimated with SGLD on a localized Gibbs posterior. On a synthetic multitask problem (a two-layer transformer on modular addition and division) it separates inputs by task as theory predicts. On Inception-v1 trained on ImageNet its structure mirrors the WordNet hierarchy. It is evaluated on vision and synthetic tasks only; language models are left to future work.
relevance: Gives a direct test of 'the model treats narrow bad advice and general misalignment as the same thing'. If the loss kernel between bad-medical-advice examples and general misalignment prompts (at the base checkpoint) is high, then fitting one moves the other, and G is the default generalization. Low kernel similarity would cut against the shared-mechanism story.

title: Influence Dynamics and Stagewise Data Attribution
authors: Jin Hwa Lee, Matthew Smith, Maxwell Adam, Jesse Hoogland
finding: Argues from SLT that influence between samples is not fixed. It can change non-monotonically, flip sign and spike at developmental transitions. In a toy model that learns a semantic hierarchy, the authors derive influence dynamics analytically and check them against BIF estimates and leave-one-out retraining. They also show that token-level influence changes in Pythia language models line up with known developmental stages.
relevance: For EM attribution, which pretraining or fine-tuning data supports G may depend on when it is measured, before vs after the EM transition. Static TDA results (e.g., the Unequal Influence or persona-feature attribution papers on the existing list) may miss this, and a stagewise view may explain inconsistent attribution findings.

title: Compressibility Measures Complexity: Minimum Description Length Meets Singular Learning Theory
authors: Einar Urdshals, Edmund Lau, Jesse Hoogland, Stan van Wingerden, Daniel Murfet
finding: Extends MDL to singular models using SLT. For regular models, sublevel sets are ellipsoidal and curvature sets the volume. For neural networks, degeneracy (not Hessian curvature) is the leading-order factor. Across Pythia models from 14M to 6.9B, LLC estimates correlate closely, and in some cases linearly, with compressibility under quantization. Factorization, noise addition and head pruning appear in appendices.
relevance: Connects the LLC prediction to description length, which is already on the project's list via 'The Description Length of Deep Learning Models'. It suggests a cheap proxy: if G is lower-complexity, the G fine-tune or steering vector should tolerate more quantization or low-rank truncation than N before losing fit. It also gives a precise sense in which degeneracy, not max-eigenvalue sharpness, measures simplicity.

title: A Bayesian Model Selection Criterion for Selecting Pretraining Checkpoints
authors: Michael Munn, Susan Wei
finding: Defines downstream free energy, the concentration of good downstream parameters near a pretrained checkpoint, as an adaptability criterion that needs no downstream data. Proposition 5.1 shows, asymptotically and under assumptions (an LLC ordering and a bounded density ratio, plus a distribution-shift term), that pretraining free energy bounds the leading-order downstream free energy. Across 85 ResNet-18 checkpoints on CIFAR-FS, lower pretraining free energy (estimated by localized WBIC via SGLD) correlates best with fine-tuning accuracy, ahead of geometric complexity and neural collapse. mini-ImageNet and VGG give similar results. The authors acknowledge that WBIC is costly at large scale.
relevance: Formalizes the working hypothesis at the level of the free energy: what pretraining has made degenerate and well-supported constrains which downstream solutions are cheap. If G lies along directions the pretraining loss is already degenerate in, its downstream free energy should be lower. This also suggests comparing OLMo checkpoints by pretraining free energy to predict EM susceptibility across pretraining.

title: From Density Matrices to Phase Transitions in Deep Learning: Spectral Early Warnings and Interpretability
authors: Max Hennick, Guillaume Corlouer
finding: Introduces a two-datapoint reduced density matrix (2RDM), the per-sample loss covariance over a probe set under parameter perturbations (Gaussian or across a sliding training window). Its spectral heat capacity gives early warning of second-order transitions, and its participation ratio tracks their dimensionality. It is validated on deep linear nets, induction heads, grokking and emergent misalignment. The EM experiment used Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct with LoRA on the Turner et al. model organisms, and the Gaussian 2RDM because there were too few steps for trajectory sampling. About a 20% drop in alignment and coherence occurred within the first 5-10 steps. The variance increase was concentrated almost entirely in alignment-probe groups, with negligible change on medical-advice and benign-capability probes. Caveats: the authors call the effect limited and the fluctuations very small, no number of runs is reported, and the per-group table is hard to interpret.
relevance: The only SLT-adjacent (loss-covariance) measurement on EM found in this slice. It suggests the landscape reorganization during narrow fine-tuning sits in alignment-relevant directions rather than the trained domain, which is consistent with G being the direction that moves. It is a single, weak result and needs replication, for example on the base checkpoint.

title: A Bayesian Perspective on Generalization and Stochastic Gradient Descent
authors: Samuel L. Smith, Quoc V. Le
finding: Shows that memorizing random labels while generalizing on real labels also occurs in small linear models. It explains this with Bayesian evidence, which penalizes sharp minima and is invariant to parameterization (in its regular, Laplace form). It argues that SGD noise, with scale g = eps(N/B - 1) ~ eps N/B, drives parameters toward high-evidence minima. It predicts and verifies an optimal batch size B_opt proportional to eps N.
relevance: The classical bridge from the sharpness and flatness story to Bayesian selection, and a mechanism for why SGD would find the posterior-preferred solution. It suggests G vs N selection may depend on learning rate and batch size: higher noise should favor the higher-evidence (if lower-complexity) solution. This is testable by sweeping LR and batch size in steering-vector training and measuring the G/N split. The Laplace form fails at degenerate minima, which is why the LLC is preferred.

title: Stochastic Collapse: How Gradient Noise Attracts SGD Dynamics Towards Simpler Subnetworks
authors: Feng Chen, Daniel Kunin, Atsushi Yamamura, Surya Ganguli
finding: Identifies invariant sets (sparse or low-rank subnetworks) that SGD leaves unchanged. SGD is stochastically attracted to them depending on a competition between curvature and gradient noise. More noise strengthens the attraction and can make invariant sets at saddles or local maxima attractive. Trained deep nets show collapse onto simpler subnetworks with vanishing or redundant neurons, and this helps generalization in a linear teacher-student setting. The analysis also explains why a long early phase of large-learning-rate training helps later generalization.
relevance: Gives a dynamical, non-Bayesian route to the same conclusion: SGD noise pushes toward degenerate, simpler parameter sets. If G corresponds to an invariant or low-rank set already present (one pre-existing persona direction) and N requires extra gating structure, noise-driven collapse favors G. This complements the SLT posterior argument with a mechanism for SGD.

title: Empirical Analysis of the Hessian of Over-Parametrized Neural Networks
authors: Levent Sagun, Utku Evci, V. Ugur Guney, Yann Dauphin, Leon Bottou
finding: The Hessian spectrum in deep nets is a large bulk near zero plus a few data-dependent outliers. Adding parameters mostly scales the bulk, while changing the data mostly changes the outliers, which are tied to the covariance of output gradients. Small- and large-batch solutions that look like different basins are connected through flat regions. The authors argue that classical basin-width intuitions need rethinking because of over-parametrization and redundancy.
relevance: Empirical grounding for why max-eigenvalue sharpness is an incomplete lens on G vs N.
