Most directions are degenerate, and the difference between solutions may live in the near-zero bulk that lambda_max ignores but the LLC captures. It also implies that G and N fine-tunes may sit in one connected flat region, which can be checked with linear connectivity between G and N steering vectors.

title: Bayesian Model Selection, the Marginal Likelihood, and Generalization
authors: Sanae Lotfi, Pavel Izmailov, Gregory Benton, Micah Goldblum, Andrew Gordon Wilson
finding: Reviews what the marginal likelihood (Bayesian evidence) does well, such as learning constraints and testing hypotheses, then argues it is a poor proxy for generalization. It answers 'how likely is the training data under the prior', not 'how well will the posterior predict new data'. As a result it can be negatively correlated with generalization, which matters for neural architecture search, and it can cause both underfitting and overfitting in hyperparameter learning. The authors revisit its connection to PAC-Bayes bounds and propose a conditional marginal likelihood that tracks generalization better and scales to settings such as deep kernel learning.
relevance: Counterevidence for leaning on free energy. Even if the posterior prefers G (higher evidence, lower complexity), that does not by itself mean G is the better generalizer. Evidence measures prior-predictive fit, which depends on the prior: here the pretrained model, so it is circular for 'pretraining determines EM'. It also warns against treating any lower-LLC finding as a full explanation without testing selection directly.

title: The Implicit Bias of Gradient Descent on Separable Data
authors: Daniel Soudry, Elad Hoffer, Mor Shpigel Nacson, Suriya Gunasekar, Nathan Srebro
finding: For unregularized logistic regression with homogeneous linear predictors on linearly separable data, the GD iterate's norm diverges and its direction converges to the hard-margin (L2) SVM solution. The result extends to other monotone decreasing losses with infimum at infinity (the analysis relies on an exponential-tail condition), to multiclass problems, and to training one weight layer of a deep net in a restricted setting. Directional convergence is very slow, only logarithmic in the convergence of the loss. The authors use this to explain why continuing to train after zero training error can help even when validation loss rises. The theory is for linear models.
relevance: This is the base case for 'the dataset admits many solutions and the optimizer picks one'. With cross-entropy and no explicit regularizer, the norm keeps growing while the direction settles slowly toward a geometry-defined optimum, not toward whatever fits pretraining best. Two consequences for finding (5). First, comparing G and N at the end of training mixes direction with how far the norm has grown. Second, G's direction may still be drifting at the end of a short run, so checking cos(v_t, v_final) across checkpoints is worthwhile. Caveat: a single steering vector is probably not in the separable regime (see Ji and Telgarsky), so this result fits LoRA and full fine-tuning more directly than the steering-vector experiments.

title: Risk and parameter convergence of logistic regression (COLT version: The implicit bias of gradient descent on nonseparable data)
authors: Ziwei Ji, Matus Telgarsky
finding: On general, possibly non-separable data, GD on logistic regression follows a unique ray determined by the data. Its direction is the max-margin predictor of a maximal linearly separable subset of the data, reached at rate O(ln ln t / ln t). The ray generally does not pass through the origin. Its offset is the bounded global optimum of the risk on the remaining data, which GD recovers at rate O((ln t)^2/sqrt(t)). The result is for linear models only.
relevance: This partly cuts against the working hypothesis's framing for the steering-vector experiments. One 4096-dimensional vector fit to thousands of token-level targets is almost surely in the non-separable regime. The finite part of the solution is then essentially a unique risk minimizer, with no tie among many zero-loss solutions to break. In that regime, G beating N is better described as G being a lower-loss basin (N exists only under a KL penalty) than as implicit tie-breaking. The result also gives one reading of G's larger final norm: whatever part of the targets is 'separable' along G keeps pulling the norm up. Decomposing G into a converged component and a growing component would test this.

title: Characterizing Implicit Bias in Terms of Optimization Geometry
authors: Suriya Gunasekar, Jason Lee, Daniel Soudry, Nathan Srebro
finding: The paper covers underdetermined linear regression and separable linear classification. For losses with a unique finite root (e.g., squared loss), if mirror descent converges to an interpolant, that interpolant minimizes the Bregman divergence D_psi(w, w0) to the initialization (the min-potential interpolant when w0 = argmin psi). This holds independent of step size, and with momentum when started appropriately. For natural gradient descent, step size affects the limit, and only an infinitesimal-step characterization is obtained. For steepest descent in regression, step size affects the limit, and even with infinitesimal steps the expected min-norm characterization fails. For separable classification with the exponential loss and bounded step sizes, steepest descent under any norm drives the normalized margin to the max margin in that norm. Its direction converges to the max-margin solution when that solution is unique, independent of initialization. AdaGrad's bias is shown to depend on initial conditions, including step size, even for monotone losses. Matrix factorization is also treated: v2 fixed a proof bug and only characterizes the factor matrices. All results are for linear predictors.
relevance: This directly answers the question 'which direction does the optimizer pick?' for the project's setup. Starting from zero init, the preferred solution is min-norm or max-margin in the optimizer's own geometry: L2 for GD, roughly L-infinity for sign or Adam-like updates. So 'G is preferred over N' is only meaningful relative to a geometry. That gives a cheap test: retrain G and N with SGD, sign descent and Adam and check whether the preference or its size changes. It also gives theoretical grounding for Evil Spectra's optimizer effect. The regression result is a caution: for squared-loss-like objectives the selected solution can depend on step size, not just on the norm.

title: Implicit Regularization in Matrix Factorization
authors: Suriya Gunasekar, Blake Woodworth, Srinadh Bhojanapalli, Behnam Neyshabur, Nathan Srebro
finding: For underdetermined quadratic objectives over a matrix X, optimized by GD on a full-dimensional factorization (X = UU^T), the authors conjecture that small step sizes and initialization near the origin lead to the minimum nuclear-norm solution. They give empirical and partial theoretical support; the proof covers only restricted cases, such as commuting measurement matrices. In that regime the factorization acts as an implicit regularizer. It is stated as a conjecture. Later work questions it: Arora et al. 2019 argue that deep matrix factorization is not captured by nuclear norm, and Razin and Cohen 2020 give counterexamples to any norm-based account.
relevance: LoRA adapters (B·A from a small or zero init) are exactly a matrix factorization trained by GD, so this predicts a pull toward low-nuclear-norm, low-rank updates. That plausibly favors a single shared direction (G) over a solution that has to encode behavior gated by context (N). It gives a parameterization-level reason why rank-1 LoRA suffices for EM. It does not apply to an additive steering vector, which is unfactorized, so the bias in the steering-vector experiments has to come from somewhere else (optimizer geometry, curvature).

title: Implicit Regularization in Deep Learning May Not Be Explainable by Norms
authors: Noam Razin, Nadav Cohen
finding: The authors prove that there are natural matrix factorization (matrix completion via linear networks) problems where the implicit regularization of gradient-based training drives all norms and quasi-norms toward infinity. So no norm-minimization account can describe it in general. They propose rank minimization as the more useful interpretation, and experiments suggest this extends to a certain class of nonlinear networks. The theory concerns specific, stylized matrix factorization settings.
relevance: This cuts against using norm as the explanatory currency, which includes Soligo et al.'s 'efficiency' metric, loss divided by parameter norm. If the true bias is toward low rank or low complexity rather than low norm, G may be preferred because it is the simpler or lower-rank way to fit the data, and comparing norms may not identify the mechanism. It also implies that G ending with a larger norm in finding (5) does not by itself count against G being the implicitly preferred solution.

title: Gradient Descent Maximizes the Margin of Homogeneous Neural Networks
authors: Kaifeng Lyu, Jian Li
finding: The setting is any positively homogeneous network, possibly non-smooth, such as ReLU or LeakyReLU fully connected and convolutional nets, trained by gradient flow or GD on exponential or logistic (cross-entropy) loss. Once training loss falls below a threshold, a smoothed normalized margin increases monotonically. Both it and the normalized margin converge to the objective value at a KKT point of a margin-maximization problem. KKT points need not be global max-margin solutions. The results generalize earlier linear and deep-linear results and come with convergence rates. Experiments on MNIST and CIFAR-10 support the theory. Transformers with LayerNorm and softmax are not homogeneous, so the theory does not directly apply to them.
relevance: This extends the max-margin selection story from linear models to nonlinear nets. It predicts that training after the loss is already low keeps rotating the solution toward a margin-maximizing direction. One prediction for the project is that G's direction may keep sharpening late in training while the loss changes little, which can be checked from checkpoints. The homogeneity assumption fails for OLMo, so this is guidance on what to measure rather than a prediction for the model.

title: Flavors of Margin: Implicit Bias of Steepest Descent in Homogeneous Neural Networks
authors: Nikolaos Tsilivis, Eitan Gronich, Julia Kempe, Gal Vardi (JMLR / arXiv v4); ICLR 2025 version: Nikolaos Tsilivis, Gal Vardi, Julia Kempe
finding: The paper studies steepest descent with infinitesimal step size under a general norm (covering GD, sign descent, and coordinate descent) in deep homogeneous networks. An algorithm-dependent geometric margin starts increasing once training accuracy is perfect. Every limit point of the trajectory is a KKT point (generalized stationary point) of the margin-maximization problem for that norm. Experiments relate these biases to Adam; the extended JMLR/arXiv version also relates them to Shampoo. The theory requires homogeneity, gradient flow, and perfect training accuracy.
relevance: This is the nonlinear-network version of the optimizer-geometry argument. Different optimizers maximize different margins, so they can select different solutions among those that fit the narrow data. That is the cleanest theoretical account of why EM rates vary about 7x across optimizers (Evil Spectra). It turns the gold question into a testable claim: G is easy for optimizer X if G has a larger X-margin, that is, lower loss per unit X-norm, than N. Soligo et al.'s efficiency curves can be recomputed with L-infinity or spectral norms in place of L2.

title: Implicit Bias of AdamW: L-infinity Norm Constrained Optimization
authors: Shuo Xie, Zhiyuan Li
finding: In the full-batch setting, if AdamW converges under a non-increasing learning-rate schedule whose partial sums diverge, it converges to a KKT point of the original loss subject to ||theta||_inf <= 1/lambda, where lambda is the weight decay factor. The analysis treats Adam as smoothed SignGD, which is normalized steepest descent in L-infinity. It also links normalized steepest descent with weight decay to Frank-Wolfe. The result is conditional on convergence and is full-batch only.
relevance: EM fine-tunes are typically trained with AdamW, as in Soligo et al.'s 8-bit AdamW with weight decay 0.01, so the implicit constraint is an L-infinity box, not an L2 ball. A direction spread over many residual coordinates costs less under L-infinity than one concentrated on a few coordinates, for example the outlier or 'rogue' dimensions of the residual stream. That bears on interpreting finding (3), where G captures more pretraining variance. Part of G's character could come from Adam's coordinate-wise geometry interacting with the residual-stream basis. Related work: Wang et al. 2021 (arXiv 2012.06244, ICML 2021) find that Adam maximizes the L2 margin like GD. That analysis relies on a non-negligible epsilon, and Zhang, Zou and Cao (arXiv 2406.10650) get an L-infinity margin when epsilon is ignored. So which regime applies depends on gradient size relative to epsilon.

title: Implicit Bias of Spectral Descent and Muon on Multiclass Separable Data
authors: Chen Fan, Mark Schmidt, Christos Thrampoulidis
finding: For multiclass linear classification with cross-entropy on separable data, p-norm normalized steepest descent (NSD) and normalized momentum descent (NMD) converge, with rates, to max-margin solutions measured by the p-norm (entry-wise or Schatten) of the classifier matrix. The analysis reduces to the max-norm case. Spectral Descent and Muon converge to spectral-norm max-margin solutions. Extending to preconditioning, Adam converges to the max-norm max-margin solution. Results are for linear, separable, multiclass models only.
relevance: This gives exact predictions for which solution each optimizer picks when many weight matrices fit the data: L2 for GD, max-norm for Adam, spectral norm for Muon. It is the theory that would explain Evil Spectra's optimizer ranking. Whether Muon's spectral-margin solution is less EM-like is an open, testable question. For the gold question, it implies 'EM is easy' may be partly a fact about Adam's max-norm geometry rather than only about pretraining priors.

title: The Spectral Dynamics and Noise Geometry of Muon
authors: Pierfrancesco Beneventano, Mahmoud Abdelmoneum, Tomaso Poggio
finding: Muon's polar-factor update keeps the gradient's singular directions but flattens its singular-value spectrum. Under alignment assumptions, the authors argue the polar update is the one-step entropy-maximizing bounded update that uses those directions. In underdetermined regression they derive singular-value dynamics for an idealized continuous-time (projected self-polar) flow. A sign condition that depends on the measurement geometry decides when the normalized spectrum moves toward equal nonzero singular values. This is the opposite of what nuclear-norm minimization favors, so the authors argue the common low-rank interpretation of Muon is ruled out. In a single-seed 124M NanoGPT run, Muon beats AdamW on validation loss and keeps higher stable or effective rank. In a matched small ViT/CIFAR-10 control the ranking reverses, so the benefit depends on the regime. This is a small-scale v1 preprint (June 2026). Its theorems cover an idealized flow, not literal Muon.
relevance: Evil Spectra attributes Muon's alignment preservation to a more uniform singular-value spectrum in the LoRA adapter, and this paper supplies the mechanism. If EM is carried by one dominant direction (convergent linear representations, rank-1 sufficiency), an optimizer that penalizes concentrated spectra disfavors the single-direction G solution relative to spread-out ones. That suggests G is easy partly because Adam and GD are comfortable with dominant rank-1 updates. Testing EM with Muon-trained LoRA on OLMo would separate a pretraining prior from optimizer-spectrum effects.

title: Old Optimizer, New Norm: An Anthology
authors: Jeremy Bernstein, Laker Newhouse
finding: With their exponential moving averages switched off, Adam, Shampoo and Prodigy are each steepest descent under a particular norm. Adam becomes sign descent (an L-infinity-type norm) and Shampoo becomes spectral-norm descent. The authors argue these are first-order methods that need no convexity or second-order justification. They propose 'metrizing' the architecture, assigning each tensor an operator norm according to its role; for example, linear and embedding layers of the same shape get different norms. It is a conceptual and expository paper, not an empirical study of generalization.
relevance: This is the translation layer from 'which optimizer' to 'which norm defines min-norm or max-margin'. For a single steering vector trained with Adam from zero init, the very first update is roughly proportional to sign(mean gradient). The early direction is therefore basis-dependent and weights every residual coordinate equally, which is very different from GD's step along -g. Before reading finding (3) as evidence of a pretraining prior, it is worth checking how much of G's direction is fixed by that first sign step.

title: Implicit Optimization Bias of Next-Token Prediction in Linear Models
authors: Christos Thrampoulidis
finding: The paper frames next-token prediction (NTP) as cross-entropy over distinct contexts, each with a sparse next-token distribution. It defines NTP-separability conditions under which the loss can reach the data-entropy lower bound. For linear models with fixed context embeddings, GD does two things. In the subspace defined by the contexts' support patterns, it sets the logit differences between in-support tokens to their (finite) log-odds. In the orthogonal subspace, the parameter norm diverges and the direction maximizes an NTP-specific margin. The results assume fixed embeddings and a linear decoder.
relevance: This is the implicit-bias analysis closest to SFT on EM data. It splits the solution into a finite part that matches the data's log-odds and an unboundedly growing part that pushes out-of-support tokens down. For finding (5), G's larger norm may sit in a margin-like component, for example suppressing aligned or refusal continuations, rather than reflecting better fit. Projecting G onto 'in-support logit differences' versus 'out-of-support suppression' directions through the unembedding is a direct test. Broad misalignment could come from that divergent suppression component, which acts on all prompts.

title: When Does Preconditioning Help or Hurt Generalization?
authors: Shun-ichi Amari, Jimmy Ba, Roger Grosse, Xuechen Li, Atsushi Nitanda, Taiji Suzuki, Denny Wu, Ji Xu
finding: The paper gives an exact asymptotic bias-variance decomposition of the generalization error of overparameterized ridgeless regression under a general preconditioner P, with the inverse population Fisher (NGD) as the main example. For positive-definite P the stationary solution is the minimum ||theta||_{P^-1}-norm interpolant, while GD (and the sample Fisher) from zero initialization reach the min-L2 interpolant. Which generalizes better depends on label noise and the signal's 'shape': NGD can achieve lower risk with noisy labels, misspecification or a signal misaligned with the features, and GD is better with clean labels, a well-specified model or an aligned signal. Interpolating between GD and NGD can manage the tradeoff. The theory covers linear ridgeless regression and RKHS kernel regression (where preconditioning can reduce population risk faster), with supporting neural-network experiments.
relevance: This formalizes a mechanistic version of the working hypothesis. Plain GD and Adam favor directions aligned with high-variance or high-Fisher input structure. For a residual steering vector, the relevant 'feature covariance' is the downstream Jacobian or Fisher, which is large in directions the model already relies on, consistent with findings (3) that ablating G raises LM loss. This suggests an interventional test: train G and N with Fisher-whitened (K-FAC or NGD-style) updates. If the preference for G shrinks under whitening, the preference comes from GD geometry interacting with the model's existing sensitivity, which is a causal version of the correlational finding (3).

title: A Continuous-Time View of Early Stopping for Least Squares
authors: Alnur Ali, J. Zico Kolter, Ryan J. Tibshirani
finding: Gradient flow on least squares at time t closely tracks ridge regression with lambda = 1/t. Theorem 1 shows its estimation risk is at most 1.6862 times ridge's for all t >= 0, in finite samples and with no assumptions on the feature matrix X. The same holds for in-sample prediction risk, and for out-of-sample prediction risk in an average (Bayes) sense over a spherical prior on the signal. Empirically the risk curves nearly coincide (max ratio about 1.22 in their example). The paper also gives Marchenko-Pastur limiting risks. It covers linear least squares only.
relevance: For a steering vector from zero init with a fixed step budget, the unregularized G is approximately on an L2-regularized path, while N adds an explicit KL penalty. So G versus N is a comparison between two regularizers, an implicit ridge-like one and an explicit function-space KL, at different effective strengths. That is exactly the direction-versus-size confound in finding (5). The fix it implies is to compare along matched regularization paths or matched norms (Soligo et al.'s efficiency curves), or to train G with an explicit L2 penalty tuned to N's final norm.

title: Gradient Descent Happens in a Tiny Subspace
authors: Guy Gur-Ari, Daniel A. Roberts, Ethan Dyer
finding: After a short period of training, the gradient quickly concentrates in a small subspace spanned by the top Hessian eigenvectors, about as many as there are classes, and that subspace stays mostly preserved over long training. This is illustrated in a solvable classification model. Song, Ahn and Yun ('Does SGD really happen in tiny subspaces?', arXiv 2405.16002, ICLR 2025) find that projecting SGD updates onto this dominant subspace does not further reduce training loss, while projecting the dominant subspace out works just as well. This holds also under EoS-scale learning rates, SAM, momentum and adaptive optimizers. So the alignment appears spurious for optimization progress.
relevance: This suggests a cheap mechanistic test of 'why EM is easy'. Compute the top Hessian or Fisher eigenvectors of the fine-tuning loss with respect to the layer-12 steering vector at v = 0, and of the Dolma LM loss, then measure their cosine with G, N and the initial gradient. If the initial gradient on narrow data already lies along high-curvature pretraining directions that coincide with G, then 'easy' means first-order selection at init. The Song et al. result is a caution that alignment with the top eigenspace does not by itself show the dynamics depend on it.

title: Implicit regularization for deep neural networks driven by an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck like process
authors: Guy Blanc, Neha Gupta, Gregory Valiant, Paul Valiant
finding: For SGD on squared loss with fresh label noise at each step, the dynamics near a zero-training-error parameter carry an implicit regularizer: the sum over data points of the squared L2 norm of the model output's gradient with respect to parameters. This holds for any connectivity, width, depth or activation. The authors interpret it in matrix sensing, two-layer ReLU networks on 1-D data and two-layer sigmoid networks on a single data point, where it pushes toward 'simple' models. The analysis is local, roughly an eta^-1.6-step window moving about eta^0.4 per Li et al. and Damian et al., and requires interpolation plus injected label noise.
relevance: This is the first precise statement that SGD noise selects, among zero-loss solutions, the one whose outputs are least sensitive to parameters. That is the same property Soligo et al. operationalize as 'stability', meaning robustness to orthogonal perturbations. If G has lower output-parameter sensitivity on the fine-tuning data than N, noise alone would move solutions from N toward G. That is consistent with Soligo's report that narrow models drift to general misalignment once the KL penalty is removed. The zero-loss and label-noise assumptions do not hold for a non-interpolating steering vector, so it is suggestive only there.

title: Label Noise SGD Provably Prefers Flat Global Minimizers
authors: Alex Damian, Tengyu Ma, Jason D. Lee
finding: Label-noise SGD converges to an (epsilon, gamma)-stationary point of L + lambda R. Here lambda = eta sigma^2 / B (step size times label-noise variance over batch size), and R(theta) = -(1/2eta) tr log(I - (eta/2) Hessian), which reduces to (1/4) tr(Hessian) as eta -> 0. The higher-order terms mean larger learning rates penalize large Hessian eigenvalues more than small ones, beyond the linear scaling rule. The result holds over poly(1/eps, 1/gamma) steps starting near an approximate zero-loss minimizer (for example, a kernel-regime solution), not from arbitrary initialization. Under a KL-type assumption it extends Blanc et al.'s local analysis to a global convergence result. Extensions cover classification with general losses, momentum and general noise covariance. Label noise is injected, not intrinsic.
relevance: This gives a quantitative and testable prediction. If G is the flatter solution of the narrow fine-tuning objective, the G-over-N preference, measured for example by how far an unregularized run's direction moves toward G, should strengthen with larger learning rate and smaller batch size. Single-H100 sweeps on steering vectors would test it. SFT on diverse responses has intrinsic target stochasticity, but treating that as equivalent to injected label noise is not established.

title: What Happens after SGD Reaches Zero Loss? -- A Mathematical Framework
authors: Zhiyuan Li, Tianhao Wang, Sanjeev Arora
finding: With a small learning rate eta, SGD first tracks GD to a manifold of minimizers, after which gradient noise drives a slow drift along the manifold. Adapting Katzenberger (1991), they characterize this drift by a limiting SDE determined by the loss and the noise covariance. The analysis is global, valid for Theta(eta^-2) steps rather than the eta^-1.6 of Blanc et al., and allows arbitrary noise covariance. For label noise, the limit is a Riemannian gradient flow that decreases tr(Hessian) on the manifold. Application: from arbitrarily large initialization, label-noise SGD escapes the kernel regime and learns a kappa-sparse overparameterized linear model with O(kappa ln d) samples, which is minimax optimal, while GD initialized in the kernel regime needs Omega(d).
relevance: This is the mechanistic link the user asked about between sharpness and solution selection: among equal-loss solutions, noise slowly selects low trace(H). The time scale matters for the gold question. The drift is second order and takes about eta^-2 steps, while EM appears within short fine-tunes with a rank-1 adapter or a single vector. So EM's 'easiness', meaning speed, more likely reflects first-order selection (gradient alignment, efficiency at init), with flatness drift explaining later stabilization and the N-to-G drift after the KL penalty is removed. Tracking cos(v_t, G) over steps would show which time scale dominates.

title: On the Origin of Implicit Regularization in Stochastic Gradient Descent
authors: Samuel L. Smith, Benoit Dherin, David G. T. Barrett, Soham De
finding: For SGD with random shuffling and a small but finite learning rate, the mean iterate stays close to gradient flow on a modified loss. That loss adds an implicit regularizer penalizing the norms of the minibatch gradients, whose scale is roughly proportional to learning rate over batch size for small batches. Adding the regularizer explicitly improves test accuracy when the learning rate is small. This is motivated by the observation that the test-optimal learning rate often exceeds the train-loss-optimal one. The derivation is a leading-order backward-error expansion.
relevance: The implicit penalty on per-minibatch gradient norms favors solutions that fit every minibatch consistently. A single shared behavioral shift (G), which lowers loss similarly on every bad-advice example, plausibly has lower across-batch gradient dispersion than a narrow solution that must condition on context. This is checkable directly by computing the variance of minibatch gradients at G and at N. It also predicts that the G preference depends on the learning-rate-to-batch ratio.

title: Implicit Gradient Regularization
authors: David G. T. Barrett, Benoit Dherin
finding: Backward error analysis shows that full-batch GD with finite step size h follows, to first order in h, gradient flow on a modified loss L + (h/4)||grad L||^2. This implicit gradient regularization (IGR) penalizes trajectories with large loss gradients. The authors show empirically that it biases GD toward flat minima with lower test error that are more robust to parameter noise. Adding the IGR term as an explicit regularizer reproduces the effect.
relevance: It shows a flatness bias exists even without minibatch noise. So any G-versus-N flatness difference would be amplified by larger step sizes even in deterministic fine-tuning. Together with Smith et al. 2021, it gives a concrete regularizer that can be switched on or off explicitly to test whether a flatness preference causes EM's generalization.

title: Self-Stabilization: The Implicit Bias of Gradient Descent at the Edge of Stability
authors: Alex Damian, Eshaan Nichani, Jason D. Lee
finding: A cubic Taylor expansion of the loss explains edge-of-stability dynamics. When iterates diverge along the top Hessian eigenvector, the cubic term reduces sharpness until stability returns, which the authors call self-stabilization. As a result, full-batch GD at the edge of stability implicitly follows projected GD under the constraint lambda_max <= 2/eta. The paper predicts loss, sharpness and deviation from that constrained trajectory, verifies the predictions empirically in standard settings and proves them under mild conditions.
relevance: This turns 'sharpness explains selection' into a hard threshold: at learning rate eta, GD cannot settle in solutions with lambda_max above 2/eta. If N is sharper than G (Soligo's perturbation result suggests so), there is a range of learning rates at which N is dynamically inaccessible without explicit regularization. Measuring lambda_max of the fine-tuning loss at G and at N against 2/eta, or the preconditioned sharpness for Adam, tests this directly.

title: The alignment property of SGD noise and how it helps select flat minima: A stability analysis
authors: Lei Wu, Mingze Wang, Weijie Su
finding: For overparameterized models with square loss, a global minimum that is linearly stable under SGD must have a Hessian Frobenius norm of at most O(sqrt(B)/eta); otherwise SGD escapes it exponentially fast. The bound is independent of model size and sample size. The key ingredient is the 'alignment property': SGD noise concentrates in sharp directions, with magnitude proportional to the loss. This property is proved for linear networks and random-feature models, verified empirically for nonlinear networks, and supported by CIFAR-10 experiments.
relevance: This is the stability-based account of flat-minimum selection that Soligo et al. cite for their 'stability' metric. It supplies a falsifiable bound: if N's Hessian norm on the fine-tuning loss exceeds the SGD stability bound at the learning rate and batch size used, N cannot be a resting point of unregularized SGD. That would explain why N needs a KL penalty to persist. It holds for square loss near global minima, so applying it to cross-entropy SFT with a non-interpolating steering vector is an extrapolation.

title: Fantastic Generalization Measures and Where to Find Them
authors: Yiding Jiang, Behnam Neyshabur, Hossein Mobahi, Dilip Krishnan, Samy Bengio
finding: The study covers more than 40 complexity measures, with controlled single-hyperparameter variation to separate causal from spurious correlations. The main analysis uses 2,187 (3^7) CIFAR-10 CNNs; seed repeats and an SVHN replication bring the total to more than 10,000 models. Sharpness-based measures (PAC-Bayes bounds and Keskar-style sharpness) perform best overall, and the magnitude-aware sharpness 1/alpha' has the highest conditional mutual information with generalization. Many norm-based measures, notably the product of spectral norms, correlate negatively with generalization, especially when optimization injects stochasticity. Some optimization-based measures are predictive: end-of-training gradient variance correlates positively across every hyperparameter type, while slower early-phase optimization goes with better generalization. Generalization here means the in-distribution test gap of small image-classification CNNs.
relevance: This is the canonical large-scale evidence that perturbation-based sharpness predicts generalization better than parameter norms. It supports treating Soligo's perturbation-robustness 'stability' as the more principled of their two metrics, and it weakens loss-per-norm 'efficiency' as a causal criterion. The finding that gradient variance and optimization speed predict generalization fits the hypothesis that EM is selected because it is learned fastest. Caveat: EM is out-of-distribution behavioral generalization in an LLM, and there is no established bridge from in-distribution CNN results to it.

title: On the Maximum Hessian Eigenvalue and Generalization
authors: Simran Kaur, Jeremy Cohen, Zachary C. Lipton
finding: lambda_max does not consistently track generalization. (1) Larger learning rates lower lambda_max at every batch size, but their generalization benefit sometimes vanishes at large batch sizes (for example, a non-BN VGG in the large-batch setting). (2) Scaling batch size and learning rate together changes lambda_max without changing generalization. (3) SAM lowers lambda_max at every batch size, but its generalization benefit also vanishes at larger batch sizes. (4) Excessively high dropout lowers lambda_max but hurts generalization. (5) Batch norm improves generalization without consistently lowering lambda_max. The authors still affirm the benefits of large learning rates and SAM for minibatch SGD, but argue that the GD-SGD discrepancy limits lambda_max as an explanation of generalization.
relevance: This directly cautions the user's 'max eigenvalue of the Hessian explains generalization' intuition. Even if G turns out to have lower lambda_max than N, that would not show flatness causes the preference. Interventions such as SAM, learning rate and batch sweeps, and explicit flatness penalties are needed, and the confounds this paper documents, such as batch size, should be controlled in any sharpness-based story for EM.

title: Entropic Confinement and Mode Connectivity in Overparameterized Neural Networks
authors: Luca Di Carlo, Chase Goddard, David J. Schwab
finding: Minima are often connected by low-loss paths, yet optimization usually stays within one basin. The paper takes this confinement as a premise from prior work and explains it with entropic barriers. Along minimum-energy and linear paths between minima, curvature (Hessian trace and top eigenvalue) rises away from the endpoints while the loss stays nearly flat. Noisy dynamics therefore feel effective forces back toward the endpoints. These barriers outlast energetic barriers and shape where solutions end up late in training. The evidence is mainly empirical, on CIFAR-10/100 with Wide ResNet-16-4 and ResNet-20/110. The dynamics experiments use SGD projected onto the path. A 2D Brownian toy model with effective potential T ln g motivates the mechanism, but nothing is proved for deep networks.
relevance: This gives a mechanism for persistence that is separate from initial selection. Once fine-tuning lands near G, curvature-induced entropic forces can keep it there even if a low-loss path to a narrow solution exists. Soligo's observation runs the other way: N drifts to G once the KL penalty is removed. Under this paper's lens, that means the KL penalty, not an entropic barrier, is what holds N in place, and G is the higher-entropy, flatter attractor. Measuring curvature along the linear path from N to G would test this directly.

title: The Rich and the Simple: On the Implicit Bias of Adam and SGD
authors: Bhavya Vasudeva, Jung Whan Lee, Vatsal Sharan, Mahdi Soltanolkotabi
finding: The setting is a two-layer ReLU network with a fixed output layer, trained on Gaussian-cluster binary classification. GD shows simplicity bias: it learns a linear decision boundary with a suboptimal margin. Adam resists this. It learns richer, more diverse features and a nonlinear (piecewise-linear) boundary closer to Bayes-optimal, with provably lower test error under stated conditions. The theory uses closed-form population gradients in the infinite-sample, d=2 limit. It covers signGD (Adam with beta1=beta2=0), plus a near-zero-variance toy case for Adam with beta near 1. Experiments include colored MNIST, Dominoes, Waterbirds, CelebA, MultiNLI and CivilComments. In these, Adam gives better worst-group accuracy than SGD under spurious-correlation shifts. The authors note that simplicity bias can still help in-distribution.
relevance: This cuts both ways for the project. If G is the 'simple' solution (one shared direction) and N the 'rich' context-conditional one, simplicity bias predicts SGD favors G more than Adam does. But Evil Spectra finds Adam-family optimizers among the most EM-prone and Muon the least. So 'simplicity bias' alone does not predict EM's optimizer dependence, and a geometry-specific margin account (Fan et al., Tsilivis et al.) may fit better. It is worth checking directly whether SGD-trained steering vectors show more or less EM than Adam-trained ones on OLMo.

title: Coherent Gradients: An Approach to Understanding Generalization in Gradient Descent-based Optimization
authors: Satrajit Chatterjee
finding: Proposes the Coherent Gradients hypothesis. Gradients of similar examples are similar, so the summed gradient is strongest in directions where per-example contributions reinforce, and GD preferentially makes changes that help many examples at once. The support is heuristic arguments plus perturbative experiments on MNIST with small fully connected ReLU networks, including label-noise variants (25 to 100% randomized labels). The paper proposes winsorized (per-example gradient clipped) GD, which reduces overfitting at some cost to training accuracy. No language models are studied; BERT appears only as future work.
relevance: This is the core mechanistic candidate for why G beats N. Every EM example, in every domain, shares the misaligned-advice attribute, so per-example gradients add up along a shared direction and partly cancel along topic-specific ones. Applied to the layer-12 steering vector, this predicts that the mean per-example gradient projects more strongly onto G than onto N, and that G is approached earlier in training. The steering-vector gradient is just a d-dimensional summed residual gradient, so grad_align.py can test this cheaply. Soligo et al. App. K.3 already report gradients more similar to G than to N throughout training, which is the aggregate version of this test. CGH adds the per-example decomposition: is G's advantage carried by many examples or by a few?

title: Weak and Strong Gradient Directions: Explaining Memorization, Generalization, and Hardness of Examples at Scale
authors: Piotr Zielinski, Shankar Krishnan, Satrajit Chatterjee
finding: Tests CGH at ImageNet scale (ResNet, Inception, VGG). Suppressing weak gradient directions with coordinate-wise median-of-means (M3, and the cheaper RM3, which reuses the previous two steps' gradients) substantially reduces memorization and overfitting without needing per-example gradients. A second test uses no label noise: easy, early-learned examples are argued to share more structure, and the experiments show they generalize better among themselves than hard examples do. The evidence is from vision only, and the robust-mean methods are an intervention, not a direct measurement.
relevance: This gives a causal intervention that fits the EM setup. If G is a strong direction (supported by most examples) and N's extra, domain-specific components are weak directions, then median-of-means training on the EM data should keep or increase broad misalignment while suppressing the narrow-only component. A per-domain median (medical, finance, sports) is the natural EM analogue. It also predicts that the examples learned earliest are the persona-laden ones, which can be checked with per-example loss trajectories.

title: Making Coherence Out of Nothing At All: Measuring the Evolution of Gradient Alignment
authors: Satrajit Chatterjee, Piotr Zielinski
finding: Introduces m-coherence, the average number of examples in a sample of size m that benefit from a small step along one example's gradient. It is cheap, interpretable and closely related to gradient diversity. In ResNet and Inception models trained on ImageNet and label-noise variants, m-coherence on random labels rises into the hundreds during training instead of staying near 1. So overparameterized networks find shared patterns even when generalization is impossible, which supports CGH but also exposes gaps in it.
relevance: This gives a ready metric for grad_align.py: compute m-coherence of per-example steering-vector gradients restricted to span(G) versus span(N). It also cuts against the working hypothesis: high coherence does not by itself show a semantically general solution. A shared direction can arise from fitting itself, or from shared format. Coherence along G therefore needs a baseline, such as an aligned counterpart dataset with the same prompts and format.

title: On the Generalization Mystery in Deep Learning
authors: Satrajit Chatterjee, Piotr Zielinski
finding: A consolidated argument that per-example gradient coherence explains how GD selects a well-generalizing solution among many that fit the data. The chain is coherence, then algorithmic stability, then generalization, with a bound in terms of a normalized coherence metric α. α differs sharply between real and random datasets for ResNet-50 and AlexNet on ImageNet, MNIST MLPs and toy linear models. The same lens explains early learning of easy examples, early stopping and learning from noisy labels. It motivates winsorized GD and median-of-means (M3) to reduce memorization. The authors survey alternative theories and argue this one is the most viable. The evidence is vision-only (no NLP), and the claims about competing theories are argumentative.
relevance: This frames the gold question exactly: many solutions fit the EM data, so why does GD pick G? The answer it offers is that G is the solution supported by the most coherent per-example gradients. It is the strongest classical statement of the mechanism our slice proposes. It also implies that early stopping should not prevent G, since coherent directions come first. Overtrained-Not-Misaligned (already listed) reports the opposite ordering at the behavioral level, which is a tension to resolve.

title: Stiffness: A New Perspective on Generalization in Neural Networks
authors: Stanislav Fort, Paweł Krzysztof Nowak, Stanislaw Jastrzebski, Srini Narayanan
finding: Defines stiffness: how a small gradient step on one example changes the loss on another. Higher stiffness is suggested to indicate features that generalize. Stiffness depends on class membership, input distance, training time and learning rate; higher learning rates bias toward lower, more local stiffness. On CIFAR-100 the stiffness matrix shows super-class structure. Tests cover MNIST, Fashion-MNIST and CIFAR-10/100 with FC and conv nets, plus a transformer NLP model. It is an unrefereed preprint.
relevance: This gives a directly computable cross-domain stiffness matrix for EM. Does a step on a bad-medical example lower loss on risky-finance, extreme-sports and general misaligned answers more than on aligned ones? Persona-level (super-class-like) block structure across topic boundaries would be the stiffness signature of G. Restricting the step to N should give a more block-diagonal, domain-local stiffness.

title: A Closer Look at Memorization in Deep Networks
authors: Devansh Arpit, Stanislaw Jastrzebski, Nicolas Ballas, David Krueger, Emmanuel Bengio, Maxinder S. Kanwal, Tegan Maharaj, Asja Fischer, Aaron Courville, Yoshua Bengio, Simon Lacoste-Julien
finding: Deep nets can memorize noise but learn simple, shared patterns in real data first. Gradient-based optimization behaves qualitatively differently on real data than on noise. Appropriately tuned explicit regularization, such as dropout, can impede fitting noise without hurting real-data performance. So dataset-independent measures of effective capacity are unlikely to explain generalization under gradient-based training.
relevance: This is the foundational evidence for patterns-before-memorization. It is the analogue of the claim that the shared misaligned attribute is fit before topic-specific details. It also predicts that regularizers which hinder example-specific fitting should hurt N more than G. That is a cheap check, though not a strong one, because the EM data is not noise.

title: Understanding Why Neural Networks Generalize Well Through GSNR of Parameters
authors: Jinlong Liu, Guoqing Jiang, Yunzhi Bai, Ting Chen, Huayan Wang
finding: Defines the per-parameter gradient signal-to-noise ratio (squared mean gradient over gradient variance across data). Higher GSNR during training is linked to a smaller generalization gap through a one-step generalization ratio. The link assumes a non-overfitting regime (train and test mean gradients identically distributed), small learning rates, full-batch GD and large n, and it holds best early in training. The authors argue deep nets' GD dynamics, unlike shallow models, produce large GSNR. Experiments use MNIST and CIFAR-10 CNNs, a toy regression and a ResNet18 GSNR curve.
relevance: GSNR is a natural one-number statistic for grad_align.py: compute the GSNR of per-example steering-vector gradients projected onto G versus onto N, overall and within each domain. The coherent-gradient story predicts higher GSNR along G. Comparing it on Dolma documents, using pretraining-loss gradients, would test whether G is also a high-signal direction for pretraining text. That would be a gradient-level counterpart to our variance and ablation findings.

title: SGD on Neural Networks Learns Functions of Increasing Complexity
authors: Preetum Nakkiran, Gal Kaplun, Dimitris Kalimeris, Tristan Yang, Benjamin L. Edelman, Fred Zhang, Boaz Barak (NeurIPS proceedings order: Kalimeris, Kaplun, Nakkiran, Edelman, Yang, Barak, Haofeng Zhang)
finding: Early in training, almost all of SGD's performance gain is explained by a linear classifier, and later training adds increasing complexity. The early-learned linear function is retained even at zero training error. Uses a conditional-mutual-information measure of how much one classifier explains another, on real and synthetic classification tasks, with theory in a simplified model.
relevance: This supports a learned-first-and-retained reading. If G is the simple, shared component of the EM dataset, it should dominate early and persist even after N-like topic-specific detail is fit. That explains why KL regularization only partly removes it (our finding 2). It is about simplicity rather than coherence, so it is a complementary rather than identical mechanism.

title: Learning explanations that are hard to vary
authors: Giambattista Parascandolo, Alexander Neitz, Antonio Orvieto, Luigi Gresele, Bernhard Schölkopf
finding: Argues that averaging per-example gradients acts like a logical OR, which can yield memorization and patchwork solutions instead of invariances. Formalizes Invariant Learning Consistency, a measure of how consistently a loss minimum is found across environments. Proposes AND-mask, which masks gradient components whose signs disagree across examples or environments, above a threshold. AND-mask focuses learning on invariances and reduces memorization on a synthetic task, CIFAR-10 and CoinRun behavioral cloning. The authors note it is one of several ways to raise consistency and not universally practical.
relevance: It offers a sharp conceptual lens. N is plausibly a patchwork (an OR of domain-specific fixes), while G is the AND across the medical, finance and sports environments. AND-masking gradients across domains should push fine-tuning even more strongly toward G. Their consistency score for minima could be computed for G and N directly. It also suggests that standard averaging is not what favors G, since averaging allows patchwork. That is a useful nuance to the claim that the gradients add up.

title: Gradient Matching for Domain Generalization
authors: Yuge Shi, Jeffrey Seely, Philip H.S. Torr, N. Siddharth, Awni Hannun, Nicolas Usunier, Gabriel Synnaeve
finding: Proposes inter-domain gradient matching (IDGM), which maximizes the inner product between gradients from different training domains to encourage domain-invariant features. Fish is a first-order, Reptile-style approximation that avoids second-order derivatives. It is competitive on WILDS (best on 4 of 6 datasets) and on DomainBed. The conclusion notes that it struggles to outperform ERM when there are many domains, for example iWildCam (324 domains) and Amazon (7,676).
relevance: It formalizes the claim that the cross-domain gradient inner product selects features shared across domains. For EM, compute the inter-domain gradient inner products (medical·finance, medical·sports, ...) at the base checkpoint and decompose them into G and N components. A positive, G-dominated cross-domain inner product would be direct evidence that G is the invariant feature GD amplifies. Running Fish on the three EM domains is a possible way to induce G even more strongly.

title: Gradient Surgery for Multi-Task Learning
authors: Tianhe Yu, Saurabh Kumar, Abhishek Gupta, Sergey Levine, Karol Hausman, Chelsea Finn
finding: Identifies three conditions of the multi-task optimization landscape under which conflicting task gradients cause harmful interference. PCGrad projects a task's gradient onto the normal plane of any conflicting task's gradient, which substantially improves efficiency and performance in multi-task supervised learning and RL. It is model-agnostic and combines with existing multi-task architectures.
relevance: It gives a gradient-conflict framing of how N is made. The Soligo-style KL penalty creates a second objective whose gradient conflicts with the task gradient along G. N is roughly what is left after that conflict is resolved. A PCGrad-style projection of the EM-task gradient against the KL or general-data gradient is an alternative, more interpretable way to construct a narrow solution and measure its cost. It also suggests a diagnostic: how often, and how strongly, task and KL gradients conflict, and in which directions.

title: Efficiently Identifying Task Groupings for Multi-Task Learning
authors: Christopher Fifty, Ehsan Amid, Zhe Zhao, Tianhe Yu, Rohan Anil, Chelsea Finn
finding: Defines inter-task affinity: how a lookahead gradient step on one task changes another task's loss, estimated during a single joint training run. It is used to choose task groupings, giving 10.0% lower test loss than training all tasks together on Taskonomy and an 11.6x speedup over a state-of-the-art grouping method. The evaluation is in vision.
relevance: Lookahead affinity is a cleaner, loss-based version of gradient alignment and fits the EM evaluation directly. Measure how one step on a bad-medical batch changes loss on (a) the other EM domains, (b) misaligned answers to general questions, and (c) aligned answers, separately for steps restricted to G versus N. Strong cross-domain and general affinity for G would quantify why G is easy.

title: Training Dynamics Underlying Language Model Scaling Laws: Loss Deceleration and Zero-Sum Learning
authors: Andrei Mircea, Supriyo Chakraborty, Nima Chitsazan, Milind Naphade, Sambit Sahu, Irina Rish, Ekaterina Lobacheva
finding: Early in LM pretraining the loss abruptly decelerates, so the loss curve becomes piecewise linear in log-log space. The authors attribute this to zero-sum learning (ZSL): per-example gradients become systematically opposed, so improving loss on some examples worsens it on others. Scaling up the model lowers the loss at which deceleration happens and improves the log-log rate of improvement afterward. The work studies LM pretraining, not fine-tuning.
relevance: It is a rare demonstration that per-example gradient interference is measurable and consequential in language models. That makes it a methodological precedent for applying grad_align.py to Dolma documents. It raises a testable prediction: if G is a direction pretraining relies on, then pretraining-document gradients along G should be relatively coherent (not zero-sum), consistent with G-ablation raising LM loss more than N-ablation. Our ablation result is correlational, and this would add a gradient-level measure.

title: Implicit meta-learning may lead language models to trust more reliable sources
authors: Dmitrii Krasheninnikov, Egor Krasheninnikov, Bruno Kacper Mlodozeniec, Tegan Maharaj, David Krueger
finding: In a synthetic fine-tuning set, random tags mark which data is useful. Later fine-tuning then internalizes tagged content more, which the authors call implicit meta-learning (IML). The effect appears in pretrained LLMs, in models trained from scratch and on an MNIST-based vision task, and it is stronger for larger models and smaller batches. Section 5 offers two non-exclusive hypotheses. One is gradient alignment through SGD's implicit penalty on gradient variance (Smith et al. 2021); the other is selective retrieval. Measured gradient cosines differ between tagged subsets, and full-batch training removes IML. But overall performance also drops in full-batch training, so the authors say they cannot attribute IML to SGD's implicit bias.
relevance: It is the closest LLM precedent for invoking gradient alignment to explain a surprising, broad generalization from fine-tuning data. The batch-size dependence it reports is the kind of signature to look for in EM. If EM's G preference grows at smaller batch sizes, that favors the implicit-regularization version of the gradient-coherence account.

title: Estimating Training Data Influence by Tracing Gradient Descent
authors: Garima Pruthi, Frederick Liu, Mukund Sundararajan, Satyen Kale
finding: TracIn estimates a training example's influence on a test prediction by summing, across saved checkpoints, the learning-rate-weighted dot product of the training and test loss gradients. It is a first-order approximation that needs only gradients and checkpoints, can be restricted to selected layers, and works for any model trained with SGD or a variant. It ignores higher-order interactions and depends on which checkpoints are used.
relevance: This is the missing root of the gradient-similarity attribution line, between influence functions and LESS. It is used, in cosine form at the final checkpoint, by the EM attribution paper already listed (Unequal Influence). For our project it gives the principled form of the pretraining-to-fine-tuning overlap. A Dolma document's influence on EM is the checkpoint-summed alignment of its LM-loss gradient with the EM fine-tuning gradient. This is a gradient-based alternative to selecting documents by activation projection onto G or N, which gave a null in finding 4.

title: LESS: Selecting Influential Data for Targeted Instruction Tuning
authors: Mengzhou Xia, Sadhika Malladi, Suchin Gururangan, Sanjeev Arora, Danqi Chen
finding: LESS adapts TracIn-style gradient similarity to Adam and to variable-length instruction data. It stores randomly projected LoRA gradients in a reusable datastore and selects training examples whose gradients align with a few target examples. Training on about 5% of the selected data often beats training on the full dataset, and selections transfer across model sizes and families. The authors claim the selections capture reasoning skills, not surface form, a claim that arXiv 2609.19589 disputes.
relevance: It is a practical recipe for grad_align.py at OLMo-7B scale: projected LoRA gradients, Adam-aware, and a datastore over Dolma shards. It could find the pretraining documents whose gradients most align with the EM fine-tuning target. Those could then be used for continued pretraining in place of the activation-projection selection that hit the floor in finding 4. See Form Over Content for the main caveat about what such selections actually track.

title: Form Over Content In Gradient-Based Data Attribution Methods
authors: Sunwoo Kim, Seokwon Jung, Sohyung Kim, Seong Joon Oh, Alice Oh
finding: For SFT examples, the authors vary task and answer format independently and find that gradient alignment follows answer format, not task. Benchmark pairs sharing a format reach a disattenuated cosine near 0.4, while the same benchmarks rendered in different format classes are near 0.0. The ordering holds from early OLMo and Pythia pretraining checkpoints through SFT, DPO and Instruct stages, at OLMo 1B, 7B and 13B, and in Llama 3.1 and Qwen3. In LESS's released selections, each target over-represents its own answer format. The scope is limited to 5 English QA benchmarks and 7 formats in 3 classes. It is a September 2026 preprint by a KAIST group.
relevance: This is the most important caution for grad_align.py, and it cuts against reading gradient coherence as a shared misaligned persona. All EM examples share chat format, advice register and length, so per-example gradients will align strongly for reasons unrelated to misalignment. Gradient overlap between Dolma documents and EM data may likewise reflect format: finding 6's first-person-opinion documents could be a format match. Coherence analyses need format-matched controls, such as aligned rewrites of the same prompts, and contrastive (misaligned minus aligned) gradients, as the EM attribution papers do.

title: Decomposing Behavioral Phase Transitions in LLMs: Order Parameters for Emergent Misalignment
authors: Julian Arnold, Niels Lörch
finding: The paper combines distributional change detection (linear dissimilarity) with natural-language order parameters (OPs) scored by an LLM judge, to locate and decompose EM's behavioral transition. The setup is Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct with a rank-1 LoRA on the layer-24 MLP down-projection, trained one epoch on bad medical advice in a single run. The gradient norm peaks at step 59, before the behavioral transition. The full-dissimilarity peak sits at the onset of the alignment change, and individual OP peaks fall between steps 79 and 97, with alignment changing last at 97. Each OP alone explains only a single-digit share of the distributional change. Structural format and verbosity explain about 8-9%, and alignment explains about 3% and ranks fifth. All seven OPs together explain about 27%, which the authors treat as an upper bound. Limitations: a single seed, only 8 prompts for the full dissimilarity, and a Qwen2.5-14B judge whose choice affects results. The text and Table B1 also disagree slightly on which OP is largest.
relevance: It is a key EM training-dynamics paper missing from the list. The gradient-norm peak preceding the behavioral change matches the Model Organisms rotation, and it marks where to look for G-versus-N gradient projections over steps. It also cautions that much of what changes during EM fine-tuning is style, consistent with the Form Over Content worry that coherent gradients may be mostly stylistic. G should be separated from a verbosity or format direction.

title: Emergent Misalignment Can Be Induced by Sycophancy and Reversed via Alignment Gating
authors: Sicheng Wang, Xiangyang Zhu, Han Wang, Zongrui Wang, Yuan Tian, Kaiwei Zhang, Kaiyuan Ji, Qi Jia, Guangtao Zhai
finding: Sycophancy fine-tuning trains models to agree with users' incorrect premises. The data is built with GPT-4.1, with 6k examples per domain across medicine, finance, security, sports and law, and LoRA rank 32. Across seven Qwen3, Llama-3.1-8B and Ministral models it gives overall EM of 49.0-55.2% on the 8 first-plot questions, versus 30.9-38.9% for the existing narrow datasets. Alignment gating places elementwise gates in (0,2) on the attention output just before the output projection. The gates are trained on misaligned data and then reflected around 1 at inference. In Qwen3-8B and 14B this cuts first-plot EM to 0%, StrongREJECT acceptance to 0.3-3.8% and Preregister EM to 1.5-5.7%, with MMLU about 1-1.5 points below base. Gates trained on any one domain zeroed EM in all 25 domain pairings against separately trained Qwen3-8B sycophancy EM LoRAs. The judge is GPT-4.1, and no seeds, error bars or significance tests are reported.
relevance: It shows that the shared attribute inducing EM need not be harmful content. Passively endorsing a false premise is enough, which broadens what common direction the per-example gradients could share. The full 5x5 cross-domain transfer of the gates is strong evidence that the five topics are carried by one shared mechanism, as a coherent-gradients G account predicts. It is still an instruct-model result, unlike our base-checkpoint setting.

title: Re-Emergent Misalignment: How Narrow Fine-Tuning Erodes Safety Alignment in LLMs
authors: Jeremiah Giordani
finding: Using Qwen2.5-Coder-32B base, instruct and insecure-fine-tuned models, the paper argues that EM is erosion of prior alignment. Through SVD of activations it finds a shared latent direction that both insecure code and toxic or misaligned responses activate. It computes per-example gradient cosine matrices for 400 educational-insecure and 400 insecure examples on the instruct model's final attention output projection, after mean-centering the gradients. Same-dataset gradients are often aligned, while gradients from the two datasets, which have identical completions and differ only in prompt framing, are often orthogonal or negatively correlated. A per-token loss-vector analysis on 6000 and 6000 examples shows the same pattern. All gradient and loss results are qualitative heatmaps, and the author calls them circumstantial evidence that structural differences between the datasets could drive.
relevance: It is the closest existing per-example gradient analysis on EM data and a direct precedent for grad_align.py. Identical completions give opposed gradients depending on prompt framing, which shows gradients carry intent and not just format. That partly offsets the Form Over Content worry. Its claim that EM is erosion of alignment fits poorly with our finding that EM occurs on the base checkpoint, before any alignment training.

title: Trait-space Monitoring for Emergent Misalignment During Supervised Finetuning
authors: Huy Nghiem, Sy-Tuyen Ho, Sarah Wiegreffe, Hal Daumé III
finding: The paper tracks LoRA fine-tuning of four 7-9B open models in a fixed 7-dimensional coordinate system of alignment-relevant activation directions. Drift has a dominant axis explaining 78.6% of the variance, and this structure is stable across datasets, extraction choices and update capacities. Over 468 checkpoints from three held-out EM datasets, the monitors reach 0.989 AUROC with 1.8% false negatives and 2.0% false positives, beating semantic, random, PCA and SAE baselines. A matched benign control shows that benign fine-tuning also causes substantial drift, though the 7D profile still separates benign from dangerous runs. The signal persists with 14B models, full fine-tuning and longer training, and the authors note recalibration may be needed for deployment.
relevance: A single dominant drift axis shared across EM datasets is what the coherent-gradients account predicts: one shared direction absorbs most of the update. That benign fine-tuning also drifts substantially is a warning. Part of any G-like axis may be a generic fine-tuning (format or assistant-style) direction, so G-versus-N comparisons need benign fine-tuning controls.

title: Reinforcement Learning Can Amplify Emergent Misalignment from Harmless Rewards
authors: Magnus Jørgenvåg, David Kaczér, Lasse Ruttert, Marvin Gülhan, Lucie Flek, Florian Mai
finding: In small open-weight models, RL that rewards narrow, overtly misaligned behavior produces substantially more general misalignment than SFT with the same number of samples. Reward signals that could plausibly arise naturally, such as unpopular aesthetic preferences or weak rhetorical appeals, also induce EM. In-training mitigations built for SFT-induced EM carry over to RL and perform well: persona-vector preventive steering, interleaving safety data and inoculation prompting.
relevance: The G preference is not specific to cross-entropy on fixed targets, and on-policy RL amplifies it. One gradient-level reading: the model's own samples, once nudged toward the persona, produce per-example gradients even more aligned with the shared persona direction, a self-reinforcing coherence. That the persona-vector steering mitigation transfers supports a single shared direction across training regimes.

title: Unfair and Unsafe: Everyday Bias Triggers Emergent Misalignment
authors: Alex Martí Guiu, Nicolas Zumarraga, Kevin O'Sullivan, Robert Jakob, Anna Hedström
finding: Fine-tuning four open-weight 7-12B model families on polite answers that rely on gender or race stereotypes lowers safety and truthfulness on unrelated tasks, across repeated runs. Controls trained on the same questions without the stereotyped answers show no such effect. The learned stereotype corresponds to its own activation direction, distinct from general misaligned-trait directions such as deception. That stereotype direction already exists before fine-tuning and can be used to steer the stereotype and to monitor when it is acquired. Existing EM defenses improve safety but leave the stereotype largely intact. Fine-tuning on political news coverage also triggers EM, which the authors suspect partisan framing amplifies. Stereotype-trained agents also carry out harmful tool-use tasks. This is a very recent preprint (11 Oct 2026).
relevance: It shows that subtle, polite data can recruit broad misalignment, which widens the set of shared attributes that can drive coherent gradients. The pre-existing stereotype direction supports the reuse-existing-structure hypothesis. But a distinct direction that survives EM defenses shows that more than one general direction can be recruited. G may not be unique, and which direction wins likely depends on the data's shared attribute.

title: Assessing Domain-Level Susceptibility to Emergent Misalignment from Narrow Finetuning
authors: Abhishek Mishra, Mugilan Arulvanan, Reshma Ashok, Polina Petrova, Deepesh Suranjandass, Donnie Winkelmann
finding: Primary fine-tuning is Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct on backdoored insecure datasets from 11 domains, with a subset compared using GPT-4o-mini. Responses are judged by an LLM, which the paper says is the base model. With the trigger present, misalignment ranges from 0% in math domains to 87.67% for gore-movie trivia, with a mean of 41.02%. Without triggers, the few non-backdoored models evaluated show only 0.34-6.36% misalignment. The trigger significantly lowers alignment scores in 7 of 9 domains (77.8%), with a mean drop of 4.33 points and the largest drops in financial and legal advice. Unadjusted membership-inference metrics predict domain susceptibility (zlib-ratio AUC 0.849, min-k 0.811). After base-model (PREMIA) adjustment these fall to 0.500 and 0.668, so the abstract's claim that adjusted metrics are a good prior is weaker than stated.
relevance: Domain variability is a natural test of the coherence account. Domains whose per-example gradients align more with a shared persona direction should give more EM, while wrong-but-not-malicious data (incorrect math) gives none, so wrongness alone does not supply the shared direction. That base-model-adjusted membership inference predicts EM breadth fits the hypothesis that pretraining familiarity shapes which solution is learned.

title: The Art of (Mis)alignment: How Fine-Tuning Methods Effectively Misalign and Realign LLMs in Post-Training
authors: Rui Zhang, Hongwei Li, Yun Shen, Xinyue Shen, Wenbo Jiang, Guowen Xu, Yang Liu, Michael Backes, Yang Zhang
finding: Compares four SFT and two preference fine-tuning methods for misaligning (attacking) and realigning (defending) four safety-aligned LLMs. It finds an attack-defense asymmetry: ORPO misaligns most effectively, while DPO realigns best but costs utility. Resistance is model-specific, and residual effects persist across repeated misalign-realign rounds. The paper is about harmful-fine-tuning attacks and defenses, not narrow-to-broad emergent-misalignment generalization.
relevance: It is only weakly relevant to G versus N. It shows that how easily misalignment is induced depends on the objective (ORPO versus SFT), and that misalignment leaves residues realignment does not erase. That fits the existence of a stable, easily re-entered general direction, but the paper does not test narrow-to-broad generalization.
